My nearly 20 years with Henry also deepened my feeling of responsibility. Was it inevitable that the US and China would be enemies? In his book On China, Henry ended by explaining that my idea of “coevolution” was the only way forward. My latest book, Darwin’s Lock, takes that idea of coevolution and spells it out in detail. I explain that the choice between the US and China isn’t who wins or loses, but something even more severe: between coevolution and coextinction.

In 2004 you coined the “Beijing Consensus” as an alternative to the Washington Consensus. In your new book, Darwin’s Lock, you argue that the US and China are locked in a relationship of “coevolution”, with the stark choice being “coevolution or coextinction”. How has your thinking evolved over the past two decades, and why do you see coevolution, rather than competition or decoupling, as the most useful framework for understanding the future of US–China relations?

When I wrote the Beijing Consensus in 2004, it was a deeply heterodox idea. “There’s only one way to develop an economy” was the general view of economists. Certainly, my own education had been firmly informed by this “Washington Consensus” confidence. What I saw in China made me question that certainty. The weight of Chinese culture and ideas was something I could really feel, from the first moment I stepped off the plane in Beijing.

The country had thousands of years of political theory and history that wouldn’t be shrugged off by new ideas. Life ran as much based on relationships as it did rules. The link between the state and market was completely different than in the West. So, I started to ask if different paths to different kinds of modernity might be possible and even necessary.

As I travelled [in] China, saw where money was made and lost, it became sharply obvious that a different logic was at work. Not one that rejected the ideas of Western economics, but that demanded a different approach.

I developed the idea of coevolution out of some work I was doing on complexity theory for my 2008 book The Age of the Unthinkable. At that time, I came to see that Darwin’s logic was perhaps the most powerful in all of science: that a simple test – are you fit or not – decides survival. And that pressure either kills something or forces it to evolve. Then I found the idea not just of evolution but of coevolution: that species can work together to become more fit over time.

Well, it was super clear to me that our world was entering a period of really revolutionary change, really an “age of the unthinkable” as I called it. This process would force a fitness test on everything. It would stress-test our politics, our economics, our security and even maybe the Enlightenment values that had organised Western society for hundreds of years.

Many people like to see the world of global affairs as an “I live and you die” sort of battle on every front. But science has shown us that is not the case. If life were only merciless competition, we’d all still be living in caves and banging each other on the head. Much human progress has come from mutually beneficial cooperation. It’s why cities work or nations thrive. The demand to be fit in a really stressful time is so extreme that species will do whatever it takes to survive. So the question is, how might we achieve this for the US and China?

China’s rise has reshaped global power structures in ways few predicted two decades ago, yet Western media and policy circles often struggle to tell nuanced stories about China, oscillating between hype and fear. Based on your experience, what are the biggest blind spots in how China’s rise is understood and covered in the West? How can journalists, policymakers and business leaders tell more accurate, multidimensional stories about China’s trajectory?

Westerners need to make a real effort to see China for what it really is, with no prejudgment, and this takes effort and modesty. Kissinger used to say: “If your mental model about something is wrong, every decision you make will be wrong.” It’s a good point. So much of the problem for Westerners is just an inability to accept Asia as it is: filled with smart, ambitious, driven figures with a rich cultural, scientific and spiritual tradition that is no better or worse than the West, just different. That is the right framework.

I recall people in Washington confidently telling me in 2023 that China was a decade away from developing large language models. Wrong framework, wrong conclusion.

One common error is to zoom in on a single aspect of Chinese life – the political structure, the real estate market, questions about the younger generation – and to tell a whole story of China from a few data points. China is so complex you can tell any story you want about it if you pick and choose your facts. The Western “experts” running around yelling about how Leninist China is cannot explain the biotech revolution or the Shenzhen nightclub scene or the emerging philosophical debate about consciousness of AI using a Daoist framework.

Doak Barnett or John King Fairbank or Ezra Vogel approached China as foreign scholars. Their writing holds up even decades later. They teach that humility is maybe the most important part of curiosity. And that understanding China is not just an intellectual game.

You have to feel China. You cannot know it from a book. I fear too many well-intentioned “experts” on China do not always have that feeling.

It’s probably also of some use to try to give up the inclination to use Western terms to label Chinese situations. That rush to label Chinese using Western political terms has always made me feel a bit uncomfortable.

There is a limit to how far Western ideas can take you in the Chinese context. It’s like trying to describe a basketball game using football terminology. I guess it’s as if Chinese analysts were warning that Trump is a “Hanfeizist”. If this is done in the spirit of opening a discussion about comparative political evolution, that is maybe of some use. But if it’s done to flatten debate and judgment? To distort something complex by simplifying it? Well, it’s not really intellectually honest or wise. For American policymakers it’s dangerous.

The mood in both Washington and Beijing has darkened considerably in recent years. Some argue that the world is entering a new Cold War. Do you agree with that characterisation? Are we entering a fundamentally new era in US-China relations, or is this another phase in a longer cycle of adjustment?

It’s popular to say we’ve entered a new Cold War. But what we face is, as I argue in the book, much more dangerous. The Cold War pitted two ideologically divergent nations against each other in an era of careful nuclear balance. There was a great discrepancy between the abilities of each nation. Our age is much more complex. And more perilous as a result.

China is not the USSR in any sense – not politically, technologically, culturally or historically. The weapons systems of our age are far more dangerous – faster, harder to control, more widespread. And we’re also living in a world that has been globalising for 40 years now, so that has left behind a network of connections that has its own evolutionary logic.

It means danger can spread super quickly. You are what you are connected to, and in our age we are all connected to each other, like it or not. I think one leap we need to make is to stop calling our age the “post-Cold War” era. No one called the Enlightenment the “post-Dark Ages”. We’ve entered a new period. I have called it the “Age of Network Power”, but no matter what you want to call it, the new logic of power is that we are all defined by what we are connected to – and that web around us is, fuelled by data and AI and zero-latency connectivity – changing at unprecedented speed.

I think we’ve entered a new phase of US-China ties. Both nations have the ability to substantially hurt the other. That is new, and it introduces a new phase of deterrence, but also of danger. We are very early in the power phase transition this is causing, in moving from one stable equilibrium to another.

It’s unclear what that next balance point will look like – and we know from science that it is the transitions between equilibria that are the moments of greatest uncertainty, risk and possibility. My point in Darwin’s Lock is that we can move to a new equilibrium of what biologists call “reciprocal helpfulness” in which each nation can become more fit and together influence our changing world.

Think of whatever particular fear might have been haunting you lately – an AI disaster, a biological risk or an economic crisis – in each case imagine a world where the US and China are working together, constantly, to manage these and other risks while also finding productive interconnection. There is no inherent reason this is not possible; it’s just a matter of finding a safe path to get there.

I think arms racing and accidents, racism and misunderstanding, these will all be a part of US-China relations for years to come. Our problem then is how to design a realistic, safe strategy to coevolve, and that is what the book tries to outline.

Many in Washington now view interdependence with China as a strategic vulnerability rather than a source of stability. Has the original case for engagement failed? Why should policymakers embrace a framework of coevolution when both countries increasingly define the relationship in terms of security, technological rivalry and strategic competition? Where does healthy interdependence become dangerous dependency?

Today the US and China have what biologists call “obligate mutualism” – each depends critically on the other. You can try to pretend that this is not the case, that somehow you could just wall off the two nations and each is strong enough to exist in isolation, but that would demand possibly catastrophic adjustments.

China depends on the US for markets, for compute, for education, for financial market discipline and for a list of other elements essential to development. And the US depends on China not only for critical minerals or pharmaceuticals or masses of imported goods, but also for talent (look at who staff most of the essential US AI research labs and companies). It’s not like this interdependence was architected by anyone; it was a result of evolutionary pressures in the global economy.

The idea of some Americans that it is possible to ‘strangle’ Chinese AI development is misguided

Joshua Cooper Ramo

China and the US both have benefited from this. And one of the lessons of nature is that when you try to unwind a system of obligate mutualism, you usually kill the participants.

But it’s not only that internal dynamic. It’s also the fact that our world is rocking with dangerous crises. The US and China are like two guys wrestling in a house that is on fire. They are fighting the wrong enemy. This lets us see that “interdependence” is not a weakness; it’s the most effective response to new evolutionary pressure.

The fundamental question of evolution is this: can you solve problems faster than they threaten to kill you? This is as true for cells in your body as it was for Greek city-states confronted with Persian attacks in ancient Western history. It’s our question too. And the US and China can best be regarded as problem-solving machines. They are engineered to address the dangers and opportunities that their citizens each face.

The result of 40 years of globalisation is that the US and China each have distinct skills that the other cannot replicate any time soon. Interdependence is important not only as a stabilising force, but because it means each nation is bringing the best ideas and skills to problems of global stability that threaten both countries.

What is the biggest misconception Americans have about China today? And what is the biggest misconception Chinese people have about the United States?

Americans have no sense of how hard-working, creative and energetic the Chinese people are, of how much they are willing to sacrifice for prosperity and stability. And they assume China wants to “beat” America and be number one in the world. I’m not sure that is correct.

Chinese people often misjudge America by only looking at the headlines. What makes America honestly amazing is the power of self-organisation. No nation on earth is as good as the US at bringing diverse groups of people – I mean not only nationally diverse, but also men and women – into productive alignment. There’s a lot that is worrisome about the US situation now, but the ability of America to fuse a sense of personal freedom with a feeling for group ambition is a wonder.

If Washington and Beijing are destined to compete, where do you still see meaningful scope for cooperation? Is there one area where cooperation is not just desirable, but unavoidable?

I think you have to reframe this. It’s a mistake to think of competition and cooperation as binary choices. Our world is full of examples of places where both occur at the same time. It’s no accident that the place where this kind of “coopertition” is most common is Silicon Valley, where firms are extremely comfortable competing and cooperating at the same time. What’s really going on here is information exchange, an understanding that knowing and doing more makes each company more fit for what is ahead. The same is true for the US and China.

It is clear the US and China have a shared interest in limiting nuclear proliferation, in stopping the spread of dangerous weapons, in global financial stability and environmental progress – and a long list of similar issues. But the key is changing how we think about our work in these areas. If the overall relationship is seen in zero-sum terms, then any cooperation becomes impossible. The right choice is to accept the shared destiny of America and China and to then use that fused “coopertition” to develop an approach to the dangers and opportunities of our age.

Taiwan remains widely regarded as the most dangerous flashpoint in the relationship. How do you assess the risks over the next decade, and what concerns you most?

First, we should remember that it’s rarely the most obvious flashpoints that lead to war. Crises can spin out of control no matter where they start. Today there are too many potential hotspots for the US and China and not enough effort to manage them.

Chinese history should reassure us that some safe path can be found. Sometimes in international relations there are issues where you want to speed up the situation, while in others you want to slow it down. It’s important to know the difference.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly becoming a new arena of strategic competition. You have said that you “cannot understand the intensity of innovation in China unless you’re there”. What are Western policymakers and executives still getting wrong about China’s AI ecosystem, and what is the biggest blind spot in America’s current AI and China strategy?

What we’re seeing in China today is what I think we can safely call a “full stack fork” in the AI ecosystem. I mean that the whole Chinese AI system – from the way large language models (LLMs) are designed to how chips are used to how systems are deployed, and even in areas like the philosophy of AI-human relations or safety – all of this is shifting into an approach that suits China’s needs and abilities.

Chinese companies have proved themselves to be excellent fast-followers and even fine-tuners in LLM development. To be sure, Westerners completely missed this for the most part. It baffles many serious US AI figures. But I think the split between the two ecosystems is more fundamental and more important. And that is what is really invisible to most Americans.

Another aspect is that success for a nation in the AI future may be less about the strength of the models or the technology, but rather about the ability of a society to absorb the shock of these systems. Chinese society has many “shock absorbers” that may be of use.

The idea of some Americans that it is possible to “strangle” Chinese AI development is misguided. It also misses the fact that Chinese AI systems are now taking paths that US systems will not take. We can see this in areas like the way Chinese are approaching energy efficiency or safety, for example. And in terms of architecture, Chinese sensor-based AI systems and world models may have some real advantages over US ones.

Even the philosophical questions about AI consciousness or human-machine ties take on different aspects when you examine them with, say, a Daoist lens.

Americans like to see AI as a race with China. But it has few characteristics of a race: it’s hard to say what the rules are. There is no clear finish line. It’s not obvious what it means to win.

A coevolutionary framework would encourage interdependence of the AI systems in the US and China, but regard this more as two nations each building gardens in the same ecosystem. Each is different; each designed for national conditions that are distinctive.

But sharing the same larger context and possibly even finding ways to share information can help each side become fitter. This is about cultivation, and careful cultivation, not racing.

Your earlier books, The Age of the Unthinkable and The Seventh Sense, argued that leaders fail because they do not understand complexity, networks and the way connection itself transforms the objects it links. Are today’s leaders any better at grasping those forces, or are we still repeating the same mistakes in new forms?

I wish I could say I see complex thinking at work in politics today, but it’s pretty rare. We have to find a way to get leaders to think in biological terms, to understand the ability of systems to evolve and change – and to accept that we live in a complex world, not a complicated one.

When we say “complicated” we mean like a jet engine, something made of lots of parts but fundamentally predictable. A “complex” system is more like a forest – also filled with lots of pieces, but interacting in ways that are hard sometimes to predict or manage.

When you accept that the world is biological in nature, it means you need to pay a lot of attention to the places where resilience could break down. But it also means you really need to find ways to encourage and trust in the self-organisation of the system.

If you could advise President Trump and President Xi on one concrete step each to reduce the risk of conflict, what would those be?

The first leap is accepting a coevolutionary framework. Rather than trying to replace the “obligate mutualism” that ties the US and China today, the right question is “What can each nation do to help both become fit for the world ahead?”

Once you get out of an “I live/you die” view, there is a long list of practical things that can be done.

The two should agree to help stop global nuclear weapons proliferation. They should work to establish treaties for space and cyber and AI weapons systems. They should reinvigorate global institutions such as the WTO or the UN. And they should also – and we have an effort trying to start this – use AI tools to help manage the relationship to avoid crises.

But the single most important concrete step is to accept the shared fate of the US and China, and then institutionalise that in deep working groups on the many problems of our age. This should be a historic, important time for diplomacy.

Looking ahead to 2030, paint us two contrasting scenarios: one in which coevolution works, and one in which it fails. What are the key turning points that determine which path the relationship takes?

Imagine in 2030 a world in which the US and China have jointly agreed to work on the major problems of our world – AI safety, global warming, economic stability, nuclear proliferation or the dozens of wars around the planet now.

Consider the possibility of the best minds from each nation asking “how can we solve this problem together” and taking the attitude of being on the same side of the table on these issues of global destiny. At the same time, competition between the countries in science or commerce or finance is intense, but grounded in rules that make for really fair competition.

The path to coextinction is one in which there is no cooperation on these issues. The planet continues to bake, species are destroyed, arms racing tips into conflict, nations struggle against economic uncertainty and face wild domestic political pressures, and racism and nationalism begin to define how each nation sees the other.

The key turning point? I don’t think there’s one. That old line about health, that “the best time to take care of your health was 20 years ago, the next best time is now” applies here. Now is the best time to reframe relations and build a safe system so coevolution can begin. Every passing day means lost opportunity.

item.title: [SCMP] Pump pressure: how rising fuel costs leave Hong Kong drivers running on fumes
item.description:
Van driver Wong Siu-po, 48, feels life is becoming more difficult than ever as rising fuel prices cost him an additional HK$5,000 (US$640) a month, about a third of his monthly income.

With an 11-year-old daughter and an unemployed wife to support, he feels the pressure mounting.

“I need to work three hours longer per day to make up for the loss of income,” he said. “I will cut down on air conditioning to save costs.”
item.content:encoded:
Van driver Wong Siu-po, 48, feels life is becoming more difficult than ever as rising fuel prices cost him an additional HK$5,000 (US$640) a month, about a third of his monthly income.

With an 11-year-old daughter and an unemployed wife to support, he feels the pressure mounting.

“I need to work three hours longer per day to make up for the loss of income,” he said. “I will cut down on air conditioning to save costs.”

Wong’s plight echoes survey findings showing that nearly 98 per cent of commercial drivers deem the government’s support “inadequate” or “very inadequate” as rising fuel prices, driven by the Middle East war and a global energy crisis, take a toll on their livelihoods.

Drivers have called for further government support after a two-month subsidy ended in June.

The poll of 770 respondents, conducted earlier this month by the Talk To You Now People Livelihood Progress Group – a concern group active in the Tuen Mun, Yuen Long and Tin Shui Wai areas – found that 98.7 per cent reported higher monthly fuel costs after a government subsidy ended.

More than a quarter said they paid at least HK$5,000 extra a month, while many said they worked longer hours, dipped into savings or cut maintenance to stay on the road.

The findings came after the price of Brent crude last week rebounded close to the year-to-date peak of US$118 per barrel in April, between US$111 and US$115 a barrel. The Middle East war has shown no signs of abating since it broke out on February 28.

Van driver Cow Lam, 38, who pays monthly car loan instalments of about HK$6,000, said rising fuel prices cost him an additional HK$3,000 per month, pushing up his living expenses by about 40 per cent.

“We need to cut down on food expenses to skimp and save,” he said.

Some 82 per cent of respondents called for immediate relief, urging transitional support for recent fuel-car buyers with ongoing vehicle loans.

Echoing 67 per cent of surveyed drivers, the group urged the government to provide clear electric vehicle replacement arrangements, increased purchase subsidies, low-interest loans, leasing or instalment plans.

“This is crucial to ensure these drivers are not left behind by the new policy simply because they cannot afford an instant vehicle swap. For drivers, securing cash flow is the first step towards a successful transition,” the concern group’s chairwoman Michelle Tsang said.

When asked whether they wanted to switch to electric vehicles that cost far less to run, nearly half the respondents, or 46.4 per cent, said they intended to switch or needed more information and time to consider. Some 11.8 per cent planned to switch within three years.

Among drivers with no present intention of switching, 61 per cent cited insufficient charging points at workplaces and overnight parking sites. More than 60 per cent said they needed more information about the net cost of switching to electric vehicles so they could better assess affordability.

Both drivers Lam and Wong called on the government to provide more subsidies to ease their burdens, such as for tunnel, vehicle licensing and examination fees.

A spokeswoman for the Transport and Logistics Bureau said the Inter-departmental Task Force on Monitoring Fuel Supply would continue to dynamically assess the situation in the Middle East and fuel supply and prices, to ensure the stability of Hong Kong’s energy reserves.

Lawmaker Mark Chong Ho-fung said the government should at least dip into its multibillion-dollar dividend payments received from the MTR Corporation every year to provide fuel subsidies for bus companies and prevent them from repeatedly raising their base fares.

“If the base fares are allowed to factor in the rise in fuel costs, the fares will keep going up if the conflict goes on. This will affect the economy and deter people from going out and spending,” he said.

Recently, franchised bus operators applied to raise fares by up to 17.7 per cent to partially offset higher fuel costs while two power companies announced an increase in fuel charges last month.

The ripple effect of the fuel crisis has spread beyond transport operators.

Clerk Wong Po-yan, 34, who earns about HK$15,000 per month and commutes daily to the airport from her Sham Shui Po home for work, is also feeling the pinch, alongside Ma Chi-hung’s family. Ma, 49, a delivery worker, earns about HK$21,000 a month and has to support two sons.

Both households said they would cut down on food spending and refrain from going out to rein in transport costs.

Ma said the family’s transport expenses alone cost HK$3,500 a month while electricity usage was over HK$2,000 a month.

“I rarely go out now,” Ma said.

Taxi driver Yuen Tak, 68, said high fuel costs had reduced his monthly income by more than HK$1,000 a month, or about 30 per cent.

“I have 20 per cent less business per month as many people want to save costs and avoid taking taxis,” he said.

Analysts warned that the government had to think of ways to relieve the livelihood pressure on residents caused by rising fuel costs, otherwise Hong Kong’s economic activity would stall.

Gary Ng Cheuk-yan, senior economist for Asia-Pacific at Natixis Corporate and Investment Bank, said the high living costs would reduce people’s willingness to spend as they cut back on food and other expenses.

“There is nothing much the government can do. It should roll out some relief measures such as subsidies to ease the impact of high fuel costs,” he said.

Apart from drivers, many residents told the South China Morning Post that they were making trade-offs due to rising fuel costs.

Low-income households also faced steeper air-conditioning costs this summer, with an unusually high number of very hot days. The Observatory recorded the city’s highest-ever temperature for the traditional Chinese calendar’s “Frost” solar term on October 23.

Among those affected was single mother Rosaly*, 44, who earns slightly over HK$10,000 a month. She began to worry about rising electricity bills since the Middle East conflict flared up early this year, as she felt an increasingly tight squeeze on her income and savings.

“In the past, I paid about HK$700 for two months. But this summer I had to pay HK$1,200 for two months. The gas bill is also rising,” she said.

She then sought to cut back on electricity use, following the cost-saving tips of former Observatory head Lam Chiu-ying, which included turning air conditioning to 27 degrees Celsius (80.6 Fahrenheit) and using fans.

She also saved gas by reducing hot water use and opening windows wide to ventilate her flat.

“Lam’s method works; my electricity use has returned to previous levels,” she said.

*Name changed at the interviewee’s request

item.title: [SCMP] Big Apple vs Pearl of the Orient? How higher taxes in New York may open door for Hong Kong
item.description:
On November 4 last year, Zohran Mamdani won the New York mayoral election on a promise to make the city more affordable, with expanded social programmes funded in part by raising taxes on the city’s wealthiest residents and most profitable corporations.

Nearly a year since his upset victory, he has secured one major piece of that agenda: a surcharge on high-end second homes. He also continues to push for higher corporate and income taxes.

The proposals have intensified criticism of Mamdani, a self-described democratic socialist, with opponents arguing that his approach to taxing the wealthy amounts to “socialism in action”.
item.content:encoded:
On November 4 last year, Zohran Mamdani won the New York mayoral election on a promise to make the city more affordable, with expanded social programmes funded in part by raising taxes on the city’s wealthiest residents and most profitable corporations.

Nearly a year since his upset victory, he has secured one major piece of that agenda: a surcharge on high-end second homes. He also continues to push for higher corporate and income taxes.

The proposals have intensified criticism of Mamdani, a self-described democratic socialist, with opponents arguing that his approach to taxing the wealthy amounts to “socialism in action”.

Speaking at the Milken Institute Global Conference in May, Citadel founder Ken Griffin warned that Mamdani was sending a clear message that New York “does not welcome success”, raising the prospect of moving parts of his firm’s operations out of the city.

Halfway across the globe, Hong Kong is charting an entirely different course. The Asian financial hub is rolling out fresh tax breaks and other red-carpet incentives to lure high-net-worth individuals (HNWIs), aiming to solidify its position as a premier global wealth management centre.

This year’s Global Financial Leaders’ Investment Summit, kicking off on Monday and bringing dozens of Wall Street and European heavyweights to Hong Kong, gives the city a high-profile platform to make its case.

Analysts and overseas scholars said New York’s tax push gave Hong Kong “a timely opening” to lure wealthy families reassessing where to base themselves, along with the capital they control.

Hong Kong could become “an attractive destination” for wealthy families considering a move away from the US, they added, although it remained uncertain how much tax policy alone influences relocation decisions.

Wall Street voices opposition

Since taking office in January, Mamdani has pushed state and city lawmakers to consider an array of proposals targeting the wealthy. His most significant win so far is the “pied-a-terre” levy on second homes, which took effect on July 1.

The annual levy applies to non-primary residences worth US$5 million or more, with graduated rates ranging from 0.8 to 1.3 per cent of a property’s value. Separate rates apply to condominiums and co-ops valued at US$1 million or more until July 2028.

Mamdani thrust the policy into the spotlight when he filmed a video outside the US$238 million Manhattan penthouse of Griffin, citing the property as an example of high-end second homes targeted by the levy.

Griffin later described the video as “creepy and weird”, saying Mamdani’s actions brought back the “trauma” of his time in Chicago, where he clashed with local leaders over crime and public policy before relocating Citadel’s global corporate headquarters to Miami in 2022. He added that Citadel would expand job creation in Miami rather than Manhattan as a result.

Beyond real estate, the mayor has proposed increasing the city’s income tax rate by 2 percentage points for residents earning more than US$1 million annually, which would lift the top rate to roughly 5.9 per cent from 3.9 per cent. He has also called on New York state to raise its top corporate tax rate to 11.5 per cent from 7.25 per cent.

While state governor Kathy Hochul rejected both tax increases this year, Mamdani’s allies are preparing another push in 2027, with Gustavo Gordillo, co-chair of New York’s Democratic Socialists of America chapter, maintaining that “we have lots of work left to do”.

Other Wall Street figures have also voiced opposition. After meeting Mamdani in May, JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon said higher taxes on the rich risked undermining the city’s position as a business hub.

Dimon said New York must compete with cities including Shanghai, Hong Kong, Singapore and Nashville, warning that people “vote with their feet”.

You do not have to pass a tax to move people. You just have to convince them it’s coming, or could come

Larry Ikard, Yuvarra

New York already collects more tax per resident than any other US state. State and local governments took in more than US$12,000 per resident in the 2024 financial year, 71 per cent above the national average, according to the Citizens Budget Commission, a New York fiscal watchdog.

New York City residents also face the country’s highest combined top income tax rate, at about 14.8 per cent, compared with 13.3 per cent in second-placed California.

Combined with high living costs and uneven public services, those fiscal burdens threatened New York’s ability to attract and retain high-income residents, the watchdog warned.

The wealth migration debate

While New York city officials described the proposed tax measures as “a fair way” to address inequality and raise revenue for essential services, some financial industry executives and analysts warned the moves could push affluent residents to lower-tax jurisdictions, taking capital with them.

Larry Ikard, CEO of Yuvarra, an independent lender serving HNWIs, said New York’s evolving tax landscape was prompting wealthy residents to rethink where they live “to a huge extent”.

“You do not have to pass a tax to move people. You just have to convince them it’s coming, or could come,” he said, adding that wealthy families treated calls to “tax the rich” as a signal to start planning ahead.

Kevin Chen Kaifeng, chief economist at Horizon Financial and a member of the Economic Club of Miami, said an exodus was already under way, with senior bankers and lawyers increasingly relocating to Florida.

Large financial firms such as JPMorgan Chase were no longer expanding headcount in New York, he said.

The bank’s New York City workforce has fallen to about 24,000 from 30,000 a decade ago, while its Texas headcount has increased to 32,000 from 26,000, Dimon said in his April shareholder letter.

Goldman Sachs was also moving hundreds of employees out of New York, asking staff to relocate to Dallas or Salt Lake City, international media reported in March last year.

Emanuele Colonnelli, a professor of finance and entrepreneurship at the University of Chicago Booth School of Business, said higher tax rates might not trigger immediate relocations, but they inevitably influence “long-term decisions” around retirement, business sales and the timing of moves after children finish school.

Long-term data points to a decline in New York’s share of high earners. The proportion of US households reporting annual income of more than US$1 million that lived in New York was 9 per cent in 2023, down from 12.7 per cent in 2010 – the steepest decline among US states, according to the Citizens Budget Commission.

The latest Internal Revenue Service data, covering tax returns filed in 2022 and 2023, showed New York lost a net US$9.9 billion in adjusted gross income to other states. Florida gained a net US$20.6 billion.

Florida has no state income tax or estate tax and offers a lower cost of living than New York. The number of tax filers there reporting annual income above US$1 million nearly quadrupled between 2010 and 2023, according to the commission.

Ikard said destinations in Latin America and Europe, including Panama, Costa Rica and Portugal, have also steadily attracted American retirees by offering a high quality of life, relatively low living costs and healthcare systems increasingly geared towards US expatriates.

What can Hong Kong offer?

Hong Kong is stepping up efforts to attract global wealth, pitching its low-tax regime, international connectivity and emerging financial sectors to affluent families.

Salaries tax is capped at a standard rate of 15 per cent on the first HK$5 million (US$637,000) of net income and 16 per cent above that level, while corporate profits are taxed at a headline rate of 16.5 per cent. The city largely taxes only locally sourced income and levies no capital gains, dividend or estate taxes.

In June, the government introduced a bill to widen tax concessions for privately offered funds and family-owned investment vehicles. The proposal would also extend the zero-tax treatment of qualifying carried interest from private equity to hedge funds and other investment strategies.

Colonnelli said Hong Kong “combines relatively low local taxes with the financial sophistication and international connections of a major business centre”. Families, he added, “do not necessarily have to choose between a tax-friendly location and being at the centre of business activities”.

The city ranked third globally in the latest Global Financial Centres Index, behind only New York and London, and placed ahead of London in business environment, human capital and financial sector development.

Boston Consulting Group reported in May that Hong Kong had narrowly overtaken Switzerland as the world’s largest cross-border wealth management hub, overseeing US$2.9 trillion in assets.

Hong Kong was also the preferred retirement destination among wealthy expatriates, chosen by 67 per cent of HNWIs polled in a survey by British wealth management and financial advisory firm St James’s Place covering 450 affluent residents in the city.

The city government is building on that foundation. Its first five-year plan places wealth management ambitions in the opening chapter as part of its “four centres and one hub” strategy, alongside efforts to expand the offshore yuan business and commodities trading.

Access to mainland China added to the appeal, analysts said.

Initial public offerings in Hong Kong raised more than HK$388 billion in the first three quarters of the year, more than double the amount recorded a year earlier, KPMG said. The consultancy attributed the growth to A+H listings, where mainland China-listed firms secure a Hong Kong listing, and specialist technology companies.

Hong Kong’s proximity and connections to mainland China and other Asian markets “can make it easier to build business relationships and pursue investment opportunities there”, Colonnelli said.

The city is also positioning itself as a digital assets hub. It has licensed cryptocurrency exchanges since 2023 and granted its first two stablecoin issuer licences in April.

The government has issued digital green bonds three times since 2023, while regulators have approved tokenised investment products. The Hong Kong Monetary Authority plans to test tokenising HK$1.3 trillion of Exchange Fund Bills by year-end.

Regulatory clarity is one of the city’s biggest draws, according to Sascha Goetz, CEO of RootstockCollective, which supports the bitcoin-linked Rootstock blockchain.

“In the US, it’s a lot of back and forth,” he said, citing the US Senate’s failure in September to advance a crypto market-structure bill. “For a family office planning 10 years ahead, that uncertainty is a real cost.”

What might hold wealthy families back?

Despite Hong Kong’s efforts to attract global wealth, analysts said tax rates were only part of the equation. Wealthy families must also consider the durability of tax policies, the predictability of regulations and whether a city could meet their needs beyond business.

A key structural constraint for American nationals is the limited relief available under US tax law.

American citizens and green-card holders are generally taxed on their worldwide income regardless of where they live. Relocating to Hong Kong could reduce their exposure to New York state and city taxes, which together carry a top marginal rate of about 14.8 per cent, but it would not eliminate federal income tax rates of up to 37 per cent.

New York also retains advantages as a global financial centre. Nasdaq was ranked first among worldwide exchanges by initial public offering funds raised in the first nine months of 2026, ahead of Hong Kong, driven by the listings of SpaceX and SK Hynix, KPMG said.

It also topped the Global Financial Centres Index, ranking five points ahead of Hong Kong.

Hong Kong is 12 to 13 hours ahead of New York, making it not a practical choice for most executives

Kevin Chen Kaifeng, Horizon Financial

Beyond tax and market access, “long-term legal and regulatory predictability, and the evolution of US-China relations” remained a key consideration for global capital, Colonnelli said.

Since the national security law took effect in 2020, followed by local security legislation in 2024, debate over Hong Kong’s autonomy has intensified. The government has said the laws restored stability and rejected criticism from Washington and other Western nations.

A February survey by the American Chamber of Commerce in Hong Kong found that 94 per cent of respondents were confident in the city’s rule of law – up from 83 per cent a year earlier – although 59 per cent cited geopolitical tensions as a primary operating hurdle.

Beijing’s tighter oversight of wealth held abroad is another consideration for families with business interests on both sides of the Pacific. China’s tax authority urged residents in January to declare overseas income earned from 2022 to 2024, and began taxing offshore trusts at 20 per cent in July.

Broader trade dynamics also cloud the horizon. A September summit in Washington between President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump produced a two-month extension of the trade truce through January 10, leaving deeper structural disputes unresolved.

“The concern is not just what is permitted today, but whether that will remain possible over the next decade,” Colonnelli said.

“A known tax bill can be planned for, but uncertainty about the rules governing a family’s wealth is harder to manage.”

For many families, however, practical lifestyle considerations outweigh macroeconomic ones. “The biggest considerations are probably very human ones: schools, housing costs, time zones and distance from family,” Ikard said.

Hong Kong remained the world’s least affordable housing market for a 16th year, according to international public policy research organisation Demographia, while 71 per cent of American Chamber of Commerce in Hong Kong members cited living costs as the top obstacle to hiring foreign talent.

Time zone differences present another challenge. Hong Kong is 12 to 13 hours ahead of New York, making it “not a practical choice for most executives”, Chen said.

“Hong Kong’s appeal to Americans has to go beyond the tax bill,” Ikard said.

item.title: [SCMP] China narrows the path to elite official training scheme for citizens graduating overseas
item.description:
China is further narrowing access to a key government recruitment programme for overseas-educated graduates, limiting their pathways into the country’s civil service and party-state system.

More than a dozen provincial-level regions, including Beijing and Shanghai, opened applications for the 2027 xuandiaosheng recruitment rounds in September and October.

Xuandiaosheng, or the “selected graduates” system, is designed to select and train university graduates to become elite cadres and officials within the party and government. Recruits must spend several years working at the grass-roots level in townships and sub-districts before moving into leading government and party roles.
item.content:encoded:
China is further narrowing access to a key government recruitment programme for overseas-educated graduates, limiting their pathways into the country’s civil service and party-state system.

More than a dozen provincial-level regions, including Beijing and Shanghai, opened applications for the 2027 xuandiaosheng recruitment rounds in September and October.

Xuandiaosheng, or the “selected graduates” system, is designed to select and train university graduates to become elite cadres and officials within the party and government. Recruits must spend several years working at the grass-roots level in townships and sub-districts before moving into leading government and party roles.

None of the local government notices released so far has offered an application channel for overseas-educated graduates, continuing a trend that was evident last year.

An Australian-educated arts graduate who called herself James said she had considered the xuandiaosheng programme among her main career options as she looked for work this year.

“Job hunting is already so difficult. I really valued the opportunity to apply for the xuandiaosheng programme but now I have no chance at all,” she said.

Part of her decision to pursue a master’s degree overseas was driven by what she perceived as welcoming signs from the programme around 2023. At least 10 provincial-level regions, including Beijing and Guangdong, explicitly listed selected top-ranked overseas universities as eligible in their xuandiaosheng recruitment notices for the 2023 and 2024 graduating cohorts.

Similar frustrations have surfaced on RedNote, a Chinese social media platform also known as Xiaohongshu. “I can’t believe it. I went to graduate school just to qualify for the programme,” one comment read.

The programme dates back to 1965, when China’s leaders saw rural assignments for university graduates as a way to train “successors to the revolution”, according to state media outlet Xinhua’s Liaowang magazine.

President Xi Jinping has backed the programme since at least 2008, when he was still vice-president. He has called for its improvement and urged officials to select outstanding university graduates to train for grass-roots positions.

In 2018, the Communist Party’s Organisation Department issued new guidelines to strengthen and improve the xuandiaosheng programme, calling for more targeted recruitment, as well as stricter training and management of recruits.

The party describes the programme as a sourcing project for “building a high-calibre, professional cadre”, according to its official website.

Entry requirements are stricter than for regular civil service recruitment and vary by region, as the central government and local governments run their own xuandiaosheng recruitment programmes.

But they generally require applicants to be party members and outstanding student leaders, and favour local universities or well-known institutions with high global rankings.

For students whose undergraduate degrees did not meet eligibility requirements, earning a further degree from an overseas university on the approved list used to offer a route into the programme. That door seems to have closed.

“From 2024 and 2025 onwards, the programme shifted to recruiting exclusively from mainland Chinese universities, effectively shutting out overseas graduates,” said Jasper Jiang, an adviser who helps overseas students prepare for civil service and public institution recruitment and posts preparation advice on RedNote.

The shift became apparent in late 2024, when provincial-level governments began releasing their 2025 xuandiaosheng recruitment notices.

[Restrictions] potentially increase the relative attractiveness of domestic education for students interested in government careers

He Qiwei, University of Edinburgh

Of those that had listed overseas universities in their 2023 and 2024 recruitment notices, only Shanghai and Henan continued to accept overseas graduates.

By this year, none did, with some provinces, including Heilongjiang in the northeast, explicitly stating in their recruitment notices that graduates from overseas universities were excluded.

Cleo, who gave only her first name, said she had once been eager to join the government, only to find the key route into government service had already closed to her when she graduated in 2025.

“Overseas-educated graduates are not eligible for the xuandiaosheng programme, leaving me with little choice but to sit the broader national and provincial civil service exams,” said the Hong Kong-educated postgraduate, who ultimately failed to enter the civil service.

Jiang said it had become more difficult for overseas-educated graduates to enter the civil service, partly due to “growing competition from returning graduates for fewer positions” now that the xuandiaosheng programme was off the table.

China has cut its national civil service recruitment for two consecutive years, with positions falling more than 10 per cent – from about 39,700 for the 2025 intake to 35,700 for 2027 – according to Xinhua.

Victor Shih, a professor at the University of California San Diego’s School of Global Policy and Strategy, said national security concerns could be among the reasons behind the restrictions.

“Senior leaders may suspect those who have lived overseas of being sympathetic to foreign perspectives, or worse, of engaging in espionage on behalf of foreign countries,” Shih said.

He said such concerns could affect “both recruitment into the government and promotions”, although there had been exceptions.

Chinese state security authorities identified overseas students among citizens considered vulnerable to recruitment by foreign espionage agencies, according to a post published by Xinhua on its social media account last year.

“The overseas student community has long been a target of foreign espionage and intelligence agencies,” the Ministry of State Security said in a post on its social media account in July 2025. The ministry also identified overseas-based personnel and people with access to classified information as recruitment targets for foreign agencies.

Ja Ian Chong, an associate professor of political science at the National University of Singapore, said competition among major powers could be one reason for the heightened emphasis on national security.

“Competition with the United States and its allies, as well as friction with places such as Europe and Australia, means it may be easier to suspect the sensibilities or even loyalties of people with significant external contact,” Chong said.

He Qiwei, an assistant professor at the University of Edinburgh’s economics school, said “eligibility for the xuandiaosheng programme is itself a valuable opportunity”, as it determined who could compete for a place in the government’s elite talent pipeline.

“The recent restrictions in certain provinces may have implications beyond the immediate recruitment process,” He said.

“They change which groups of graduates have access to this career pathway and could potentially increase the relative attractiveness of domestic education for students interested in government careers.”

While studying abroad was once seen as a route to better jobs and higher pay, the value of an overseas degree appears to have declined in China’s increasingly competitive job market in recent years.

A 2006-07 survey found that returnees from Japan, Canada and Hong Kong earned about twice as much as their locally educated counterparts, according to David Zweig in a 2018 article for the University of Hong Kong’s Centre for Higher Education Research.

By 2015, the premium had narrowed. Returnees with postgraduate degrees earned about 20 per cent more than their domestic counterparts, while overseas bachelor’s degrees offered no significant earnings advantage, according to a 2021 study by Du Zaichao, Sun Yuting, Zhao Guochang and Zweig and published in The China Quarterly.

A 2025 résumé experiment published in China Economic Quarterly, conducted by He Haoran, An Lulu and Lin Jiayue, also found that applicants educated overseas were 16.2 per cent less likely to receive interview feedback than comparable applicants educated in China.

item.title: [SCMP] In Malaysia’s largest state, ‘Sarawak First’ faces a Dayak election test
item.description:
Ethnicity plays out differently across Malaysia. On the peninsula, identity politics is comparatively rigid: Malay vs non-Malay, with Islam and Malay identity fused not just culturally but constitutionally. In the Borneo states of Sabah and Sarawak, however, the picture is less binary. Religion plays a smaller role in daily life, cultural identities are more diffuse, and ethnic lines are less clear-cut.

The Dayaks, a collective term for Sarawak’s non-Muslim indigenous peoples, are the state’s largest ethnic group at 42 per cent of the population. They comprise the Iban (28 per cent), Bidayuh (8 per cent), Orang Ulu (“people of the interior”) and other indigenous groups (6 per cent). Malays (24 per cent) and Melanau (5 per cent), most of them Muslim, make up much of the rest of the population, alongside Chinese (24 per cent).

Power struggles within the Dayak community – and between the Dayak, Malay-Melanau and Chinese blocs – are layered with personality politics and, increasingly, “Sarawak First” nationalism. The ruling Gabungan Parti Sarawak (GPS) coalition formally broke away from Barisan Nasional in 2018 and champions Sarawakian identity over ethnicity. Its dominant component party, Parti Pesaka Bumiputera Bersatu (PBB), has anchored the state government since the 1970s.
item.content:encoded:
Ethnicity plays out differently across Malaysia. On the peninsula, identity politics is comparatively rigid: Malay vs non-Malay, with Islam and Malay identity fused not just culturally but constitutionally. In the Borneo states of Sabah and Sarawak, however, the picture is less binary. Religion plays a smaller role in daily life, cultural identities are more diffuse, and ethnic lines are less clear-cut.

The Dayaks, a collective term for Sarawak’s non-Muslim indigenous peoples, are the state’s largest ethnic group at 42 per cent of the population. They comprise the Iban (28 per cent), Bidayuh (8 per cent), Orang Ulu (“people of the interior”) and other indigenous groups (6 per cent). Malays (24 per cent) and Melanau (5 per cent), most of them Muslim, make up much of the rest of the population, alongside Chinese (24 per cent).

Power struggles within the Dayak community – and between the Dayak, Malay-Melanau and Chinese blocs – are layered with personality politics and, increasingly, “Sarawak First” nationalism. The ruling Gabungan Parti Sarawak (GPS) coalition formally broke away from Barisan Nasional in 2018 and champions Sarawakian identity over ethnicity. Its dominant component party, Parti Pesaka Bumiputera Bersatu (PBB), has anchored the state government since the 1970s.

Over the ensuing decades, every Sarawak chief minister has come from the Muslim bumiputra – a Malay word meaning “sons of the land” – in an unbroken 56-year run: Melanau (Abdul Rahman Ya’kub, 1970–81; Taib Mahmud, 1981–2014) or Malay (Adenan Satem, 2014–17; Abang Johari, 2017 to present). That dominance traces back to 1966, when Kuala Lumpur used emergency powers to remove Iban chief minister Stephen Kalong Ningkan for resisting federal control. It has endured because Muslim bumiputra voters consolidated behind one party while the Dayak vote split across several.

The coming state election could be Abang Johari’s last as chief minister. With GPS’ return to power virtually assured, the more consequential question is succession: will a Dayak finally lead Sarawak? A Dayak successor would show that GPS’ “Sarawak First” slogan is inclusive. Another Malay-Melanau-Muslim successor would only keep alive the grievance on which ethnonationalist appeals, or “Dayakism”, thrive.

As Sarawak heads to the polls, the contest for the Dayak vote is once again under way. In a state where no ethnic group commands a majority on its own, no party can govern without the Dayak, the largest bloc.

Yet Dayak representation remains fragmented and uneven. Of the 82 seats in the state legislative assembly, 34 are Dayak-majority, meaning Dayaks make up more than 50 per cent of voters. GPS won all but two of them in 2021, spread across its component parties: PBB, Parti Rakyat Sarawak (PRS), the Progressive Democratic Party (PDP) and the Sarawak United Peoples’ Party (SUPP). PRS, the coalition’s main Dayak-based party, held 11 seats. No opposition party currently represents Dayaks in the assembly.

Social media has been awash with Dayak grievances, from calls to reclaim ancestral land to complaints of underrepresentation in government. One widely circulated table purported to show Dayaks far behind their Malay-Melanau-Muslim counterparts in key management positions. GPS’ response was pointed. At the PBB Special Convention in August, Abang Johari rejected the marginalisation narrative, declaring “siapa nya pandai, nya lah naik” (whoever is capable will rise), and framing leadership as a matter of merit, not ethnicity.

Past election results suggest Dayak bids for top leadership roles face steep odds. Even a clean sweep of all 34 Dayak-majority seats would leave a Dayak party short of the 42 needed to govern, forcing it into partnership with Malay-Melanau or Chinese parties already locked into GPS. In 2021, opposition parties, chief among them Parti Bansa Dayak Sarawak Baru (PBDS), dangled the prospect of a Dayak chief minister, but failed to shift loyalties in any meaningful way.

That appeal has a long history. Founded in 1983, PBDS mobilised Dayak sentiment more consistently than any other party and coined the rallying cry “Dayakism” during its failed 1991 bid to install a Dayak chief minister. Deregistered in 2004, it was revived in 2013 as PBDS Baru before reclaiming the PBDS name in 2022. Another opposition party, the now-defunct Parti Sarawak Bersatu (PSB), was formed in 2014 after a SUPP breakaway and dissolved in March 2024, with its members absorbed into GPS coalition party PDP. That leaves PBDS as the only visible Dayak-based challenger to GPS, though a far less formidable one than the online noise around it suggests.

GPS’ edge also lies in its track record of delivering development to rural, Dayak-majority areas. That record, paired with its skilful use of Sarawak nationalism, helped it comfortably win most of those 34 seats in 2021 – a measure of how little electoral purchase Dayakism holds.

The more significant contest is within GPS itself. Since PRS president James Jemut Masing died in October 2021, Dayak politics has lacked a leader of comparable stature. Many are asking whether PBB secretary general and Kapit MP Alexander Nanta Linggi might fill that void. He has said he will not defend his parliamentary seat at the next general election and has signalled his intention to contest a proposed new state seat in Melekun, within Kapit, pending gazettement.

In the coming election, the odds look unfavourable for anyone tempted to weaponise ethnicity to mobilise support

But Nanta would need the backing of Abang Johari and his deputy Douglas Uggah Embas, PBB’s most senior Dayak figure. The Dayak challenge facing GPS, then, is less external than internal: a quiet contest among its own Dayak leaders to become the community’s next standard-bearer.

Adenan, the former chief minister, brought Sarawak First into the political mainstream in 2014, framing demands under the Malaysia Agreement 1963 that Abang Johari has since carried forward. But Sarawak First sentiment is more than GPS’ state-level winning formula; it underwrites the coalition’s pivotal role in federal politics, where its 23 MPs are a pillar of Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s unity government. More uncomfortably, it also entrenches PBB, and with it Malay-Melanau-Muslim predominance within GPS, unless the coalition proves genuinely willing to hand power to a Dayak leader.

In the coming election, the odds look unfavourable for anyone tempted to weaponise ethnicity to mobilise support. Those stoking Dayak sentiment for electoral gain will have to convince not only the Dayaks but all Sarawakians of what matters more: Dayak First or Sarawak First.

Dr Arnold Puyok is a Visiting Senior Fellow at ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute. He is a Senior Lecturer in Politics and Government Studies at the Faculty of Social Sciences and Humanities, Universiti Malaysia Sarawak (UNIMAS). This article was first published on the institute’s commentary website fulcrum.sg.

item.title: [SCMP] ‘I’m terrified’: AI comes for Southeast Asia’s graduate jobs
item.description:
Nafeesa Azman has applied for hundreds of jobs over the past two months, yet the 24-year-old Malaysian marketing graduate is yet to find a permanent role that pays what she needs or uses the skills she spent years, and a good deal of money, developing.

Natthanicha Intawong, a final-year media arts student in Bangkok, describes the terror many of her peers feel as they prepare to enter a jobs market that artificial intelligence is already beginning to scythe through.

For Joshua Nai, a Singaporean graduate, the writing was quite literally on the wall. He completed a three-year diploma in animation and game art at Singapore Polytechnic in 2024, but abandoned his dream of a career in gaming after seeing the increasing amounts of AI-generated artwork being used in the industry and elsewhere.
item.content:encoded:
Nafeesa Azman has applied for hundreds of jobs over the past two months, yet the 24-year-old Malaysian marketing graduate is yet to find a permanent role that pays what she needs or uses the skills she spent years, and a good deal of money, developing.

Natthanicha Intawong, a final-year media arts student in Bangkok, describes the terror many of her peers feel as they prepare to enter a jobs market that artificial intelligence is already beginning to scythe through.

For Joshua Nai, a Singaporean graduate, the writing was quite literally on the wall. He completed a three-year diploma in animation and game art at Singapore Polytechnic in 2024, but abandoned his dream of a career in gaming after seeing the increasing amounts of AI-generated artwork being used in the industry and elsewhere.

It was “a slap in the face”, he said. “It seems like people have forgotten the human ingenuity that makes art meaningful.”

Nai has since changed course on his career ambitions and now works full-time in a gym.

Across Southeast Asia, millions of graduates are entering a workforce that has been irrevocably changed by generative AI: the software behind popular chatbots ChatGPT, Claude, DeepSeek and the like that produces text, images and code from short written instructions.

The International Labour Organization (ILO) estimates that nearly 80 million Southeast Asian workers – or more than one-fifth of the region’s total workforce – will be affected by the rise of AI. Some 11.7 million could lose their jobs outright or see their tasks entirely reworked, it said.

Though an ILO report published in July found no evidence of large-scale AI-driven regional job losses as yet, the first effects are beginning to be felt at the bottom of the career ladder.

Graduates, who traditionally learn on the job during their first few years in a role doing routine work such as taking notes, preparing slides and compiling data, are increasingly finding that AI can now do those tasks faster and cheaper.

“If you are in a repetitive task job, kiss it goodbye,” Kristalina Georgieva, managing director of the International Monetary Fund, told a panel discussion on AI in Bangkok earlier this month for online.

Spreading strain

Singapore, the Association of Southeast Asian Nations’ wealthiest member, is already showing early signs of slower graduate hiring as it struggles to match the aspirations of the region’s best-educated young people with suitable work.

A survey by the city state’s six public universities conducted late last year and released in March found that the share of job-seeking graduates who found work within six months of their final exams fell to 83.4 per cent in 2025 from 87.1 per cent in 2024.

Whether the change is gradual or sudden, every country in the region is now grappling with the fallout from a new technology that pits professional experience and judgment against machine minds that are at once faster and cheaper.

In the Philippines, concerns are mounting that AI could replace at least some of the nearly 2 million people employed in the business process outsourcing sector that handles administrative tasks for foreign clients – and provides about 850,000 graduates with their first job every year.

In Indonesia, where the ILO estimates around 13 per cent of young people are already unemployed, a further hollowing out of entry-level work carries political risks among restive students who have repeatedly taken to the streets in recent months to protest against government policies.

For young people without the means to retrofit their education, catching the AI wave is becoming increasingly difficult.

The technology has already ravaged Malaysia’s marketing sector, according to Nafeesa, taking away copywriting and visual-content production work with the stroke of a few well-aimed chatbot prompts.

She finished an internship around two months ago and says she has since applied for “200 to 300 jobs” without success as the rise of AI pares back the available roles and employers armed with machine assistants lowball on pay.

“My expected [monthly] salary is at least 3,000 ringgit [US$730], but many offers fall short and don’t seem to reflect the skills and knowledge I have gained,” Nafeesa said.

“AI can be useful but it shouldn’t replace the entire creative process,” she said, arguing that the technology was best employed to help generate ideas “rather than supplanting human creativity”.

‘Creative destruction’

The big beasts of AI are fond of prophesying about a machine-scripted future that is as as unpredictable and dangerous as it is abundant and exciting.

In Bangkok this month, Anthropic co-founder Jack Clark called AI a form of “creative destruction”, using an economist’s term for new innovations and industries replacing old ones.

He said job losses were likely in fields with high exposure to AI, such as call centres, while simultaneously predicting employment would grow in other areas such as scientific research – and calling the technology’s potential to create jobs in entirely new industries a major unknown.

Anthropic, whose chatbot Claude is among the world’s most used, is preparing for an initial public offering that could value the company at up to US$2 trillion – making Clark and his fellow founders unfathomably rich.

At the other end of the spectrum, the advent of the AI age has those who are about to join the workforce overcome by a sense of powerlessness.

“I’m terrified,” Natthanicha said. “AI technology keeps getting more advanced and I’m worried it will replace human labour.”

She dreams of becoming an actress, already a tough calling, but as AI-generated scripts and videos increasingly pervade the entertainment industry, the 25-year-old is realistic about her chances of success.

“Businesses will not waste money hiring when they know there’s technology available that’s faster, better and costs [next to] nothing,” she said.

“I guess at the end of the day I’d rather just make a living than wait for the right opportunity to come so I can do my dream job.”

Natthanicha is among the six in 10 Thai graduates who study humanities and social sciences, fields that feed many of the jobs most exposed to AI.

And the ranks of unemployed graduates are growing. About 44 per cent of Thailand’s unemployed are graduates aged 20 to 24, many with skills that do not match the jobs market, according to a recent briefing paper from the Kasikorn Research Centre.

At the same time, jobs are being created thanks to the billions of US dollars’ worth of investment in AI infrastructure that is pouring into the country – but a chronically underfunded and unreformed education system has left it short of the science, technology, engineering and mathematics graduates these industries need.

The government must therefore bring its universities up to speed to teach young people about a technology that is already here, according to observers. Yet while it scrambles to fund plans to upskill the graduates leaving university in their thousands every year, entry-level roles are quietly disappearing.

“Normally, fresh graduates learn on the job,” said Thongnuakao Kampim, co-founder of AEIOU, an AI consultancy for Thai businesses.

“It might take one or two years for them to get through the learning curve and become proficient at what they do, but now AI can already handle those initial tasks, and in many cases, it can do them even better. As a result, business owners no longer have the same need, or the time, to train them.”

Secretaries, clerks, administrators and those who made presentation decks, kept records or entered data were all becoming redundant, the 37-year-old said – the selfsame roles that once gave newcomers an entry point and an understanding of a company’s systems, culture and expertise.

“A company that once employed thousands of people might shrink to just 100,” she said. “There will simply be fewer seats available within organisations, fewer positions to fill. It will become a game of musical chairs when it comes to hiring people and competing for jobs.”

New roles, such as that of office “AI champion”, who helps a firm compete using AI agents and expertise, may also prove out of reach for graduates gradually being frozen out of the jobs market.

“It’s not just about being good at using AI,” Thongnuakao said. “They need other skills … like the ability to develop and upskill people across the organisation so that employees can effectively use AI in their work.”

The very nature of work is changing, according to business analysts, demanding constantly updated skills from workers and pushing employers to embed AI throughout their operations just to stay ahead.

“Delayed adoption risks widening skill gaps and weakening competitiveness,” consultancy PwC Malaysia said in a July report. “Ultimately, the advantage will come not just from technology, but from effectively integrating and managing it – across people, processes and AI.”

For jobless graduates, adapting to the AI age is easier said than done. Andy Iskandar Baharudin, 23, a finance graduate from a Malaysian public university, has applied to more than 100 companies since finishing an accounting and administration internship in July.

He spends his days slogging through job applications, trying to stay upbeat about his prospects as he completes round upon round of speculative emails and calls.

“As fresh graduates, we not only have to compete with other applicants, but also continually upgrade our skills to keep up with technological developments,” he said, lamenting the amount of competition for entry-level jobs that often called for two years’ prior experience.

“How are we supposed to gain experience as fresh graduates if even getting an opportunity to work is difficult?” he added.

“Not every fresh graduate who is still unemployed is being too picky or isn’t trying to find work. We do want to work, gain experience and build our own careers. It’s just that sometimes the opportunities are so hard to come by.”

Singapore’s stand

In Singapore, the promise of employment and “the good life” in return for working hard in school and college is, in many respects, part of the social contract. But with that well-worn path no longer as certain as it once was, policymakers are speaking frankly about what the future might look like.

AI might have already broken the “bottom rung” of the career ladder, Prime Minister Lawrence Wong said at the DBS Asia Future Forward Conference on October 12. Routine tasks such as note-taking, speech drafting and preparing PowerPoint slides would soon be obsolete, he said.

“So employers will need to be more deliberate in thinking about training and mentoring of their young officers,” Wong said. “And that is something we are studying in Singapore, sector by sector.”

As part of that push, the government has agreed to subsidise companies that take on students as interns, with the aim of teaching them the systems, culture and soft skills they will need before graduating into a transformed workforce.

So far, job losses in the city state attributable to AI appear to be little more than a trickle, but that could become a flood as use of the technology expands across industries.

Of those Singapore firms that have adopted AI, 6.2 per cent reported lowered headcount and another 8.5 per cent reported lower hiring activity, an April report by the Manpower Ministry found.

Wong said there was still time to retrain workers affected by AI and match them to new job opportunities. This year, the city state unveiled ambitious plans to do just that, including a S$1 billion (US$780 million) investment in worker upskilling, infrastructure upgrades, securing advanced hardware and research and development.

“That is what we are doing in Singapore and hopefully that is what, over time, the global economy will be able to do for the rest of the world as well,” he said at the October 12 conference.

Singapore has won praise for its foresight and preparation. But it is a small, wealthy state with a strong record in planning, adopting technology and implementing policy.

For other Southeast Asian nations, the outlook is bleaker. The IMF has warned that already unequal economies risk becoming even more so as a few people earn a premium for harnessing AI technology while most stay trapped in a service class.

“You get young people, who would normally have gone into professional routine jobs, now serving coffee in Starbucks,” IMF chief Georgieva told the Bangkok summit. “That is not what young people aspire for.”

item.title: [SCMP] Hong Kong’s wider yuan push: a gateway to the world?
item.description:
In September, Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu unveiled the city’s first five-year plan along with his policy address, highlighting Hong Kong’s strategic role in promoting the greater use of the yuan outside mainland China as a key priority. In the last of a four-part series on the internationalisation of the yuan, Lam Ka-sing examines Hong Kong’s push to make the currency part of everyday life – from vending machines and retail payments to government spending and cross-border trade.

At Hong Kong’s Central Ferry Pier No 8, mainland Chinese tourist Lei is surprised to find that the digital currency e-CNY can be used to buy drinks from a vending machine.

Lei, a logistics worker in his twenties from Guangxi, had never encountered the digital currency and related payment system developed by the country’s central bank, the People’s Bank of China, in real life.
item.content:encoded:
In September, Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu unveiled the city’s first five-year plan along with his policy address, highlighting Hong Kong’s strategic role in promoting the greater use of the yuan outside mainland China as a key priority. In the last of a four-part series on the internationalisation of the yuan, Lam Ka-sing examines Hong Kong’s push to make the currency part of everyday life – from vending machines and retail payments to government spending and cross-border trade.

At Hong Kong’s Central Ferry Pier No 8, mainland Chinese tourist Lei is surprised to find that the digital currency e-CNY can be used to buy drinks from a vending machine.

Lei, a logistics worker in his twenties from Guangxi, had never encountered the digital currency and related payment system developed by the country’s central bank, the People’s Bank of China, in real life.

Hong Kong has been testing the use of e-CNY in a pilot scheme, with the aim of making cross-border retail payments more convenient.

“I remember when I was in senior secondary school, my politics class talked about this,” he said of the e-CNY. “But we haven’t seen this in real life. I saw this for the first time today in Hong Kong.”

The excitement did not move him, however, to use the option; he went with Alipay instead.

As China seeks to expand international use of the yuan amid rising geopolitical uncertainties and growing import-export trade, the Hong Kong government has made wider use of the currency a priority in its annual policy address and the city’s first five-year plan, covering 2026-30.

From vending machines to government receivables and payments for cross-border bills, yuan settlements are gaining momentum – although consumer habits and currency unpredictability during conversion into Hong Kong dollars remain obstacles.

Government-led yuan adoption

Hong Kong has the world’s largest offshore yuan liquidity pool. As of July 31, renminbi deposits in the city had reached 1.3 trillion yuan.

In an interview with the SCMP earlier this month, Secretary for Financial Services and the Treasury Christopher Hui Ching-yu said the city had taken steps to pave the way for broader yuan use among businesses and residents.

For example, he said the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, the city’s de facto central bank, had earlier injected more liquidity into the offshore renminbi market by expanding its renminbi business facility to 500 billion yuan.

“Another thing that we should do is about education,” he said. “Try to share more use cases of renminbi in the region, either in the form of trade settlement and others, in such a way that there is greater interest and eagerness across the region using renminbi.”

He conceded that bottlenecks in yuan adoption needed to be addressed.

Hui cited market feedback on insufficient direct quotes between local currencies and the yuan.

With Asian economies trading more heavily among themselves after the Covid-19 pandemic, and the renminbi offering lower interest rates than the US dollar, Hui said there were stronger reasons for regional businesses to raise financing and settle trades in the yuan without touching the dollar.

In June, the Monetary Authority signed a memorandum of understanding with Bank Indonesia, the country’s central bank, and the People’s Bank of China to establish a bilateral transaction framework for direct offshore renminbi-Indonesian rupiah trading, reducing exchange-rate risks and transaction costs for businesses.

“[Through this] there will be greater willingness for market participants to use RMB,” Hui said.

Yuxuan Tang, Asia head of rates and foreign exchange strategy at JP Morgan Private Bank, said global fragmentation could be manifested by the fact that rising geopolitical tensions and supply chain reconfiguration were encouraging countries and businesses to diversify their settlement arrangements.

Direct currency transaction frameworks, such as the mechanism between the offshore renminbi and rupiah mentioned in the policy address, could reduce transaction costs, limit foreign exchange risk and lessen operational dependence on a single settlement system.

“The broader implication is a gradual evolution towards a more multicurrency global financial system,” Tang said. “Over time, this could deepen regional currency liquidity pools and support the development of local financial markets.”

The current situation highlighted the transition of the offshore renminbi from a pure trade-settlement currency into an investment and diversification asset amid global fragmentation, Tang said.
