Hong Kong authorities are also taking the lead in adopting more yuan in government revenue and expenditure.

On the revenue side, Hui said the government had recently changed the law to allow it to collect stamp duty in renminbi when mainland investors bought and settled Hong Kong-listed shares directly in yuan through renminbi-denominated stock counters under the cross-border Stock Connect scheme.

Trading in these stock counters is due to be rolled out by July next year.

Receiving stamp duty in yuan would also help the government manage exchange-rate risks, Hui said.

“When we have the RMB counters collecting stamp duty in RMB, it will also be an additional source of RMB,” he said.

“Having them directly deployed will be a way for us to avoid the need for managing the exchange-rate risk. Fundamentally, it is to manage use – RMB in and RMB out.”

On the expenditure side, settlement in yuan is already a reality.

The government has made renminbi payments for a cross-border infrastructure project, the Western Cross-River Link Bridge connecting two parks in Hong Kong and Shenzhen in the Hetao Shenzhen-Hong Kong Science and Technology Innovation Cooperation Zone.

More significantly, it is discussing with mainland authorities the possibility of settling the 2027-29 Dongjiang water supply agreement in renminbi. The city paid HK$5.28 billion for Dongjiang water in 2025-26.

Through the Dongjiang-Shenzhen water supply scheme, Hong Kong has relied on water from the Dongjiang, or East River, for the past 60 years, supplying up to 80 per cent of the city’s fresh water.

Cross-border social welfare payments are also shifting to renminbi.

According to the Social Welfare Department, the government spent about 37.7 million yuan in the 2025-26 financial year on places at residential care homes in Guangdong province.

As of September, 1,600 Hong Kong seniors were staying in 29 homes for the elderly taking part in the department’s subsidised residential care services scheme in the province.

An additional 5.77 million yuan was paid out in medical subsidies to 762 elderly participants who opted to receive the funds in the currency.

Use cases

At the retail level, e-CNY is another point of focus. Hui revealed that the number of local retail outlets accepting the digital currency had jumped from 300 in May 2024 to about 5,200 currently.

“They cover a whole value chain in terms of retail stores, hotels, travel agencies, restaurants, convenience stores [and] supermarkets,” Hui said.

“So fundamentally, we try to provide at the more retail level as much convenience as possible, in such a way that for the users who are really ready and willing to use e-CNY, they can do that more conveniently in Hong Kong.”

As of January this year, 79,600 e-CNY wallets had been registered, according to data from the People’s Bank of China.

The city’s Faster Payment System (FPS), a real-time payment platform, mirrors this rapid growth.

Daily renminbi transaction volume on the system surged from about 30 million yuan across 700 transactions in the fourth quarter of 2018 to an average of 21,500 transactions worth about 1.1 billion yuan daily by the third quarter of this year, according to bureau data.

To further fuel the momentum, the Monetary Authority is actively preparing to link FPS directly with the mainland’s UnionPay, a bank card and payment system, in a move expected to enable seamless cross-border retail payments across a vast merchant network.

Despite the rapid growth of QR-code payments, a banking source pointed to a lingering hurdle in the city’s infrastructure: settlement banks automatically convert these renminbi payments into Hong Kong dollars for local merchants at the back end as goods are priced in the local currency.

Asked about the instant conversion, Hui said authorities were trying to develop an ecosystem in which banks encouraged merchant acceptance by expanding support, noting that the number of retail banks supporting e-CNY top-ups through FPS had risen from 17 to 19.

“So, what we try to do is really identify more players in the market that are ready and also willing to take on e-CNY in such a way that for people or for tourists who are coming here and also want to use it, they have the right means to do so,” Hui said.

Mainland tourists are believed to make up the largest group of e-CNY users in Hong Kong.

Mainlanders accounted for 78 per cent, or 31.9 million, of the tourists visiting the city in the first nine months of this year, according to the Hong Kong Tourism Board.

Hong Kong-based FreshUp, a major operator of vending machines, including those at the Central pier, is part of the private sector driving the wider use of the yuan in the city.

Founder and executive director David Lam said the company rapidly upgraded about 800 of its more than 5,000 machines to accept e-CNY.

In the weeks before the 15th National Games, co-hosted by Guangdong, Hong Kong, and Macau last November, there was a coordinated push to expand e-CNY acceptance and use in the city, mainly a bank- and merchant-led adoption campaign.

Appointed by Bank of China (Hong Kong), FreshUp spearheaded the roll-out in October last year.

“We helped them modify many things, such as installing QR-code scanners, ensuring back-end data accuracy, and integrating the API [application programming interface],” Lam said. “We spent a lot of effort on this project.”

He said the company had deployed the payment option across targeted tourist-heavy transport hubs.

“The response has been very good. It has achieved Bank of China’s expectations for the project,” Lam noted, declining to reveal exact transaction data.

By capturing what Lam described as “high-frequency, low-amount” daily transactions, these micro-purchases are quietly building consumer habits around the use of the digital yuan.

However, mainland tourist Mr Wu said more promotion and marketing was needed to raise awareness of e-CNY in the city, given the prevalence of Alipay and WeChat Pay. Alipay is owned by Ant Group, an affiliate of Alibaba Group Holding, which also owns the South China Morning Post.

“It has not been [widely] promoted,” said Wu, who is in his fifties. “Someone sent this [to me] previously but most people have not used it because Alipay and WeChat Pay are there already.”

Bank of China (Hong Kong) deputy chief executive Huabin Wang recently said that a growing range of renminbi products was among the advantages the city possessed that would ensure broad prospects as a global offshore renminbi hub.

“First, Hong Kong’s first five-year plan provides clearer guidance for the development direction of its renminbi business,” Wang said.

“Second, the city’s renminbi business ecosystem has become increasingly mature with its expanding range of offshore renminbi products.

“Third, Hong Kong has a unique advantage in telling the story of the international use of the renminbi, and its ability to reach emerging markets is strengthening.”

item.title: [SCMP] ArchipelaGoGo! The Inter-Island Festival is back to celebrate Hong Kong’s more laid-back lifestyles
item.description:
What do the curators and organisers of the 2026 Inter-Island Festival have in common? All three of them – Yip Kai-chun, Chan Chun-kit and Gloria Furness – traded life in urban Hong Kong for one of the city’s outlying islands for similar reasons: to be close to nature, experience a sense of community and enjoy a quiet lifestyle.

However, they got more than they bargained for: connection. Peng Chau specifically “has a lot of people from the creative industries who move out [of the city] and start over”, says Furness, the newer resident out of the three. It’s how the compact land-mass, measuring less than one sq km, became ground zero for the Inter-Island Festival, a month-long event celebrating the coastal societies on Hong Kong’s outlying islands through exhibitions, workshops, installations and talks.

Founded in 2019, the Inter-Island Festival takes inspiration from the inter-island ferry (“cross-water ferry”) connections between the outlying islands of Cheung Chau and Peng Chau and Lantau’s Chi Ma Wan and Mui Wo. Its first iteration, in 2021, came to fruition through the efforts of more than 50 collaborators, who put together 40-plus tours, workshops, exhibitions, performances and screenings, attracting more than 10,000 visitors to experience island culture.
item.content:encoded:
What do the curators and organisers of the 2026 Inter-Island Festival have in common? All three of them – Yip Kai-chun, Chan Chun-kit and Gloria Furness – traded life in urban Hong Kong for one of the city’s outlying islands for similar reasons: to be close to nature, experience a sense of community and enjoy a quiet lifestyle.

However, they got more than they bargained for: connection. Peng Chau specifically “has a lot of people from the creative industries who move out [of the city] and start over”, says Furness, the newer resident out of the three. It’s how the compact land-mass, measuring less than one sq km, became ground zero for the Inter-Island Festival, a month-long event celebrating the coastal societies on Hong Kong’s outlying islands through exhibitions, workshops, installations and talks.

Founded in 2019, the Inter-Island Festival takes inspiration from the inter-island ferry (“cross-water ferry”) connections between the outlying islands of Cheung Chau and Peng Chau and Lantau’s Chi Ma Wan and Mui Wo. Its first iteration, in 2021, came to fruition through the efforts of more than 50 collaborators, who put together 40-plus tours, workshops, exhibitions, performances and screenings, attracting more than 10,000 visitors to experience island culture.

After a three-year hiatus, the Inter-Island Festival finally makes its return for a third edition, taking place on Cheung Chau, Lantau and Peng Chau across five consecutive weekends, from November 1 to 29. Yip and Chan are among the founding members, while Furness joins the team for the first time after previous involvement as a volunteer coordinator.

When asked how the trio got together, they point to the very connection already present among the creative communities of the outlying islands. “I feel like everybody knows everybody,” says Yip, an independent artist and curator who has organised other events on the island. It was Chan, a co-founder of social enterprise and research lab Islanders and a long-time resident of Peng Chau, who introduced Yip to life on the island, leading the latter to eventually make the move from Sham Shui Po.

Furness became acquainted with Chan and Yip through various arts and cultural gatherings, and they invited her to join the Inter-Island Festival team this year to “deepen their collaboration” and leverage her experience in events planning and curation, gained from working with the biennial Hong Kong International Photo Festival exhibition and Koon Man Space, a photography-resource centre in Tsuen Wan.

“We all have similar backgrounds and networks,” says Furness. “We moved at various times [to Peng Chau] from the same circle, which is also part of our lore now.”

Yip conceived the idea for the Inter-Island Festival after moving to Peng Chau in 2017 and learning of the ferry network, little known to non-residents. “We mostly think of Victoria Harbour when riding the ferry [in Hong Kong], but the inter-island ferry is different. You see unfamiliar mountains and waters; that’s very special,” he says.

It sparked something in him, encouraging him to explore more of the city’s outlying islands.

Moreover, learning of the Lantau Tomorrow Vision project, a government land-reclamation initiative formally proposed in 2018, with the goal of building artificial islands off Lantau near Kau Yi Chau and Hei Ling Chau, further ignited his fervour, as the anticipated marine-habitat destruction and carbon emissions were expected to cause irreparable harm and “irreversibly change” the treasured environment of the islands. “Maybe a festival [about the islands] will create a bond between each of the ports that will be affected by the construction” and demonstrate their need to be preserved, Yip decided.

Dr Michael Rivera, a biological anthropologist at the University of Hong Kong who grew up in Mui Wo, shares that recent urban developments and events that “highlight traditional island culture” have also accelerated the desire for preservation. Largely, Hong Kong’s outlying islands are “marketed as tourist destinations”, he says. “But, at the same time, that [creates] an urgency, where people on those islands or who care about those islands feel that they need to share and conserve the narratives, livelihood and memories that are in these places.”

Conceived as a response, the Inter-Island Festival becomes a physical anchor to the stories of the islands’ inhabitants – such as the kaito captain, surnamed Wong, and his team, who bring Peng Chau residents across the water, and a fish-farm owner, Mo Lo, who commutes from Mui Wo to his farm in Chi Ma Wan – in living form. Between the islands, the connections are felt through daily life: a Peng Chau resident hikes in Chi Ma Wan, goes to the beach in Cheung Chau and dines in the cooked-food market in Mui Wo. Yip, Chan and Furness, together with local curators, exhibitors and artists, preach the gospel of their islands as a self-sustaining network of people and culture rather than being dependent on the city.

But it wasn’t smooth sailing upon launch, despite the evident passion driving the project. Yip admits that “the first edition was a pain”. Originally scheduled for 2020, the Inter-Island Festival was postponed three times due to Covid-19 social-distancing measures. In the weeks leading up to the event, there was concern that “attracting more visitors to the islands could overwhelm the community and inconvenience the residents” during the pandemic. After multiple delays, they decided to host it anyway, over three days on the last weekend of March 2021, focusing on the art, tradition, nature and environments of the four locations. Yip even organised an open house showcasing his life as an islander and his artworks.

A reprise followed in November 2023, with an expanded agenda taking place across four weekends. As part of the programme, visitors could listen to the sounds of the islands’ non-human neighbours – a running river, the chirping of birds and a buffalo bathing – and examine an installation designed as a home for bees. Peng Chau resident Jiming Lu, who serves as a local curator and coordinator for the upcoming edition, held two guided tours, one of Peng Chau cinema and the other of the island.

It took longer than expected for the curator-organisers to come back with the next instalment. “We really needed to take a break after the last edition, because it was quite overwhelming. It’s a lot of work,” says Chan.

Instead, they used the time to reflect on how to improve the event. One change that Yip, Chan and Furness are making this year is to “centralise” the festival on a different island each weekend, rather than host programmes simultaneously across all four, as it was done in the past, to help reduce the inter-island travel strain on visitors during their day trips.

Another challenge is timetabling. Entirely volunteer-run, the Inter-Island Festival is “really a bottom-up initiative, so we have to organise it according to everyone’s schedule”, says Furness. Plus, the islands are going through post-pandemic changes. “People are developing new creative spaces”, which take time to be incorporated into the event. In a way, the economic and structural development of the islands – such as the opening of new shops and businesses, adding another layer of self-reliance for the islanders who choose to live outside urban Hong Kong – and the festival have a “symbiotic relationship”. Even as a co-founder, Chan still encounters something new each time he visits the other islands to meet people who can represent the communities and business owners. “I’m still discovering more about these islands, including Peng Chau, through the festival.”

Next month, the Inter-Island Festival will include local co-curators and coordinators who reside in or are deeply familiar with Cheung Chau, Chi Ma Wan and Mui Wo, as the core team members all live on Peng Chau.

“We [want to] give more curatorial power to the local [collaborators] and allow our neighbours to be more involved within the umbrella of the festival,” says Yip. Compared with other public revitalisation projects, the Inter-Island Festival focuses on uplifting residents. “We want them to realise how precious island life is” and not take it for granted, he adds.

Centred on the theme “ArchipelaGoGo!”, this year’s edition will explore what living together as a cluster of islands looks like in 2026 through the lens of inter-island mythologies and the tidal beings that live on, around and under the ocean. Feature Projects, which pair researchers with creative practitioners over a six-month period to develop works around a specific theme, will include a literature scholar from Lamma Island working with a dancer, a woodworker partnering with a bamboo artist and a marine paleobiologist teaming up with two ceramic artists.

Moreover, the festival team selected 20 Micro Projects and 20 self-initiated Satellite Projects from the open call. Some of these include a hands-on workshop using oyster shells as a palette to create textured artwork in Peng Chau; a photography exhibition on the Cheung Chau Bun Festival; a community walk of Mui Wo to map out the neighbourhood through smell, touch and sound; and a tour across the mudflats in Pui O, which are home to snails, mangroves and fiddler crabs. Local businesses will also organise their own activities and discounts during the Inter-Island Festival.

Recruiting on-the-ground expertise is essential to fully represent the diversity of these islands. The four communities at the heart of the Inter-Island Festival each have their own distinct culture and rich tradition, though they share deep historical roots tied to maritime trade, fishing and, eventually, integration through the inter-island ferry network.

Peng Chau’s past can be traced back to the Neolithic period; a substantial fishing community called the island home, drawn by its sheltered bays and freshwater sources. In the 1960s, Peng Chau became a manufacturing powerhouse, with more than 30 types of factories, including the Great China Match Factory, once Southeast Asia’s largest producer of matches.

Mui Wo’s history has been recorded as far back as the Southern Song dynasty (1127-1279), when fleeing imperial court officials sought refuge from the invading Mongols in the area in 1277. Mui Wo’s silver mine, used to extract galena, operated until the end of the 19th century. In the 50s, the community blossomed as a farming hub, focusing on rice and vegetables.

Chi Ma Wan, a bay on southeastern Lantau, was a melting pot for Hong Kong’s early settlers, including the Hakka, Hoklo, Punti and Tanka. Farming and fishing dominated the peninsula, and its Shap Long Reservoir was once the main water source for Cheung Chau, Peng Chau and Hei Ling Chau. Later, camps housing Vietnamese refugees were built there.

Cheung Chau flourished as a fishing and trading port during the early Ming dynasty (1368-1644). Given its propensity for attracting mariners, it’s little wonder early-19th century pirate Cheung Po-tsai chose to hide his loot in one of the caves there – or so the legend goes. Nowadays, it’s the annual Cheung Chau Bun Festival, celebrating Pak Tai, the Taoist water deity and protector of fishermen and seafarers, that sees travellers scrambling to the island.

“We have always been a maritime society, reliant on coastal resources and seafood to survive. About a century ago, the population really expanded when more and more waves of boatpeople moved to these islands,” says Rivera. With the inception of the inter-island ferry route, closer ties between the islands were established, allowing them to have a connected, archipelagic relationship, rather than exist as isolated places.

But just as the islands have evolved into the coastal societies they are today, there has also been a shift in the way people see them, particularly during and after the Covid-19 pandemic.

In 2021, homes on Hong Kong’s outlying islands saw an almost 30 per cent increase in transactions, according to Midland Realty. While reports from the Census and Statistics Department do not detail urban-to-island migration trends, demographic data from last year reveals that the Islands district, which includes Cheung Chau, Mui Wo and Peng Chau, grew to about 196,000 residents. (Chi Ma Wan, while also part of the Islands district and once populated with villages and settlements, is largely uninhabited these days. Some descendants visit regularly but don’t “live” there year-round any more.)

“Part of what makes the [outlying] islands attractive is the cheaper rents,” says Rivera. “You can also expect a stronger network with your neighbours and a stronger sense of place.” He adds that, on the islands, “your entire space is a third space”, in that “your house is also part of the third space – there’s no barrier between them any more”.

In September 2025, the Hong Kong government shelved the Lantau Tomorrow Vision blueprint until further notice, but the mission of the Inter-Island Festival continues.

For Yip, Chan and Furness, living on Peng Chau is an exploration of how individuals can grow together, away from gentrification or “city mentality”, mirroring the connection, community, culture and creativity they hope to preserve with the Inter-Island Festival.

Furness believes that one can only fully understand the “islander” way of life through lived experiences. What might seem unusual to urbanites is second nature to them. By simply looking out the window, “I can tell the time based on which boat is coming in”, she says. For Yip, he can guess the typhoon signal by observing how the trees move in the wind.

Chan hopes that the Inter-Island Festival can grow to become like the Hungry Ghost Festival, where “people get together regardless of their backgrounds”. Different generations nurture their own traditions while still growing organically, much like the stories and lives on the islands. When you live the “island life” long enough, says Chan, “you start changing to its ways”.

The 2026 Inter-Island Festival runs until November 29. Tickets for individual events in the programme are sold separately here

item.title: [SCMP] Scary deals? What makes Hong Kong shun death-linked homes while France embraces the risk
item.description:
Even as Hong Kong remains the world’s least affordable housing market, many buyers still shun heavily discounted homes linked to an “unnatural death”, such as murder or suicide, according to property agents.

Prices for such properties could fall by as much as 50 per cent, while rents were typically about 20 per cent below market rates, they added.

The aversion stands in stark contrast to parts of Europe, particularly in France, where buyers are often willing to purchase homes under a “vente en viager” arrangement that can see properties sold at discounts of up to 80 per cent below market value.
item.content:encoded:
Even as Hong Kong remains the world’s least affordable housing market, many buyers still shun heavily discounted homes linked to an “unnatural death”, such as murder or suicide, according to property agents.

Prices for such properties could fall by as much as 50 per cent, while rents were typically about 20 per cent below market rates, they added.

The aversion stands in stark contrast to parts of Europe, particularly in France, where buyers are often willing to purchase homes under a “vente en viager” arrangement that can see properties sold at discounts of up to 80 per cent below market value.

Under the system, an elderly homeowner agrees to sell a property in exchange for an upfront payment and a monthly annuity that continues for the rest of their life.

The arrangement allows sellers to supplement their retirement income while remaining in their homes. For buyers, the main attraction is the steep discount, even if they may have to wait for years before taking possession.

In effect, buyers are betting on how long sellers will live before they can claim the property.

“In Hong Kong, there is no official definition or registry for ‘haunted houses,’ or xiong zhai in Chinese,” said Ivy Wong, managing director of Centaline Mortgage.

“The term generally refers to properties associated with unnatural deaths, such as murders, suicides or fatal accidents, which are distinctly separated from natural deaths such as passing away from old age.”

The “haunted houses”, particularly those linked to sensational murder cases, could receive a zero valuation or be deemed ineligible for valuation, making it difficult to secure a mortgage, according to Eric Tso Tak-ming, chief vice-president at mReferral Mortgage Brokerage Services.

“Because the difficulty of reselling these properties in the future is exceptionally high, valuation firms significantly reduce their valuations,” Tso said. “Consequently, it is very difficult for banks to approve the buyer’s desired loan amount, and they often lower the loan-to-value ratio.”

Recently, a low-floor flat with a private podium in Metro Town in Tseung Kwan O was sold for HK$4.5 million (US$574,000), significantly below the more than HK$7 million valuation for a comparable home on a similar floor in another tower of the same project.

The reason, according to one agent, was that a person had fallen from a higher floor and landed on the flat’s private podium, stigmatising it as a “haunted house”.

Murders, especially those involving multiple victims, grisly details or extensive media coverage, tend to have the most severe impact on home assessments and could result in outright mortgage rejections

Ivy Wong, Centaline Mortgage

In some cases, online mortgage valuation platforms operated by banks do not generate valuations for homes associated with such incidents.

There were also cases where the “negative impact even spilled over, causing online valuations for the entire floor to become unavailable”, Centaline Mortgage’s Wong said.

Banks and surveying firms relied heavily on internal databases and media reports of tragic incidents to conduct case-by-case assessments, she added.

Banks, however, do not all take the same approach. “While some adopt a highly conservative approach and outright reject mortgage applications for stigmatised properties, the majority rely on individual assessments to determine approval and set conditions,” Wong said.

Assessments depend on factors including the nature and severity of the incident. Murders, especially those involving multiple victims, grisly details or extensive media coverage, tended to have “the most severe impact” and could result in “outright mortgage rejections”, she said.

Suicides involving charcoal burning, jumping or hanging, as well as fatal accidents such as falls or gas explosions were generally viewed as less severe, and more open-minded banks could still consider mortgage applications for such properties, Wong added.

Valuations for homes linked to high-profile murder cases would typically fall by 50 per cent or more, while those associated with suicides or fatal accidents could decline by at least 30 per cent, she said.

However, if an incident occurred decades ago and the property had changed hands or been leased multiple times since, some banks could “view the negative impact as diluted, resulting in a more favourable assessment”, Wong said.

France and several other European countries, including Belgium, Switzerland, Spain, Italy and Germany, take a markedly different view of death in relation to property transactions under the “vente en viager” arrangement.

“What sets France apart is how common private, person-to-person ‘viager’ sales are, with a well-developed legal framework around them,” said Alex Balkin, head of Savills French Riviera.

The arrangement offered advantages to both sellers and buyers, Balkin added.

For sellers, the benefits included additional retirement income while remaining in their homes, annuity payments indexed to inflation and part of the income receiving a “favourable tax treatment”, he said.

Sellers were also well-protected, as contracts typically contained clauses allowing them to reclaim the property and retain payments already received if buyers stopped paying.

For buyers, the property’s price was discounted to reflect occupancy and the seller’s life expectancy, while payments were spread over time, removing the need for a traditional bank mortgage, according to Balkin.

Some Hong Kong-based buyers had inquired about purchasing French property through a “vente en viager” arrangement, said Sebastien Salin, a Hong Kong-based French entrepreneur and the founder of Acheterpourlouer, a real estate advisory firm that helps expatriates and foreigners to buy properties in France remotely.

“There’s a number of clients who have shown an interest, but it’s a limited percentage,” Salin said.

Depending on the seller’s age, discounts could reach as much as 80 per cent of market value, he added.

“This arrangement is getting more popular because a lot of people are getting older and don’t have much income, but they have a nice flat,” Salin said. “So they want to get some extra funds to make sure they have enough income during the remaining years of their life.”

There is, however, a famous example of a transaction that went badly wrong for the buyer.

In 1965, Jeanne Calment sold her home in Arles, France, at age 90 under a “vente en viager” arrangement to Andre-Francois Raffray, a 47-year-old lawyer.

Raffray paid Calment 2,500 French francs a month for 30 years before dying in 1995. His widow continued the payments until Calment died in 1997 at the age of 122. By then the family had paid more than twice the home’s value, according to Savills. France replaced the franc with the euro in 1999, when 2,500 francs equalled around US$405.

“It’s a little bit like gambling,” Salin said.

In Hong Kong, the aversion to properties linked to unfortunate circumstances stemmed from “the prevailing cultural beliefs and superstitions that are deeply ingrained in local Chinese society,” according to a spokesman from Centaline Property Agency.

There were, however, prospective buyers or tenants willing to consider these properties, he said.

“Individuals who do not subscribe to local superstitions, such as Catholic buyers, expatriates and atheists, are much more open to living in these homes,” he said.

“This is particularly driven by budget constraints or a desire to save money, as the significant rental discounts of around 20 per cent below standard market rates make these properties a highly cost-effective option.”

Even so, the long-term value of these properties generally does not fully recover or keep pace with the broader property market.

“While general market growth may result in a slight increase in value, these properties almost invariably continue to trade at a significant discount relative to comparable, unaffected properties in the same neighbourhood,” the spokesman said.

item.title: [SCMP] Ellora and Ajanta: the history and mystery of India’s ancient cave-temples
item.description:
The view of the Kailasa Temple from above takes my breath away – and I am not referring just to the huffing and puffing of the climb to the top of the hillock that overlooks this 8th century marvel.

Its sheer scale and significance seen from on high make me literally gasp in wonder. In an archaeological complex strewn with ancient Buddhist, Jain and Hindu temples, this one – dedicated to the Hindu destroyer god, Shiva – is the show-stopper.

It’s the middle of the monsoon season in central India and I have plodded along the rough stone pathways elsewhere at the Ellora Caves complex in incessant, if mild, morning showers. But any discomfort is forgotten when I look down upon this 1,200-year-old temple that was carved top-down out of solid basalt rock.
item.content:encoded:
The view of the Kailasa Temple from above takes my breath away – and I am not referring just to the huffing and puffing of the climb to the top of the hillock that overlooks this 8th century marvel.

Its sheer scale and significance seen from on high make me literally gasp in wonder. In an archaeological complex strewn with ancient Buddhist, Jain and Hindu temples, this one – dedicated to the Hindu destroyer god, Shiva – is the show-stopper.

It’s the middle of the monsoon season in central India and I have plodded along the rough stone pathways elsewhere at the Ellora Caves complex in incessant, if mild, morning showers. But any discomfort is forgotten when I look down upon this 1,200-year-old temple that was carved top-down out of solid basalt rock.

That’s worth repeating; this temple – with its central shrine, multi-storey gateway, assembly halls, free-standing pillars, life-size elephant statues and surrounding side galleries – was not built from the ground up, but hewn into shape from the top, slowly, painstakingly over the course of many years. It is estimated that more than 200,000 tonnes of rock were chiselled by hand to create the basic shapes, to which carvings and flourishes were later added. Measuring 30 metres in height, 90 metres in length and 53 metres in width, this is the world’s largest monolithic structure.

“How was this possible in the 8th century,” asks guide Vilas Mitkar, giving voice to the question uppermost in my mind. How did those Rashtrakuta artisans have access to such sophisticated theoretical and technical skills? And where did all the excavated rock and rubble go?

I hired this licensed guide at the main gate of the caves complex in the hope of learning more about Ellora’s history but, in this case, I am to be disappointed, because even archaeologists and historians have been unable to solve the puzzle of how this particular masterpiece was built.

Mitkar makes up for his lack of rational explanations with a plethora of far-fetched theories that have been repeated and embellished over the centuries. The one alleging the temple was constructed by aliens is particularly bizarre. There again, looking at the temple walls glistening in the weak post-rain sunshine, it is easy to believe that superhuman, if not actual otherworldly, hands were involved in their creation.

Within the temple, Mitkar stops to point out the splendour of the statues of assorted divine beings lining the corridors and edges of the pavilions, and the elaborate details in the carvings along the inner walls of the main sanctum. Depicted are scenes from the Hindu epics Ramayana and Mahabharata; flying angels and warring demons; and myriad incarnations of popular gods and goddesses. One could spend days deciphering these stories in stone.

Hundreds of such cave-temple complexes – most of them Buddhist – exist in the central Indian state of Maharashtra, having been built centuries ago to serve as both centres of worship for resident monks and places of rest for travellers. Many are in ruins or inaccessible to tourists, but the Karla and Bhaja caves, just off the highway linking the cities of Mumbai and Pune, have been fairly well preserved. And even within the urban chaos of Mumbai, there are the neglected Kanheri Caves, deep inside Sanjay Gandhi National Park, with similar architecture and iconography to those in the more significant sites.

Of these, the Ellora complex, roughly 320km from Mumbai and spread along 2km of a high escarpment, is one of the largest, with shrines dug directly into the basalt rock. And while the word “cave” may bring to mind dank and musty subterranean formations, these are massive, true to the etymology of the word “cavernous”.

Of the original 100 excavated between AD600 and 1000, only 34 of Ellora’s caves are open to the public, and it takes an entire morning to do just a cursory round of the most significant ones. Along the way, Mitkar generously colours his narrative with stories of hidden trapdoors and underground cities; he points to carved figurines of “extraterrestrial beings” on the walls. Many of Ellora’s pillars depict the yali: a mythical creature with the face of an elephant and the body of a lion – the epitome of strength and bravery.

Its Unesco World Heritage listing declares that Ellora “brings the civilization of ancient India to life”. While that is true, what is more significant, especially in today’s climate of frenzied communalism in India, is this statement: “Not only is the Ellora complex a unique artistic creation and a technological exploit but, with its sanctuaries devoted to Buddhism, Hinduism and Jainism, it illustrates the spirit of tolerance that was characteristic of ancient India.”

Tourists who have been quick to whip out selfie sticks and wisecracks fall into a respectful silence at Cave No 10 (also known as Vishwakarma Cave), a Buddhist chaitya, or prayer hall, with an imposing Buddha statue dominating its central altar. With a high domed roof and a wood-like polish to its rock pillars, this cave feels sparse and severe, but evokes the same sense of awe as the Kailasa Temple.

It’s a mystery how so much of Ellora has managed to withstand the ravages of time, and indeed, the plundering invaders who desecrated other monuments of the age, particularly those with a religious slant. It is known, however, how Ajanta – another cave complex, located a two-hour drive away and often mentioned in the same breath as Ellora – pulled it off.

At Ajanta, guide Naseeb Khan begins his tour not at the entrance to the caves but on a hilltop a few hundred metres away, from where the complex is visible in its entirety, sprawled along a horseshoe-shaped vertical cliff and concealed – as if by design – by a lush emerald forest.

It is believed the oldest of these 30 caves (although some sources say there are only 29) dates back to the 2nd century BC, with a second phase of building having taken place between AD480 and AD600. Not too long afterwards, Buddhism began to decline in popularity in the region, and the caves were eventually abandoned.

Ajanta simply slipped from view and remained hidden for more than 1,200 years – until 1819, when John Smith, a British Army officer hunting in the area, chanced upon the caves. One can only wonder at his amazement at finding these Buddhist monuments hewn into sheer rock.

We follow an easy downhill trail to the caves, passing seasonal waterfalls and panoramas.

Unlike at Ellora, which is under an hour’s drive from the nearest big city, Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar (named Aurangabad until 2023), we have Ajanta’s caves almost to ourselves, save for a few other domestic tourists.

Despite having been shielded from human interference for such a long time, the older Ajanta is in an overall more fragile state than Ellora, its cliff-edge, forested location having taken a toll. The damage is most evident in the erosion of the wall and ceiling frescoes, which were created with natural dyes and are considered the highlight of the complex. The few much-needed preservation measures in place include a ban on shoes and flash photography inside the caves, and a limit on the number of visitors at a time.

Walking barefoot on the cold stone floors seems appropriate and once my eyes get used to the darkness, I find it easy to trace the lines of the floral, geometric and even human shapes that adorn the walls. Themes include stories from the Jataka tales – ancient Buddhist literature conveying lessons and guidelines for ethical living; snippets from Buddha’s life; animals in conversation with humans; divine beings in silks and gold; and lithe creepers and intricate flowers. In one of the caves, Khan flashes a slim torchlight upon depictions of traders with Central Asian and African features, which attest to this region’s importance in a flourishing network of trade and commerce.

The most arresting of Ajanta’s frescoes is to be found in a crowded cluster in Cave No 1 and depicts Avalokiteshvara (called Guanyin in China) as the Bodhisattva Padmapani, or “Lotus Bearer”. The colours are faded, the paint is peeling, but my breath slows as I stand in the darkness, taking in the finer details of this 5th century painting of the bodhisattva of compassion.

Caves are denoted as either prayer hall or monastery (vihara), with the latter possessing the more advanced carvings and paintings. This is not surprising given that, at Ajanta’s peak, there were hundreds of Buddhist monks living and worshipping in these stone quarters. They enjoyed royal patronage, which in part allowed them to create art in such profusion.

“Painting was perhaps a form of meditation,” Khan muses. After all, Buddhist monks to this day engage in the act of creating delicate mandala paintings with coloured sand or rice flour. Once finished, the mandala is wiped out, to reinforce the idea that life is impermanent.

In the case of Ajanta, it is time that has been slowly destroying the art – another reminder that nothing lasts forever. There have been occasional rumblings about the need to close these caves to visitors to preserve them. But for now, I am grateful for this fleeting monsoon morning in the presence of such magnificence.

item.title: [SCMP] How Cantonese became mainland China’s regional cuisine of choice
item.description:
In a restored siheyuan courtyard residence, nestled amid 600-year-old hutong alleyways in Beijing’s Caochang neighbourhood, diners dip porcelain spoons into steaming bowls of double-boiled black Silkie chicken, conpoy and bamboo-pith soup. Overseen by celebrity culinarian Huang Jinghui, better known as chef Fei, Yan Garden also serves sweet red-bean soup lifted by aged tangerine peel, succulent char siu and deep-fried pigeon, its paper-thin skin glossy and taut.

Set amid the sea of softly curved, ash-grey rooftops and maze of walls of the Mandarin Oriental Qianmen, Beijing, Yan Garden may be thousands of kilometres from the homeland of the cuisines in which it specialises, but the scents, flavours and textures of its dishes evoke the lushness and humidity of southern China.

Few people would be surprised to find classic Cantonese fare in the centuries-old streets of northern China – the cuisine is, surely, almost everywhere. Look through the Michelin and Black Pearl Restaurant guides and it is striking how the gastronomy of the old coastal province of Canton – today’s Guangdong – dominates. In Beijing, seven of 32 Michelin-star restaurants focus on Cantonese cuisine. In Shanghai, 15 of 50.
item.content:encoded:
In a restored siheyuan courtyard residence, nestled amid 600-year-old hutong alleyways in Beijing’s Caochang neighbourhood, diners dip porcelain spoons into steaming bowls of double-boiled black Silkie chicken, conpoy and bamboo-pith soup. Overseen by celebrity culinarian Huang Jinghui, better known as chef Fei, Yan Garden also serves sweet red-bean soup lifted by aged tangerine peel, succulent char siu and deep-fried pigeon, its paper-thin skin glossy and taut.

Set amid the sea of softly curved, ash-grey rooftops and maze of walls of the Mandarin Oriental Qianmen, Beijing, Yan Garden may be thousands of kilometres from the homeland of the cuisines in which it specialises, but the scents, flavours and textures of its dishes evoke the lushness and humidity of southern China.

Few people would be surprised to find classic Cantonese fare in the centuries-old streets of northern China – the cuisine is, surely, almost everywhere. Look through the Michelin and Black Pearl Restaurant guides and it is striking how the gastronomy of the old coastal province of Canton – today’s Guangdong – dominates. In Beijing, seven of 32 Michelin-star restaurants focus on Cantonese cuisine. In Shanghai, 15 of 50.

According to chefs and Chinese-food experts, there are past and present reasons for its prominence – and opinion is divided on its future status. Cantonese cuisine’s legacy of being the most well-known Chinese regional food can be traced back to the waves of emigrants who took their food culture from southern China to Southeast Asia and the West, a centuries-long migration.

“Hong Kong didn’t experience the Cultural Revolution and the other turbulent events of mainland China in the second half of the 20th century, so their Cantonese cuisine flourished, unhindered by all this historical mayhem,” says British writer, author and cook Fuchsia Dunlop, an authority on Chinese food. “A lot of people think that, during this period, the best Cantonese food was to be found in Hong Kong. These days, Hong Kong is still a centre for Cantonese gastronomic excellence, but the mainland has caught up, with many Hongkongers now popping over to Shenzhen to eat food of a very high quality that is less expensive than at home.”

With its special economic zones, Canton was the first region in China to become wealthy, colouring people’s perception of the cuisine. “In the 1990s, if you wanted to go for an extravagant meal, even in Sichuan, you would go to a Cantonese restaurant with live seafood – it signified spending a lot of money and giving face,” says Dunlop. A “snobbery” about fiery food, the stereotype being that lots of spice is added “when you don’t have great ingredients and you’re just trying to xiàfàn [send the rice down]”, also made Cantonese gastronomy prestigious.

Spicy food, such as that from Sichuan, and the folk cooking of Hunan and Guizhou provinces, may be popular, but traditionally high-ranking cuisines are delicate. “Cuisines such as Cantonese and Jiangnan have an emphasis on incredibly fresh, seasonal ingredients and not using too many seasonings; the whole point of the cooking is to show off your great ingredients,” she says.

Chef and restaurateur Du Jianqing, of the Amazing Chinese Cuisine (Jing Xi Hui) restaurants in Shanghai – the Changning original of which has two Michelin stars, while the branch on the Bund has three Black Pearl diamonds – agrees, adding that Cantonese cuisine has always carried the potential for broad appeal.

“Whether among the elderly, children, or people from diverse backgrounds, this light, fresh and ingredient-focused style of dining is universally well accepted,” he says.

In 2024, he opened Selection by Du, with executive chef Chen Shaoxiong at the helm, as a “modern Chinese family banquet” and a “dialogue with the international market”. It involves a multi-course set menu accompanied by wine and tea, and what Du calls “East-meets-West post-meal experiences”, including petit fours and a souvenir. While still very much haute cuisine, the restaurant itself has a relatively relaxed atmosphere.

Du hails from Puning, in Guangdong’s Chaoshan region, and specialises in the cuisine of his home, known for its braised goose, beef hotpot and raw-marinated seafood. Some argue that Chiuchow is separate from Cantonese fare, while others see it as a subcategory of the cuisine. Either way, Du attributes Cantonese cuisine’s success to the replicability of its fundamental precepts.

“Its respect for ingredients, pursuit of original flavours and high standards for basic techniques – such as heat control, broths and knife skills – show exceptional stability,” he says. But while sophisticated cooking processes are the cuisine’s backbone, it is also versatile.

“Cantonese cuisine has a strong tradition but remains highly adaptable, allowing chefs to innovate while retaining its identity. I believe this combination of culinary depth, adaptability and international recognition has contributed to its strong presence in today’s fine-dining landscape,” says Chaoshan-born Fei, who also oversees, along with Yan Garden, two-Michelin-star restaurants in Shenzhen and Guangzhou, a newly starred spot in Singapore and a Bangkok outpost, all in partnership with Mandarin Oriental.

Singaporean group Imperial Treasure runs more than 20 – mainly Cantonese – restaurants around the world, including Michelin-star spots in Shanghai and Guangzhou. CEO Kenny Leung Tak-shun says that, while the fundamentals of Cantonese cooking remain the same – an “emphasis on fresh ingredients, balance, texture, timing and technique” – his chefs adjust the ingredients, seasoning and portion sizes according to the market.

“Availability, seasonality and quality of certain ingredients can vary significantly between Shanghai and the Greater Bay Area,” he says. “Guangzhou and the Pearl River Delta have a wider, more immediate supply of southern Chinese vegetables and produce. Naturally, this has an impact on what we put on the menu.

“This is an important part of authentic Cantonese cooking. Authenticity doesn’t mean using the same ingredients in every city. It means applying the same philosophy, sourcing the best ingredients and allowing them to speak for themselves.”

Cantonese cuisine’s adaptability is taken to bold heights by the trio of chefs behind one of the most in-demand restaurants in Shanghai. Fabula – just six seats in an attic above a wine bar – was opened in August 2025 by Zee Zheng Yunze and Ricky Deng Yongjun, both formerly of Taian Table in Shanghai, and Charles Tan, an alumnus of Hong Kong’s Amber.

Although primarily Western, the restaurant’s dishes incorporate the culinary heritage of all three chefs: Zheng is from Ningbo, in Zhejiang province; Deng from Shanghai; and Tan from Foshan, in Guangdong province. Cantonese air-dried lap cheong inspired the trio’s pigeon-blood sausage, bulked up with Ningbo-inspired rice cake, with hints of rose-fragranced baijiu and soy sauce. Elsewhere, they draw on the legacy of rice-less congee, famous in Guangdong’s Shunde district, by making a soup infused with matsutake mushrooms diced finely to resemble rice grains. Referencing the Cantonese technique of flash-frying fish with hot oil, they then pour the soup over raw botan ebi in front of guests.

Cantonese ingredients are used instead of Western ones in some dishes. “Instead of asparagus, for example, we use choi sum that’s grown in Guangzhou, known as ‘late-harvest choi sum’, that reaches over a metre tall,” says Zheng. “It’s not a very regular variant, and only available for a short season.”

Deng points out that the structure of the Cantonese kitchen, with its clearly defined stations – for making dim sum, roasting meats and wok-cooking – also makes it easily translatable into different contexts. “It’s more like the French system, where they have stations, so it’s easier for Cantonese chefs and restaurateurs to move to different cities and copy what they do back home,” he says.

For these young chefs, the lengths that Cantonese cuisine has travelled are not just measured in physical distance. In Tan’s case, cooking more than 1,000km from where he spent his childhood, Shanghai has an openness to the new while the Cantonese tend to be “more rigid about tradition”.

Hong Kong has long had progressive gastronomes expanding the boundaries of Cantonese fare, and Chinese cuisine more generally, but Shanghai chefs see the southern city as the place where tradition is honoured.

“Shanghai gathers talent, ingredients and cultures from across the country and the world, offering chefs space to experiment,” says Du. “Hong Kong excels at preserving traditions, Shanghai excels at driving evolution; these two cities form the most significant facets of high-end Cantonese and Chiuchow cuisine today.”

Cantonese restaurants face increasing pressure across China, however. A growing number of new openings are serving regional cuisines such as Jiangnan or Sichuan, for example, with Michelin, Black Pearl and the 50 Best rankings firmly in their sights. Despite the challenges and competition, Cantonese chefs remain positive.

“As living standards improve, diners are paying more attention to the quality of ingredients, flavours and the overall dining experience. At the same time, both Cantonese and Chiuchow cuisine continue to evolve, finding new ways to express their traditions,” says Fei. “I believe this balance between tradition and innovation gives them strong potential for continued growth.”

item.title: [SCMP] Big dreams, growing pains in Indonesia: Prabowo’s turbulent 2 years in power
item.description:
When 35-year-old Bekasi resident Ika Kartika voted for Prabowo Subianto in Indonesia’s 2024 presidential election, she hoped the former general would restore a “Suharto-like” era of stability, when everyday essentials were affordable and life felt more predictable.

Growing up, she had often heard her parents reminisce about the “good old days” under the late strongman, whose rule had brought a sense of order to their lives.

Two years into his presidency, however, rising food prices have left Ika questioning whether Prabowo, who was once Suharto’s son-in-law, can deliver on that vision.
item.content:encoded:
When 35-year-old Bekasi resident Ika Kartika voted for Prabowo Subianto in Indonesia’s 2024 presidential election, she hoped the former general would restore a “Suharto-like” era of stability, when everyday essentials were affordable and life felt more predictable.

Growing up, she had often heard her parents reminisce about the “good old days” under the late strongman, whose rule had brought a sense of order to their lives.

Two years into his presidency, however, rising food prices have left Ika questioning whether Prabowo, who was once Suharto’s son-in-law, can deliver on that vision.

“I thought he would turn things around. Now I feel cheated and disappointed,” Ika said.

Her disillusionment reflects a broader loss of confidence in the 75-year-old former special forces commander – a sharp reversal from the position of strength he enjoyed after finally winning the presidency on his third attempt.

Taking office with virtually no parliamentary opposition after bringing former rival parties into a sprawling governing coalition, Prabowo rode a post-inauguration honeymoon that saw his public approval rating hit 79 per cent at the start of his term as he began implementing his blueprint to transform Southeast Asia’s largest economy and elevate its global standing.

At home, he staked his legacy on eradicating child malnutrition through his universal free nutritious meals programme – initially projected to cost 450 trillion rupiah (US$25 billion) a year at full scale – and reviving rural economies through Red and White Village Cooperatives, a state-backed network of retail and logistics hubs.

For investors, his pitch was that these and other state-led initiatives would create millions of jobs and propel annual GDP growth to 8 per cent, with sovereign wealth fund Danantara central to his plan to put state assets to work in strategic industries and accelerate development.

Abroad, he championed Global South diplomacy in the Brics bloc alongside a pledge to remain a stabilising anchor in Southeast Asia.

Yet as Prabowo marked his first 24 months in the top job on Tuesday, those lofty ambitions have collided with harsh realities on all three fronts.

An October survey by Saiful Mujani Research and Consulting (SMRC) found that Prabowo’s approval rating had fallen to 44.5 per cent, below the 50 per cent mark for the first time. A separate survey by the Centre of Economic and Law Studies (Celios) found that 75 per cent of respondents felt stressed by government policies, with high prices for basic necessities and a lack of job opportunities among their chief concerns.

Simultaneously, a looming global index downgrade has triggered a bruising stock market rout, while raging forest fires have blanketed the region in toxic smog, choking neighbours Malaysia and Singapore.

In the face of those challenges, analysts say Prabowo has oscillated between reactive damage control and stubborn resolve.

Rather than fundamentally rethink his agenda, he has made adjustments, such as slashing the budget for the free meals programme but refusing to abandon it, and repeatedly reshuffling his cabinet. His government has also sent confusing signals abroad, approving foreign firefighting help to battle the haze before subsequently putting the offers on hold.

While ruling party allies defend his adjustments as “dynamic moves” to protect fiscal stability, observers argue they merely paper over the deeper structural flaws of his administration.

The question now is whether Prabowo can genuinely change course or whether the setbacks of his second year will define the rest of his term.

Prabowo himself remains publicly defiant. Brushing off economic pessimism at a nickel-processing project launch on October 8, he pointed to robust state-backed investments as proof that his administration was succeeding.

“Every month, they predict that we will collapse. But today, I have come here and I see a bright future for Indonesia,” he declared.

Fraying mandate

At the heart of the public mood shift is the troubled roll-out of the signature welfare schemes that once anchored Prabowo’s popularity. The SMRC survey showed that 61 per cent of citizens familiar with the free meals initiative were unhappy with its execution, while 71 per cent doubted the village cooperatives plan would succeed.

Saidiman Ahmad, a researcher and programme manager at SMRC, said the poll exposed a broad defection of supporters across all demographic groups, pinpointing mismanagement of the president’s flagship initiatives as the main cause of public censure.

Both the free meals initiative and village cooperatives plan “were significant factors”, Saidiman said.

Those missteps are glaring to voters like Lugas Limojoyo, 31, a resident of Purwokerto in Central Java who backed Prabowo in 2024 among the three presidential tickets.

Lugas, a former hotel chef, described the free meals programme and the cooperatives as Prabowo’s “main red flags”.

Pointing to recurring mass food-poisoning cases, he noted a lack of basic food safety protocols – an observation echoed by Indonesia’s food and drug agency, which has repeatedly cited poor sanitation and untrained staff as the primary causes behind thousands of students falling ill.

Lugas saw a similar lack of coordination in the village cooperatives initiative, noting that many state-funded warehouses “have already been built but aren’t operational, sitting there like empty husks”. Reuters has also reported concerns from analysts about the scheme’s top-down approach, the commercial viability of some locations and whether the cooperatives can respond to local needs.

Still, the programmes retain pockets of support. Anissa Fadhilah, a 29-year-old greengrocer in Surabaya, said she remained satisfied with Prabowo’s performance and would vote for him again in 2029 after her daughter received school meals and her business landed supply commissions from the scheme.

“I think [the free meals initiative] has the desired effect of lifting ordinary people economically, so I’m for it,” Anissa said.

Officials also defended the administration’s two-year track record.

Jasmine Herawan, a spokeswoman for Indonesia’s Government Communications Agency, said the administration had expanded the social safety net, with its free meals programme reaching 57 million recipients, while nearly 1.5 million people had been lifted out of extreme poverty within a year.

She also cited gains in food security, saying Indonesia produced 34.71 million tonnes of rice in 2025 without importing any that year.

On the extractive sector, Jasmine said: “We’ve also affirmed our mineral sovereignty by setting up a single-door export system for our key commodities.” The system is intended to give the government greater oversight of mineral exports and make it harder for companies to understate the value of what they sell overseas, potentially depriving the state of tax revenue.

Market reckoning

Costly spending commitments, however, have raised broader concerns about fiscal sustainability. Earlier this year, the government cut 67 trillion rupiah from the free meals programme before imposing further spending curbs across ministries in the final quarter to help keep the budget deficit within its legal ceiling of 3 per cent of GDP.

But fiscal tightening did little to reassure investors. On October 16, index provider MSCI warned that Indonesia could be downgraded from “emerging” to “stand-alone” market status over concerns about opaque corporate ownership and trading manipulation, triggering a bruising sell-off in Indonesian assets. The Jakarta Composite Index plunged 11.6 per cent and the rupiah fell to 18,050 per US dollar.

Despite emergency regulatory fines against market manipulators and bourse officials pledging swift governance reforms during a meeting with MSCI on Monday, the benchmark index hit a six-year low this week, as investors continued to digest the warning and the risk of billions of dollars in passive capital outflows.

Siwage Dharma Negara, co-coordinator of the Indonesia Studies programme at Singapore’s ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute, said regional investors continued to view Prabowo’s economic policy as unpredictable.

“He will not give up his populist programmes, like the free meals and rural cooperatives, but it is not clear what the economic benefit for the country will be,” Siwage said.

Siwage noted that the recent fiscal correction was too small to satisfy investors, many of whom viewed the free meals as a waste of state resources that should be redirected towards education, health or struggling regional governments.

“Prabowo fundamentally does not trust anyone else to advise him on economic direction,” Siwage said, warning that such moves were creating a poor investment climate. “If we want to restore market confidence, the most urgent fix is reducing this state intervention in the economy.”

Inside Prabowo’s ruling Gerindra party, lawmakers reject assertions that the administration’s economic agenda is faltering. Gerindra spokesman Sugiat Santoso dismissed Celios’ two-year study as “over the top” and “deliberately dramatised” to create mass panic.

Defending the village cooperatives as a path to financial independence for disadvantaged communities and the free meals as an ongoing investment in future generations, Sugiat added, “The president is definitely not here to please analysts, but to bring about real changes for the welfare of the people.”

Musical chairs

Unwilling to abandon his core populist pledges, Prabowo has instead turned to frequent personnel changes to tighten his grip on the bureaucracy – reshuffling his cabinet or installing new officials three times in the first two weeks of October alone, bringing his total number of cabinet shake-ups to eight in two years.

Arya Fernandes, head of politics and social change at the Centre for Strategic and International Studies Indonesia, said these shake-ups stemmed from the president’s underlying political vulnerability – specifically Gerindra’s lack of parliamentary dominance and the lingering influence of his predecessor, Joko Widodo.

This has forced Prabowo to consolidate power by accommodating a wide political spectrum, Arya noted. But the high cost of maintaining that stability – through an oversized cabinet and increased military budgets – has driven up fiscal pressure and forced the central government to slash local funding.

“In sum, Prabowo has secured elite support and lost mass support,” he said.

Yoes C. Kenawas, a researcher at Lembaga Survei Indonesia, said this dynamic reflected a leader whose authoritarian instincts make him insecure about elite loyalty.

“He remains deeply paranoid about elite betrayal and being backstabbed by coalition partners,” Yoes said. “Even with an 80 per cent parliamentary majority, he does not feel secure.”

Siwage said swapping out officials would not solve the administration’s deeper flaws: “We have seen many cabinet reshuffles so far, and he will likely continue shuffling officials, thinking a new person will fix the problem. But the real issue is that the entire system of governance is currently ineffective at implementing sound economic policy.”

Fanning flames

Nowhere has that administrative strain spilled beyond Indonesia’s borders more visibly than in the transboundary haze crisis.

Since August, severe forest and peatland fires across Sumatra and Kalimantan have sent thick smoke across the region, forcing school closures in Malaysia, prompting diplomatic protests and leading Singapore’s prime minister to warn of action against errant companies.

Siwage linked the resurgence of the fires directly to Prabowo’s domestic fiscal squeeze, which he said left local governments “without enough operational funds to fight the fires”.

For months, Jakarta resisted regional offers of firefighting help, while public remarks by officials only inflamed tensions – most notably when the newly appointed communications agency head suggested neighbours should remember Indonesia’s forests “send oxygen” when there is no haze.

Rifki Dermawan, an international relations lecturer at Universitas Andalas in West Sumatra, says the episode highlights a stark contrast: while Prabowo frequently travels globally, “Asean does not seem to be a priority”.

Pointing to the president’s failure to apologise or engage with regional counterparts over the pollution, Rifki said it suggested the bloc “might not be among Prabowo’s interests”. He attributed Jakarta’s reluctance to accept outside help to Prabowo’s suspicion of foreign involvement and repeated rhetoric blaming “foreign agents”.

A diplomatic thaw seemingly arrived on October 15 when Foreign Minister Arrmanatha Nasir announced Prabowo had approved regional firefighting help. But the administration later abruptly backtracked when security chief Dudung Abdurachman put the offers on hold, declaring Indonesia was “still capable” of managing the blazes.

Prabowo then railed against “countries that like to insult” his nation over the wildfires, amid growing public anger and calls for Indonesia to be treated as an “outcast” in the region.

“Indonesia is a polite and patient nation. Our country is often insulted, but believe me, our nation does not want to be insulted all the time,” Prabowo said on Wednesday.

⁠⁠Prabowo also told his cabinet ‌on Wednesday that MSCI was trying ⁠to “scare us”, adding ‌that Indonesia was “not afraid” ‌and would not ⁠buckle, Reuters reported.

Despite plunging approval ratings, a market sell-off and diplomatic fires, Yoes warned Prabowo might not feel compelled to change course because the pain of his second-year slump had not hit his immediate political centre.

“The crisis is fragmented,” Yoes said. “The toxic haze chokes Sumatra and Kalimantan, but it does not blanket Jakarta or Java.”

Because the distress was clustered outside the capital, it looked manageable on paper, he added, “but underneath the surface, this is a crisis in the making”.

Defiance or adaptation

Analysts say moving beyond short-term diplomatic firefighting to rebuild his popular mandate and calm financial markets over the remaining three years of his term could depend on Prabowo’s willingness to look outside his inner circle.

So far, however, the president has framed mounting resistance not as a symptom of policy missteps but as a manufactured campaign by entrenched elites bankrolling paid protesters and online influencers – known locally as “buzzers”.

“We have no doubts. Even if they have hundreds of trillions of rupiah, they pay buzzers, they pay for algorithms, they attack us on social media, and they finance demonstrations, we are not afraid. We stand with the people, we are ready to die for the people,” Prabowo said during a fiery speech on October 6.

That defiant posture worries observers who believe Prabowo must adapt his approach to meet the challenges he is facing.

SMRC’s Saidiman argued that reversing the polling slide would require structural reform – starting with shrinking the cabinet, pulling back from the ongoing militarisation of the civilian sphere and conducting a “radical review of the administration’s costly yet ineffective populist programmes”.

“The president needs to step up and enact fundamental changes to how he governs the nation,” Saidiman said, adding Prabowo “should let opposition forces fulfil their function as a democracy should”.

Siwage warned that without an effective parliamentary opposition to check the president’s instincts, financial market tremors could eventually spiral into a wider political reckoning.

“Prabowo currently controls most of the government coalition and the parliament. With essentially no opposition, why would he change course when nobody dares to oppose his policies?” he said.

Outside Jakarta’s corridors of power, voters who helped put Prabowo in the presidential palace say he still has a window to turn things around – if he starts listening to ordinary Indonesians.

In Central Java, Lugas urged the president to break out of his palace echo chamber.

“My suggestion for Prabowo is to cross-check the reports he gets from those closest to him, because obviously he is only being fed information on the good things,” he said.

And in Bekasi, despite feeling let down by rising living costs, Ika said she was not ready to give up on Prabowo’s presidency just yet.

“Maybe these are growing pains for us,” she said. “I’m still optimistic about Prabowo’s leadership and I pray he won’t prove me wrong.”

item.title: [SCMP] JW Marriott Hotel Hong Kong redefines luxury dining with zero-waste culinary innovation
item.description:
For Tony Wong Chi-chuen, the executive chef of JW Marriott Hotel Hong Kong, waste is never the conclusion of an ingredient’s story. Lemon ends can be used to perfume seafood, shrimp shells to deepen the nuance of a broth and fishbones to build a base for pasta dough. In Wong’s kitchen, food waste is simply ingredients waiting for a second life.

“Discarding something is easy,” says Wong. “[Reusing] is not about saving cost; saving is about reinvesting in more quality ingredients.”

In person, he doesn’t mince his words. As the conversation turns to his craft, Wong – who has 38 years of experience in the industry – becomes animated, revealing a passion honed over decades, rooted in a lesson learned long before he entered a professional kitchen.
item.content:encoded:
For Tony Wong Chi-chuen, the executive chef of JW Marriott Hotel Hong Kong, waste is never the conclusion of an ingredient’s story. Lemon ends can be used to perfume seafood, shrimp shells to deepen the nuance of a broth and fishbones to build a base for pasta dough. In Wong’s kitchen, food waste is simply ingredients waiting for a second life.

“Discarding something is easy,” says Wong. “[Reusing] is not about saving cost; saving is about reinvesting in more quality ingredients.”

In person, he doesn’t mince his words. As the conversation turns to his craft, Wong – who has 38 years of experience in the industry – becomes animated, revealing a passion honed over decades, rooted in a lesson learned long before he entered a professional kitchen.

His parents used to run a dai pai dong-style stall behind the Yau Ma Tei Police Station, peddling steaming bowls of fish-ball noodles, before it closed more than 40 years ago. From the age of 12, Wong would help out after school. He watched his parents work hard, stretch ingredients and make full use of what they had.

He recalls that “they didn’t throw anything away”: fishbones were simmered into broth for the noodles – an ingrained reflex that later inspired his fishbone fettuccine at JW Marriott Hotel Hong Kong, showing how every ingredient could be made to work harder. Wong came to understand that saving on food waste only mattered if it was turned into something better eventually.

“When I was 18, I realised being thrifty is not enough,” he says. “You have to use what you save and make it into something good for customers.” His philosophy – waste not, but elevate – became the bedrock of his kitchen. It is an exercise not in austerity, but in wringing maximum quality and flavour out of scraps.

Wong joined JW Marriott Hotel Hong Kong in 1990, a year after its opening. He started as a senior cook at the former Marriott Cafe, now JW Cafe, and steadily moved up the ranks: sous chef in 2003, executive sous chef in 2009 and, finally, executive chef in 2018.

As a young cook, he noticed how quickly bins filled up. Celery ends, carrot peels, onion trimmings and other offcuts were tossed aside because only the neatest parts were used. When he became sous chef, he began making changes: a bucket near a chopping board was added to hold bones, end cuts and trimmings to be reused.

Now, the system has become part of kitchen culture. Watermelon rind is blended into a light breakfast drink, valued in traditional Chinese medicine for its refreshing sweetness and cooling effects; leftover pieces from Peking ducks are shredded into a braised rice-vermicelli dish.

What it has done for food-waste numbers is significant – the hotel repurposes around 8.2 tonnes of watermelon rind a year, along with 900kg of lemon peel, more than 3.6 tonnes of fishbones and 3.65 tonnes of shrimp heads and shells, says Wong. At its core, however, his philosophy remains simple: an ingredient should have as many “lives” as possible before it leaves the kitchen.

“I see an ingredient and think, ‘How can it be used again?’”

Tony Wong

“I see an ingredient and think, ‘How can it be used again?’”

Across JW Marriott Hotel Hong Kong’s eight dining venues and multiple event spaces, Wong’s strategy goes beyond creating isolated “green” dishes – it is about building a circular kitchen system. His approach aligns with Marriott’s Serve 360 sustainability and social-impact platform, which is guided by the belief of “doing good in every direction”.

Furthermore, the culinary initiatives sit within the property’s broader push towards responsible luxury – a commitment that has won prestigious recognition, recently from the US Green Building Council for sustainable building operations and maintenance, and the International WELL Building Institute for health and wellness, ensuring that guest well-being and environmental stewardship are both fully considered.

In a five-star hotel, sustainability has to meet the expectations of luxury dining. Wong does not see a contradiction. He believes that responsible cooking should make food better, not lesser, and the clearest expression of this thinking is Fish Bar’s lobster fishbone fettuccine, one of the restaurant’s signature dishes. Instead of treating grouper bones as waste, Wong’s team dries and pulverises them into a fine powder, then blends the meal with gluten-free flour to make pasta. No mere sustainability gimmick, the bones add calcium and deepen the pasta’s umami, turning scrap into part of the dish’s flavour structure.

If anything, Wong says, zero-waste practices allow him to be more generous. Financial savings from careful portioning and cross-kitchen reuse are channelled back into premium buffet offerings, such as abalone, fish maw, sea cucumber, lobster and crab.

High-quality offcuts receive similar care: Australian Wagyu trimmings are crafted into burger patties, while at the hotel’s Michelin-star Man Ho Chinese Restaurant, prime cuts of Iberico pork are reserved for char siu and flavourful remnants are minced for xiaolongbao fillings at The Lounge.

For banquets and functions, Wong’s team makes enough food for no more than 10 per cent above the expected number of guests. At the buffet, dishes are prepared in smaller, more frequently replenished batches, ensuring that food does not sit for long periods. It is a more labour-intensive practice, but one that benefits the environment and creates a better experience for diners. “Other places refill food maybe twice; we do it 20 times,” says Wong.

Luxury diners used to fixate on origin – lobsters from France, tomatoes from Italy, sea urchin from Japan – but these priorities have shifted. “I think guests mainly care about the taste, quality and freshness of the ingredients – these are the three things they focus on now and they care less about where they come from,” says Wong.

For him, this change has widened the meaning of luxury. Premium dining is no longer defined only by provenance or price, but by how thoughtfully an ingredient is sourced, handled and cooked. If a dish tastes good and aligns with sustainable values, guests will often see it as something better.

JW Marriott Hotel Hong Kong prioritises local sourcing where possible, which helps reduce transport time, spoilage and carbon emissions. Suppliers are screened for certifications – including from organisations such as the Marine Stewardship Council (MSC) and Aquaculture Stewardship Council (ASC) – and traceability. Purchasing decisions made by the procurement team are guided in part by monthly WWF recommendations of vetted seafood suppliers and sources, says Wong. Endangered species, such as bluefin tuna and shark, are off the menu, replaced by alternatives like yellowtail and vegetarian shark’s fin – a plant-based ingredient that replicates the texture of the original.

At Fish Bar, renovated in 2024, sustainability is built into the space as well as the dining programme. An open design allows for natural ventilation, reducing reliance on air conditioning. Uniforms were designed in partnership with the Caritas Bianchi College of Careers and incorporate coffee-ground materials. Bottled water has been replaced with a filtered system.

Meanwhile, JW Garden grows herbs such as rosemary, basil and perilla, which are used in drinks, dishes, amenities and even canned beverages that extend the farm-to-table idea into a “farm-to-home” experience. Edible surplus, such as croissants and muffins, is donated to organisations serving people in need, while food waste that cannot be reused is sent to recycling partners for renewable energy or composting. JW Marriott Hotel Hong Kong also works with The Nature Conservancy, turning discarded oyster shells into reef substrate for local marine restoration.

From Wong’s point of view, these hotel-wide initiatives connect back to the same principle: resources should circulate, not dissipate. His message for the next generation is clear: cooking well is no longer enough, because a chef must also think about impact.

His 180-strong team, many of whom have worked with him for decades, now closely follow his doctrine.

It has created a virtuous cycle: the kitchen grows increasingly efficient as reuse practices are streamlined; diners enjoy fresher, higher-quality food; staff develop discipline and pride – all while protecting the environment. Wong shares of his team that “they feel this is a good habit; they feel like they can be good people”.

Some might label the rethinking of food waste as accumulating good karma, but in hospitality terms, it’s simply good business.

item.title: [SCMP] Hong Kong’s 700-year-old oyster industry goes hi-tech with ‘super’ specimen
item.description:
Out on Deep Bay, between Hong Kong and Shenzhen, the first thing you notice is what doesn’t seem to belong there.

Many of the oyster-farming rafts here are old. Weathered wood, greyed by salt and sun – the kind that has floated in these waters for generations. A few look abandoned, but this is inevitably the appearance a 700-year-old industry takes on when it is running out of time.

And then, there are the newcomers – bobbing buoyantly in a bright, unmistakable shade of blue – made of fibreglass. Pacing back and forth on one in a pink shirt and dark trousers is Professor Thiyagarajan Vengatesen, a marine biologist from the University of Hong Kong (HKU) who is better known as Professor Rajan.
