The firm’s CEO, Gan Tian, pointed to the recent Middle East crisis as a major “stress test” that demonstrated the Chinese currency’s resilience, noting that the renminbi remained firm even as the US dollar surged and Asian peers like the Japanese yen fell sharply.

“On the path to yuan internationalisation, in this stress test in the first half, the People’s Bank of China has already sent a clear message to the smartest investors in the world,” Gan said.

“If de-dollarisation is a medium- to long-term trend, once you pull your money out of the US dollar, where exactly should you put it? The renminbi is the unparalleled choice.”

Driven by intensifying US-China rivalry and the strategic need to mobilise mainland capital safely abroad despite capital controls, Hong Kong is rapidly transforming its market infrastructure – building a larger offshore renminbi ecosystem, developing independent gold clearing and testing alternative payment channels.

Once primarily a bridge for Western capital entering the mainland, Hong Kong is now positioning itself to support China’s financial resilience, analysts say. The aim, they add, is to establish the city as a launch pad for financial products and payment channels that rely less on traditional Western networks.

Earlier this year, Financial Secretary Paul Chan Mo-po expressed confidence that Hong Kong, currently behind New York and London in the global ranking of international financial centres, would climb to at least second place within 10 to 15 years.

In a recent interview with the South China Morning Post, Chan explained the city’s efforts on yuan internationalisation and their relevance to Hong Kong’s status as an international financial centre.

Chan singled out Hong Kong’s unique role as a firewall for China’s financial security, with yuan-related products and services tested in the city.

“From China’s standpoint, to build a strong country, we need to have a strong currency. But this needs time,” Chan said.

“To strengthen the global utilisation and influence of renminbi, it is the user-case scenario, a substantive business-user case.”

‘Tremendous room for growth’

Chan said he expected global use of the yuan to rise amid geopolitical tensions.

He noted that China accounted for 14 to 15 per cent of global imports and exports combined, but only about 4 per cent of trade was invoiced in yuan last year. The ratio had grown a lot compared with a year earlier, he said.

Foreign investors have shown a strong appetite for trading in mainland stocks through cross-border schemes such as Northbound Stock Connect.

“There is tremendous room for future growth, particularly given the geopolitical context. Most countries are trying to use their own currency in terms of trading,” Chan said.

Hong Kong is the world’s biggest offshore renminbi market, with about 1.3 trillion yuan of deposits as at the end of July, according to the Financial Services and the Treasury Bureau.

A high-profile move to tap international capital took place in August when China’s Ministry of Finance sold 15 billion yuan worth of sovereign bonds in Hong Kong to a strong response from institutional investors.

The sale took place just days after the city launched a long-awaited tool designed to help global investors hedge against risks in the mainland bond market.

Ho Lok-sang, adjunct professor of economics at Lingnan University, said the renminbi remained very much underutilised and did not reflect China’s economic strength, leaving huge potential for wider use.

“What we are after in the long run is that we want to build a more inclusive kind of system,” Ho said.

“At present, the current system, which is very much predominated by the US dollar, is not really an inclusive system, and especially as it has been weaponised.”

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent advocated in early September for Washington to use its financial power as a foreign policy tool to advance the interests of American allies, including ‌in financial and political situations abroad.

Meanwhile, the US Treasury Department has warned under its “Operation Economic Outcast” that entities facilitating money laundering or sanctions evasion on behalf of Iran risk being cut off from the US financial system, citing several Hong Kong-based companies that did business with Iran.

“China has been thinking strategically against the possibility that the US might impose different kinds of sanctions, and China is really extremely alert … strategically very, very smart,” Ho said.

Testing ground

Hard data shows the shift away from US dollar-centric systems is well under way in Hong Kong’s capital markets.

Beijing is using Hong Kong to test a China-led multilateral central bank digital currency platform, mBridge, as a potential alternative to the traditional US dollar-dominated payments system. The effort has gained momentum in recent years amid heightened tensions between the world’s two largest economies and growing concerns over the reliability of the US dollar as it becomes politicised.

The project faced a setback late last month after a key participant – the Saudi Central Bank – confirmed its departure after completing what it described as “a limited proof-of-concept” trial in May last year.

Secretary for Financial Services and the Treasury Christopher Hui Ching-yu told the SCMP in an interview earlier this month that the Saudi departure would “not really” affect the wider experiment.

“Fundamentally, what we try to do is, through Hong Kong, at the same time through these measures, to engage different players across the industry in such a way that they can work on some live cases or new cases to test out this technology,” Hui said.

“So technology as it is, people still see the benefit. At the same time, what Hong Kong should do is continue contributing our expertise and also our relevance here.”

Beyond payments infrastructure, Hong Kong is also seeking to make the yuan more attractive for corporate financing.

Multinational firms need to borrow large sums of cash to run their global operations. Historically, many borrowed yen because Japan had the lowest interest rates.

But recently, the script has flipped. Japan’s 10-year sovereign bond yield rose above 3 per cent in early September, while China’s dropped below 1.7 per cent, Gan of ChinaAMC (HK) said.

Global companies were now flocking to Hong Kong to borrow yuan by issuing dim sum bonds – offshore renminbi-denominated bonds – because they offered cheaper funding, Gan said.

He noted that this rush for cheap borrowing had caused the dim sum bond market to explode to 1 trillion yuan, making it significantly larger than Hong Kong’s traditional stock IPO market.

When massive Chinese companies, such as appliance maker Midea, made profits overseas, they faced a huge problem: exchange rates were swinging wildly, Gan said.

Midea suffered a foreign exchange loss of almost 6 billion yuan in six months because the value of the currencies it was holding dropped. Normally, companies buy financial “insurance” with hedging to protect against these US dollar swings, but that insurance can cost 2.5 per cent of the hedged amount every year.

To reduce losses from volatile exchange rates, Chinese companies were simply refusing to convert their cash. Instead, they were parking their overseas profits directly into offshore yuan funds in Hong Kong, Gan said.

Liquidity boost

Chan, the finance chief, has pledged a multipronged strategy to boost yuan liquidity through an array of products. In addition to Chinese treasury bonds, he has pointed to opportunities in stock trading.

He said authorities would consider expanding the number of listed companies whose shares investors could trade using offshore yuan. At present, there are 23 such companies with renminbi business counters.

Chan said another strategy was to allow China-based investors to use renminbi to trade in Hong Kong-listed shares through the Southbound Stock Connect scheme.

“If we can achieve that, the liquidity will be quickly increased,” he said. “In summary, we want to have more product offerings.”

For Hong Kong’s manufacturers and traders, the stakes extend beyond financial markets.

Anthony Lam Sai-ho, chairman of the Federation of Hong Kong Industries, said that pricing commodities in renminbi would link finance more directly with physical supply chains, giving manufacturers a “natural hedge” against exchange rate volatility.

“If we can trade commodities in renminbi … it provides manufacturers and stakeholders with an additional method to hedge and predict procurement costs, reducing currency fluctuation,” Lam said.

He added that while markets were accustomed to US dollar pricing, importing raw materials such as rice or base metals directly in local currencies or renminbi would reduce the risk of being caught between shifting exchange rates.

“It is less about avoiding the US dollar out of fear, and more about giving the market an additional option to balance trade,” Lam added.

Commodity trading had so far started with gold but could extend to other metals, energy, grains, soft commodities and even livestock, Lam said.

Alternative clearing networks, meanwhile, are expanding their reach. China’s Cross-border Interbank Payment System (CIPS) processed 180 trillion yuan in cross-border payments in 2025, up 373.6 times the 2015 level, according to its website.

CIPS said it provided secure, efficient, convenient and low-cost cross-border renminbi payment and settlement services for global users, offering an additional channel beyond the US-dominated financial system.

That existing US dollar-based system relies heavily on Swift, the Belgium-based Society for Worldwide Interbank Financial Telecommunication, which connects more than 12,500 institutions across more than 220 countries and territories and enables global trade.

Dollar payments are also settled through the Clearing House Interbank Payments System (Chips), a private-sector, high-value clearing and settlement system that helps financial institutions move domestic and cross-border wire payments, according to its website.

Under Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu’s policy address in September, the government has established the Hong Kong Precious Metals Central Clearing Company and will implement targeted measures to boost the trading and settlement of gold futures contracts using the offshore renminbi.

Kenny Shui Chi-wai, vice-president of think tank Our Hong Kong Foundation, said market participants would have another option if access to dollar-based channels were restricted.

“A gold clearing system allows gold transactions via a local central ledger without relying on the Swift messaging network or the Chips payment system, thereby providing an alternative store of value,” Shui said.

“Unlike fiat currencies, gold is a physical commodity that inherently holds value, making it a trusted safe asset not directly tied to any jurisdiction.”

Gan of ChinaAMC (HK) said that having huge physical gold reserves in Hong Kong provided foreigners using offshore renminbi in the city with a “Plan B” if they wanted to convert or transfer those funds.

“They do not need to convert their assets into US dollars, British pounds or Japanese yen to move them globally; they can directly exchange them for physical gold in Hong Kong and have it delivered anywhere in the world,” he said.

“Therefore, gold, acting as a ‘Plan B’ and the most important collateral asset of the future, will support the development of the offshore renminbi in Hong Kong.”

The peg question

The Hong Kong Securities and Futures Professionals Association warned that an overnight shift away from the US dollar was unrealistic.

“If de-dollarisation is overemphasised, international investors might interpret it as a signal of declining openness,” said the association’s chairman, Mofiz Chan.

Chan said Hong Kong had to strike a delicate balance between securing multiple sources of capital and maintaining its international free-market reputation with compliance, transparency and neutral standing.

To make this “financial armour” truly functional, the association called for specific technological and regulatory upgrades.

Gregory Yu, head of markets at Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing, told the SCMP that the exchange was focused on building a more comprehensive offshore renminbi ecosystem spanning equities, fixed income, currencies and commodities, and it was actively exploring opportunities to expand the range of yuan-denominated products.

“Initiatives including the continued expansion of the LME’s warehouse network in Hong Kong strengthen the market infrastructure that supports trading, storage and delivery activities across the region,” Yu said, referring to the London Metal Exchange.

Yu added that the bourse continued to explore opportunities to enhance market efficiency through innovation, including in digital assets and tokenisation.

“Together with ongoing market infrastructure enhancements, these efforts strengthen Hong Kong’s role as the world’s leading offshore renminbi hub and reinforce its position as an international financial centre connecting China and the world,” Yu said.

But any push to reduce reliance on the US dollar runs up against a basic constraint: the Hong Kong dollar remains pegged to it.

Ho Lok-sang argued that linking exclusively to the US dollar exposed Hong Kong to extreme economic swings, recalling the 1985 “super dollar” phase, when the city lost its export competitiveness.

“It’s much, much, much better if we can peg a basket of currencies … and now devise a way to seamlessly adopt the system without any shock at all,” Ho said.

“We can continue with the linked exchange rate system, but we just link with the basket,” he added, referring to a GDP-weighted basket that would include the renminbi, euro, yen, British pound and the US, Australian and Canadian dollars.

Chan, the finance chief, along with city leader John Lee Ka-chiu have said repeatedly the government has no intention of changing the 43-year-old peg, which has been underpinning the city’s economy.

At the end of the day, the key buzzwords are hedging and strategic planning, analysts say.

And the official regulatory response has been to rapidly deepen the multi-asset ecosystem and expand mutual market access to facilitate this capital transition.

“For Hong Kong, this means strengthening its role as a resilient international financial centre while supporting the financing of Chinese technology companies and renminbi internationalisation,” Shui of the think tank said.

item.title: [SCMP] Five takeaways from US midterms as Democrats sweep Congress and Trump faces Iran reckoning
item.description:
A Democratic victory that reached from Texas to Kansas changed the terms of Donald Trump’s final two years in office.

When the new US Congress convenes in January, Democrats will control both chambers. They can block his legislation, challenge spending on the war in Iran and scrutinise the deals he strikes with Beijing.

The day after his party lost control of Congress, Trump invited reporters to the construction site of his new White House ballroom to watch workers raise the final steel beam.
item.content:encoded:
A Democratic victory that reached from Texas to Kansas changed the terms of Donald Trump’s final two years in office.

When the new US Congress convenes in January, Democrats will control both chambers. They can block his legislation, challenge spending on the war in Iran and scrutinise the deals he strikes with Beijing.

The day after his party lost control of Congress, Trump invited reporters to the construction site of his new White House ballroom to watch workers raise the final steel beam.

Asked about the prospect of impeachment, he dismissed the idea, then turned back to the reason he had brought them there. “Watch the beam go up,” he said.

The visit also gave Trump a chance to respond to his vice-president, J.D. Vance, who had blamed the Iran war for the defeat.

Many voters who backed Trump in 2024 had turned out again on Tuesday and voted for Democrats, Vance said.

Trump put the emphasis on higher fuel prices and stood by his decision to go to war. “If I had it to do again, I’d have to do it again,” he said.

Here are five takeaways from the US midterms.

1. The Democratic wave reached deep into Trump country

In Texas, James Talarico defeated Republican Ken Paxton to become the first Democrat to win a US Senate race in the state since 1988. In South Carolina, doctor Annie Andrews defeated Republican Senator Darline Graham. Trump had carried both states by double digits just two years earlier and had backed both losing candidates.

Kansas delivered the longest break with the past. Adam Hamilton defeated Republican Senator Roger Marshall, ending a Senate winning streak that dated to 1932. In Ohio, Democrat Sherrod Brown won the seat Vance had vacated to become vice-president.

The final size of the majority was still taking shape on Wednesday.

At noon Eastern time, the Associated Press had yet to call the Senate races in Alaska and Mississippi. Democrats had already secured control without either seat.

2. Vance blamed the war. Trump blamed the price of fuel

Republicans had spent much of the campaign watching whether the people who backed Trump in 2024 would turn out again. Vance said the party had drawn too much comfort from seeing those voters show up. Many came back, he said, and cast their ballots for Democrats.

“The reason we lost is the war,” Vance wrote on X. He cited an unnamed pollster who had asked former Trump voters what it would take to win them back.

Ending the conflict topped the list, Vance said, followed by tackling the cost of living. An NBC News exit poll found that 62 per cent of voters thought the US had made the wrong decision in taking military action against Iran.

Speaking from the ballroom site, Trump offered a narrower explanation. He said the war had hurt Republicans by driving up petrol prices, but defended his decision to take military action.

He also maintained that Republicans would have won had his name been on the ballot. “We weren’t able to transfer the love to candidates,” he said of the crowds at his rallies.

3. Schumer put household costs first and pointed to Congress’s leverage over Iran

Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer described his party’s first assignment in terms of choices families faced at home: buying petrol to get to work or groceries to feed their children, paying for healthcare or keeping the heat on.

Lowering those costs, he said, was the first thing Democrats had to do to earn the trust of voters who had given them another chance.

On Iran, Schumer was emphatic about the goal and less specific about the means. “This war must end. It must end,” he said.

Asked whether Democrats would use defence funding as leverage, he pointed to Congress’s “power of the purse” and said some Republicans already supported ending the conflict. He stopped short of proposing a funding cut.

Schumer also pledged to tackle government corruption. His warning on investigations came with a condition: if Trump defied the law or the will of the American people, Democrats would investigate and take him to court. “The days of Trump’s supplicant Senate are over,” he said.

4. House Republicans need a new leader

As recently as October, House Speaker Mike Johnson expected to keep leading Republicans even if Democrats took the chamber. “I intend to stay and lead,” he told CBS News.

On Wednesday, the Louisiana Republican, who won re-election to his own seat, told staff he would not seek the minority leader’s job.

House Majority Leader Steve Scalise of Louisiana and Judiciary Committee chairman Jim Jordan of Ohio looked like the strongest candidates to replace him. The two had sought the speakership in 2023, when neither could assemble enough support and Johnson emerged as the compromise choice.

This time, only Republican members will vote, in a leadership election scheduled for November 10.

Asked at the White House whether he would take sides, Trump offered a short answer: “We’ll stay out of it.”

5. Trump can still negotiate with Xi, but he may have less to offer

Beijing called the election a US “domestic affair”, and Chinese foreign ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning said China wanted to build on the understandings Trump and President Xi Jinping had reached. Trump will still be able to negotiate directly with Xi, but Democratic control of Congress could narrow what he can offer Beijing in return for concessions.

One example is a waiver from US technology export restrictions. Feng Chucheng, founder of Beijing-based consultancy Hutong Research, told the South China Morning Post that a Republican Congress might have granted such a waiver, giving Trump something to offer Xi at the negotiating table. Democrats would be less inclined to grant one, Feng said.

Technology is also an area where lawmakers could press Beijing harder. Fudan University professor Zhao Minghao expects a Democratic Congress to take a tougher stance on artificial intelligence, export controls and Taiwan, even as Washington’s broader strategy towards China holds steady.

California congressman Ted Lieu said on Wednesday that House Democrats would use their new majority to hold public hearings on the AI industry and advance legislation to regulate it.

Lieu, a co-chair of the House Democratic Commission on AI and the Innovation Economy, accused the Trump administration and House Republicans of making a “conscious decision to let the AI industry run wild”.

He called that a mistake both as policy and as politics, citing growing public opposition to the rapid expansion of data centres.

item.title: [SCMP] Armour vs altitude: India’s light tank dilemma along China border
item.description:
India’s new high-altitude combat tank was designed to go where its heavier armoured fighting vehicles cannot: the thin mountain air, narrow roads and small bridges along its disputed border with China.

In its base configuration, the Zorawar weighs some 25 tonnes – light enough to be flown all the way to the Line of Actual Control – but a push to make it strong enough to withstand high-calibre autocannon fire could add an extra seven tonnes to that loadout.

Reports of renewed stand-offs between Indian and Chinese troops at the border, including one carried by The Hindu newspaper on October 23, have injected fresh urgency into the debate surrounding how much the tank should weigh.
item.content:encoded:
India’s new high-altitude combat tank was designed to go where its heavier armoured fighting vehicles cannot: the thin mountain air, narrow roads and small bridges along its disputed border with China.

In its base configuration, the Zorawar weighs some 25 tonnes – light enough to be flown all the way to the Line of Actual Control – but a push to make it strong enough to withstand high-calibre autocannon fire could add an extra seven tonnes to that loadout.

Reports of renewed stand-offs between Indian and Chinese troops at the border, including one carried by The Hindu newspaper on October 23, have injected fresh urgency into the debate surrounding how much the tank should weigh.

First phase of developmental field firing trails of Indian Light Tank successfully conducted. The field trials have successfully met the intended objectives in desert terrain. During trials the tank demonstrated required accuracy on the intended targets. @DefenceMinIndia https://t.co/cm9qr4uHsJ

— DRDO (@DRDO_India) September 13, 2024

During previous confrontations, India airlifted its older, Russian-origin T-72s and T-90s, which weigh between 45 and 50 tonnes each, to the border territory of Ladakh, where they have faced off against China’s lighter Type 15, weighing 33–36 tonnes.

But question marks hang over the performance of these heavier main battle tanks in the sub-zero conditions and low-oxygen environment of the high Himalayas, as the Observer Research Foundation, an Indian think tank, noted in a 2021 report.

China’s Type 15, by contrast, is easier to run and maintain at altitude and has been in service since the end of 2018.

The Zorawar was developed by India’s state-run Defence Research and Development Organisation and the private engineering group Larsen & Toubro over a two-year period, from its formal approval in March 2022 to the first public unveiling of a prototype in 2024.

It comes equipped with a 105mm rifled gun in a Belgian-designed Cockerill turret – the rotating upper section of the tank – that is hardened against small arms fire and artillery shrapnel, but not the armour-piercing shells designed to punch through metal that are fired by Chinese autocannons.

India’s army is reportedly pushing for the tank’s armour to be upgraded to Nato’s highest standards of ballistic protection, known as STANAG Level 6, able to withstand 25mm and 30mm armour-piercing rounds.

Doing so would not only add weight, but also force redesigns and prolong the tank’s development cycle. As a result, army chief General Upendra Dwivedi told Indian media earlier this year that he expected the Zorawar to enter service in 2028–29, overshooting the original 2027 target.

‘The urgency is real’

Ashok Bhim Shivane, a retired lieutenant general who previously led the Indian Army’s mechanised forces and commanded a strike corps – one of its major offensive formations – delivered a blunt assessment of why such a delay was a problem.

“The urgency is real,” he told This Week in Asia. “A light tank for areas where the medium-category T-90/T-72 cannot reach or operate is a critical requirement as of the day before yesterday.”

Heavier armour needs a stronger engine. At altitudes above 4,500 metres (15,000 feet), where the Zorawar would have to operate, thinner air could result in a 20 per cent drop in engine power, Shivane said – unless the tank’s current 764-horsepower engine was upgraded to a 1,000-horsepower one.

“There is also a design question. The Belgian turret cannot take the heavier armour,” said Shivane, who helped build the case for a home-grown light tank and has been closely involved with its development.

The additional armour could add up to seven tonnes to the tank’s weight, he said, arguing that to rectify some of these issues, India should further localise its design, which he described as currently between 40–45 per cent indigenous by value.

India plans to field an initial 59 Zorawars and 354 in total. Shivane said he wanted to see the first batch inducted by 2028 “with a documented baseline, instrumented trials and funded upgrade lots”, meaning a thoroughly tested, finalised design with funding already secured for upgrades.

He proposed a “spiral approach” to production that gradually added capability in stages, with stopgap measures to plug any vulnerabilities that should arise.

“A tank that does not exist cannot be trained on. A user trial under real conditions teaches what no laboratory can,” he said.

Sanjay Iyer, a retired Indian Army brigadier, agreed that fielding the first batch of Zorawar tanks that had already been through trials would be preferable to waiting for a heavier version that so far existed mostly on paper.

“I do understand where the army is coming from. No commander wants to send crews up to the LAC in a vehicle they don’t fully trust,” he said, referring to the disputed India-China border by the abbreviated form of its official name. “Still, these tanks won’t be arriving in an empty theatre.”

An armoured brigade of T-72s and T-90s, typically ranging from 135 to 150 tanks, was already in Ladakh “and the Zorawar brings what those tanks can’t easily give you”, Iyer said.

“It can be flown in, it can use the smaller bridges and narrow roads, and it can get up to heights where a 45-tonne tank struggles,” he said. “Used alongside the heavier tanks on the flatter ground, even 59 of them would give the brigade a good deal more flexibility.”

China’s decade lead

The Zorawar is part of a broader overhaul of India’s armoured forces, which includes upgrading the T-72 and T-90 fleet using Soviet-era and Russian engineering drawings, alongside developing indigenous systems.

India has the world’s fifth-largest tank fleet with an estimated 3,900 main battle tanks, while China has the largest with more than 5,800 units, according to data compiled by US-based military tracking site Global Firepower.

Iyer said China was nearly a decade ahead of India in light tanks, noting that its Type 15, launched eight years ago, had a 1,000-horsepower engine and came equipped with a 105mm gun.

“On paper the baseline Zorawar is lighter,” he said, describing the power-to-weight ratio as “broadly similar” and the guns as “comparable”.

But other factors must also be taken into account, including road, rail and air links, and the industrial capacity to build tanks at scale, Iyer said.

India’s tank fleet was older and behind on protection technology, he said, but not hopelessly so – further noting that the army had moved more T-90s and T-72s into Ladakh in a bid to narrow the gap.

Neither the Zorawar nor the Type 15 had yet seen combat, Iyer said. “The advantage India has in acclimatised troops and high-altitude experience is real and should not be underrated,” he added.

item.title: [SCMP] US midterm shift could squeeze China on AI, but bring clarity to bilateral talks
item.description:
Follow the SCMP’s live coverage here

Beijing has vowed to continue working with Washington towards a “constructive relationship of strategic stability” following the Democrats’ sweeping victory in the US midterm elections on Wednesday.

But analysts said a Democratic-controlled US Congress would ramp up pressure on Beijing over Taiwan, artificial intelligence (AI) and export controls, though it might also eliminate uncertainties in negotiations.
item.content:encoded:
Follow the SCMP’s live coverage here

Beijing has vowed to continue working with Washington towards a “constructive relationship of strategic stability” following the Democrats’ sweeping victory in the US midterm elections on Wednesday.

But analysts said a Democratic-controlled US Congress would ramp up pressure on Beijing over Taiwan, artificial intelligence (AI) and export controls, though it might also eliminate uncertainties in negotiations.

When asked by reporters about the results on Wednesday, Mao Ning, spokeswoman for China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, pledged to continue to work with Washington towards a constructive relationship of strategic stability based on respect, fairness and reciprocity.

She described the election as an “internal matter” for the US and said China stood ready to work with Washington to implement the consensus reached by Chinese President Xi Jinping and his US counterpart Donald Trump to “enhance communication, properly manage differences and expand cooperation”.

Trump’s Republican Party lost control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate, handing Democrats the power to block parts of his legislative agenda and intensify congressional scrutiny of his administration’s policies, including its approach to China.

Wu Xinbo, dean of the Institute of International Studies at Fudan University in Shanghai, said the power shift would certainly affect the China-US relationship.

“One possibility is that the Democratic Party would put pressure on Trump regarding the Taiwan issue, criticising him for betraying Taiwan and developing ties with Beijing and pushing Trump to resume arms sales to Taiwan,” Wu said.

The United States paused a US$14 billion arms sale to Taiwan before Trump and Xi met in May. The US is considering postponing the announcement of major arms sales to Taiwan until after November’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit in Shenzhen, the South China Morning Post reported in September.

“The US-China Board of Investment may discuss easing restrictions on Chinese investment in the US, but the Democratic Party has the backing of labour unions, so it seeks to protect many industries, particularly the automotive industry. So they would also oppose this,” Wu said.

In September, 27 House Democrats sent a letter to Trump to urge him not to open the US market to Chinese carmakers through imports, local manufacturing or other arrangements ahead of Xi’s state visit to the US.

Beijing and Washington agreed to establish a US-China Board of Investment during Trump’s summit with Xi in Beijing in May. The White House announced that the mechanism had been established during their second summit in Washington in September, providing a government-to-government forum to discuss investment opportunities and barriers.

Wu said the House Select Committee on Strategic Competition Between the United States and the Chinese Communist Party would also play up bilateral flashpoints, which would in turn influence US public opinion, policy and legislation on China.

On US-China trade talks, Wu said Democratic control of Congress might benefit these talks because the Democrats “will limit Trump constantly playing the tariff card”.

“I feel this might actually be a good thing [for China],” he said.

His view was echoed by Feng Chucheng, founder and partner at Hutong Research, a Beijing-based strategic consultancy, who said a Democratic-controlled Congress would eliminate uncertainties in US-China negotiations.

Feng noted that Congress could constrain the White House’s China policy by influencing the implementation of technology and export restrictions, particularly by denying Trump legislative waivers or exemptions that a Republican-controlled Congress might have been willing to grant. Such waivers, or even delays in implementing certain restrictions, would be valuable bargaining chips for Trump in negotiations with Beijing.

“From Beijing’s perspective, this actually removes a significant element of uncertainty from the US-China negotiating equation. Beijing no longer has to factor in the possibility that Trump could secure congressional waivers or exemptions in exchange for Chinese concessions,” Feng said.

He said a Democratic-controlled House would have limited ability to shape the leader-level diplomacy between Trump and Xi. Feng added that the US president retained considerable discretion to negotiate with his Chinese counterpart, but Trump’s ability to deliver on certain promises to Beijing would be more constrained.

“This makes the boundaries of any potential US-China deal clearer, even if it narrows the scope for bargaining,” Feng said.

In addition to their reunion in Shenzhen later this month, Xi and Trump are set to meet in Miami for a Group of 20 (G20) summit in December.

Zhao Minghao, a professor at Fudan University’s Institute of International Studies, called the election results so far a “blue tsunami” and a “big win” for the Democrats that would turn Trump into a “lame duck”.

Zhao said a Democratic-controlled Congress was likely to launch sweeping investigations into Trump, his family and senior officials once it convened in January, pushing back on the president’s agenda across legislation and the budget.

Zhao suggested that the midterm elections would not change the overall direction of Washington’s China policy, since stepping up strategic competition with Beijing was a bipartisan consensus. But the results could affect the tools Washington uses.

“For one, a Democratic-led Congress will certainly further intensify pressure on China on Taiwan, AI and export controls,” he said.

“Democrats will also scrutinise the Trump administration’s China policy more closely, including how it conducts diplomacy with Beijing. All of this will affect how the executive branch handles relations with China in the next phase.”

As artificial intelligence – from data centres to regulation – took centre stage in the midterm elections, Zhao said the debate was likely to become more closely tied to US-China competition once the Democrats take control of Congress.

“The Democrats may instrumentalise China policy as a tool to pressure Trump. This is a very big challenge for Beijing,” he said.

“Going forward, the decline of Trump’s personal political authority will also pose a major challenge to the new positioning of a strategically stable relationship that China and the US have formed … and the progress made on it.”

Chen Fengying, a Beijing-based expert on US-China relations, said election results could have implications for Trump’s foreign policy, particularly in the Middle East and the Pacific.

She said the US economy was relatively strong apart from inflation, describing this election as one “tied to Trump’s Middle East policy”.

With Democrats gaining ground and placing greater constraints on the president, efforts to resolve the Iran issue could accelerate, according to Chen.

“His room [to] manoeuvre in foreign policy will narrow, and US foreign policy could become more restrained. I don’t believe he will stir up trouble in the Pacific again,” Chen said.

Additional reporting by Ji Siqi

item.title: [SCMP] ‘I wasn’t on the ballot’: Trump deflects blame as Democrats on track to control Congress
item.description:
Follow the SCMP’s live coverage here

In what appears to be an early attempt to distance himself from the Democrats’ historic gains, US President Donald Trump has sought to shift attention away from his party’s performance in the midterm elections, taking to social media to remind voters that he “wasn’t on the ballot”.

“I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE! Thank you for your attention to this matter,” Trump wrote as early results showed Democratic gains in places Republicans expected to hold.
item.content:encoded:
Follow the SCMP’s live coverage here

In what appears to be an early attempt to distance himself from the Democrats’ historic gains, US President Donald Trump has sought to shift attention away from his party’s performance in the midterm elections, taking to social media to remind voters that he “wasn’t on the ballot”.

“I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE! Thank you for your attention to this matter,” Trump wrote as early results showed Democratic gains in places Republicans expected to hold.

This came weeks after Trump told supporters to “just close your eyes and pretend I’m on the ballot”.

Shortly after his election night social media post, in a New York Times interview, Trump said he would accept the election results and was willing to work with lawmakers on the other side of the aisle.

He once again blamed Republican losses on the fact that he himself was not on the ballot.

Trump’s willingness to accept the midterm results stands in contrast to his long-running refusal to concede the 2020 presidential election, which he lost to Joe Biden. For years he has continued to insist, without evidence, that the 2020 contest was stolen from him.

Here is the latest on how the midterm elections are unfolding:

An eventful evening

Earlier on election day, Trump told Fox News that if Americans ever got tired of him, he would move to Israel and become prime minister, claiming that he had a 99 per cent approval rating there.

“In fact, if people ever got tired of me in the US, I’ll move to Israel, become prime minister,” he said. “So, I’m the No 1 … I was 99 per cent approval rating in Israel,” he added.

“Can you believe it? In fact, if people ever got tired of me in the US, I’ll move to Israel and become prime minister.”

Decisive rebuke for Republicans and Trump

Democrats are projected to seize control of both chambers of Congress.

Setbacks started emerging early on for Trump and the Republican Party, even in historically deep-red territory, as voters registered dissatisfaction with his new wars and the economic pressure that has accompanied them.

What initially appeared to be scattered losses soon took shape as a broader and decisive rebuke of the Trump administration.

In Texas, Democrat James Talarico is projected to defeat Republican Ken Paxton, according to NBC News and Decision Desk HQ. Paxton has conceded defeat.

It is the first Democratic Senate victory in the state since 1988 and, so far, the biggest and most significant loss for Republicans of the night.

In the Texas governor’s race, Democrat Gina Hinojosa is projected to defeat Republican incumbent Greg Abbott, who has also conceded defeat.

In South Carolina, Democrat Annie Andrews is on track to defeat Republican Darline Graham, sister of the late Senator Lindsey Graham, who was appointed to the seat after her brother’s death earlier this year.

She was hand-picked by Trump to run for a full term, in a race which would be a major upset if it flipped a long-time Republican seat.

The AP projected former North Carolina governor Roy Cooper as the winner of the state’s Senate race, flipping a Republican-held seat. Democrats entered the night needing a net gain of four seats to take the Senate.

In Ohio, former senator Sherrod Brown is projected to defeat Republican incumbent Jon Husted in the special election, flipping the seat. Brown, who lost re-election in 2024, returns to the Senate two years later.

In Ohio’s governor’s race, Democrat Amy Acton is projected to defeat Republican Vivek Ramaswamy, according to NBC News and the Associated Press. Ramaswamy has conceded defeat.

Acton becomes the first woman to be elected governor of Ohio and the first Democrat to win the office in 20 years, ending a long stretch of Republican control in a state Trump carried by a wide margin in 2024.

In Iowa, Democrat Josh Turek is projected to defeat Republican Ashley Hinson, flipping the open Senate seat. It is the first Democratic Senate victory in Iowa since 2008.

The AP also called Democratic holds for Senator Jon Ossoff in Georgia, Representative Chris Pappas in New Hampshire’s open seat and Senator Cory Booker in New Jersey.

In the House, the Associated Press projected Democrat Jamie Ager as the winner in North Carolina’s 11th congressional district, in the first Democratic flip of the night.

In Michigan’s 13th district, Democratic Socialist of America-endorsed Democrat Donavan McKinney is projected to win a heavily Democratic Detroit-area seat, though the Associated Press has not yet issued its own call.

The remaining contests that will decide control are in Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Michigan, Ohio and Texas.

High turnout and Chinese-American candidates

More than 59 million Americans cast ballots before election day, according to an Associated Press analysis, surpassing early-voter turnout from the 2022 midterms and setting a new midterm record.

Candidates of Chinese-American descent are also running in several races. The most prominent is Connie Chan, a San Francisco supervisor seeking the California seat being vacated by long-time Democratic leader Nancy Pelosi.

There are roughly 16 million eligible Asian-American and Pacific Islander (AAPI) voters in 2026, including about 1.6 million who are newly eligible since 2022.

Pre-election surveys showed AAPI registered voters leaning strongly Democratic in congressional races, typically in the range of 55–64 per cent Democratic versus 20–25 per cent Republican, with cost of living and the economy as their top issues.

Historic victories

Several historic victories have already made headlines.

Republican Byron Donalds is projected to become Florida’s first Black governor.

In Georgia, Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms is projected to make history as the first Black woman to be elected governor of a US state, defeating a self-funded opponent who spent more than US$200 million of his own money.

In New Hampshire, Democrat Chris Pappas is projected to become the first openly gay man elected to the US Senate.

Close races can take days to resolve. Most of the country has finished voting, though polls in Alaska remain open until midnight Eastern Time in most of the state.

item.title: [SCMP] US voters unleash blue wave, handing Congress to Democrats and rebuking Trump
item.description:
Follow the SCMP’s live coverage here

After weeks of insults, fearmongering and eye-popping spending on advertising, Americans settled down to vote on Tuesday, unleashing a blue wave that saw Democrats projected to take the House and the Senate, in a sharp rebuke to US President Donald Trump and his controversial governing style.

In a stunning development, Associated Press also projected that Democrat James Talarico won the Texas US Senate election, defeating Republican nominee Ken Paxton and earning the first statewide win for a Democrat in 32 years. This came after billionaire Elon Musk threw over US$200 million of his own money into defeating Talarico.
item.content:encoded:
Follow the SCMP’s live coverage here

After weeks of insults, fearmongering and eye-popping spending on advertising, Americans settled down to vote on Tuesday, unleashing a blue wave that saw Democrats projected to take the House and the Senate, in a sharp rebuke to US President Donald Trump and his controversial governing style.

In a stunning development, Associated Press also projected that Democrat James Talarico won the Texas US Senate election, defeating Republican nominee Ken Paxton and earning the first statewide win for a Democrat in 32 years. This came after billionaire Elon Musk threw over US$200 million of his own money into defeating Talarico.

Kansas’ Adam Hamilton chalked up another historic win, becoming the first Democrat to be elected senator in the state in nearly 100 years.

Despite urging voters to act as if he were on the ballot, Trump quickly pivoted to sidestep any blame as the electoral map turned increasingly blue.

“I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE! Thank you for your attention to this matter. President DONALD J. TRUMP,” he posted after tearing into Fox News’ coverage a few hours earlier, complaining that the network was spending “too much time” covering Democrats – who he labelled “Trump Deranged Dumocrats”.

As the evening unfolded, seat after seat long considered safe Republican strongholds swung to increasingly competitive Democrats.

Exit polls suggested voters were strongly motivated by inflation – petrol prices hit a national average of US$4.14 per gallon, their highest ever, on election day – as well as the future of democracy, corruption and the Iran war, much of which was tied directly to Trump.

Democratic control of Congress will almost certainly result in more investigations into many of these issues, especially the war, tariffs and corruption.

It could also see lawmakers become more assertive on Taiwan policy, including required reports on delayed weapons deliveries, calls to notify Congress of new arms sales and demands that the administration explain any decision to pause them, according to Bonnie Glaser, managing director of the Indo-Pacific programme at the German Marshall Fund of the United States.

Atlantic Council economist Josh Lipsky also predicted that Democrats could reshape US-China tariff policy by seeking to restore congressional authority over trade, including by demanding that tariffs be approved by lawmakers. While Trump would almost certainly veto such bills, he said, that could set the policy agenda for 2028 and beyond.

Voter enthusiasm approached all-time highs for a midterm election. Early voting surpassed 59 million ballots nationwide, according to the University of Florida’s Election Lab, compared with 46 million ballots for 2022, a then-record fuelled by the pandemic and wariness over in-person voting.

A key group that appeared to make a big difference Tuesday was Hispanic voters who heavily supported Trump in 2024 but became increasingly disenchanted with his aggressive immigration crackdown.

Trump told The New York Times that he would accept the results, a shift in tone from his pre-election statements that indicated he would only accept them if they were “honest”. “We’ll work with the Democrats,” he reportedly said. “We’ll probably work something out.”

Because Trump had so effectively remade the Republican Party in his image and urged voters to “pretend I’m on the ballot, ’cause in a way I am”, the results were tied to him personally, analysts said. With Trump unable to run again, that could accelerate his descent into lame-duck status.

At times, Trump’s efforts to support Republicans in recent weeks appeared almost designed to do the opposite. Two months before the election, he slapped 50 per cent tariffs on Canada, undercutting the economies of several important swing states along the border.

And while the 80-year-old has campaigned energetically, making some 30 appearances in 20 states over the past month, Trump often avoided swing states in favour of deep red districts where he could find a friendly audience. Yet as the election approached and the map turned bluer, even those traditional sure bets increasingly wobbled.

As his popularity fell, as the Iran war trundled on and as anger over his policies grew, some Republican candidates quietly dropped references to the president from their campaign websites and quietly suggested he not appear in their districts.

Where Trump did appear, he seemed at times to highlight party weaknesses rather than strengths and thumb his nose at voter concerns.

“They said, ‘President Trump is talking about all the money they’re making while people are suffering at the pump.’ That’ll be the headline,” he told a crowd in Georgia. “But I said, ‘I don’t give a damn, I’m gonna say it: We’re making a freaking fortune.’”

Tuesday’s results came amid record spending, especially by Republicans, which focused on key battleground states and now raises questions about the torrent of money in US elections and its effectiveness.

Texas saw overall spending of some US$635 million. Senate races in Ohio attracted an estimated US$450 million, Michigan’s some US$384 million, Iowa’s over US$220 million and Maine’s US$190 million.

Trump also doubled down on support for data centres as these became increasingly unpopular among voters in both parties. “The only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. should not want Data Centers is if they want to end up being backwards and poor,” Trump wrote on social media.

Likely galling for Trump were races where he prominently staked his clout and prestige, not only with Paxton in Texas but giving his full backing in South Carolina to the late senator Lindsey Graham’s sister, Darline Graham, who was also defeated.

The results will almost immediately start the clock ticking on the race for president in 2028. The results are likely to seriously dent the outlook for perceived Republican front-runner Vice-President J.D. Vance, likely to be saddled with his boss’s legacy.

And it could complicate the prospects for the other early Republican front runner, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

On the Democratic side, the midterm is expected to spur a host of announcements by wannabes in the next few months. These could include Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro and Georgia Senator Jon Ossoff, both of whom won re-election handily on Tuesday, and California Governor Gavin Newsom and Kentucky Governor Andy Beshear, among others, who were not on the ballot this time.

But a strong Democratic performance on Tuesday risked overconfidence, analysts said, and the chance that the party failed to develop a strategy beyond “not Trump” and failed to focus on a positive agenda.

In effect, the showing may be less of a “blue wave” or overwhelming vote of confidence for Democrats, political operatives warn, than a “red undertow” reflecting deep anger and disenchantment with Trump and Republicans.

As Republicans faltered, meanwhile, Trump’s rhetoric and accusations intensified, leading to his referring to Democrats as “Radical Left lunatics”, “extremists”, “Marxists”, “thugs” and “fascists”.

Even races that Republicans won or held Tuesday saw often double-digit erosion from the huge margins that they enjoyed in Trump’s historic 2024 win, highlighting his huge fall from grace.

“Character matters, and this president didn’t deliver it,” said former New Jersey governor Chris Christie, a Republican.

item.title: [SCMP] Why North Korea’s Kim sees no need for another Trump ‘photo-op summit’
item.description:
Kim Jong-un’s powerful sister on Wednesday rejected holding any further talks with the United States, days after the FBI accused North Korea of stealing more than US$6 billion from a cryptocurrency exchange and Washington launched a new round of sanctions aimed at Pyongyang.

Analysts say the latest developments have all but killed off the chances of another Trump-Kim summit, despite the US president’s continued warm words for North Korea’s supreme leader and apparent openness to meeting him again.

In a statement on Wednesday, Kim Yo-jong called the Federal Bureau of Investigation’s allegations regarding the Binance hack proof of Washington’s “hostile policy” towards Pyongyang and said there was “no need” for further talks.
item.content:encoded:
Kim Jong-un’s powerful sister on Wednesday rejected holding any further talks with the United States, days after the FBI accused North Korea of stealing more than US$6 billion from a cryptocurrency exchange and Washington launched a new round of sanctions aimed at Pyongyang.

Analysts say the latest developments have all but killed off the chances of another Trump-Kim summit, despite the US president’s continued warm words for North Korea’s supreme leader and apparent openness to meeting him again.

In a statement on Wednesday, Kim Yo-jong called the Federal Bureau of Investigation’s allegations regarding the Binance hack proof of Washington’s “hostile policy” towards Pyongyang and said there was “no need” for further talks.

“They talk about peace but prefer above all war drills and strengthening military alliances,” she said. “It is our clear position that there is no need to sit face to face with such untrustworthy and hostile people.”

Her remarks also followed last week’s sanctioning by the US Treasury Department of eight North Korean operatives, two Russian financial facilitators and one North Korean-controlled entity over an overseas IT worker fraud scheme.

Hundreds of North Korean nationals, officials and front companies have been sanctioned under the US sanctions framework, which typically freezes assets subject to US jurisdiction and bars Americans from dealing with those named.

The Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control, which administers the sanctions, on October 28 accused the sanctioned group of running a state-directed scheme in which North Korean IT workers, often posing as freelancers, had defrauded American companies to generate revenue for Pyongyang’s weapons programmes.

“The North Korean regime continues targeting and exploiting American companies through fraudulent activities conducted by its overseas IT operatives, who weaponise sensitive data and extort businesses for substantial payments,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a statement.

Trump’s mixed signals

Trump and Kim Jong-un met three times during the US president’s first term in office, most recently at the demilitarised zone in June 2019.

The US president has repeatedly touted his “very good” relationship with the North Korean dictator and said in August that he planned to meet Kim again this year, but has since walked back these remarks, telling reporters on October 19 that he was “not sure that anybody’s asking for a meeting”.

Washington has said Trump would meet Kim again if Pyongyang was willing to discuss issues of concern to the US and its regional allies, including South Korea. Speculation has linked a potential meeting to the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen later this month.

But analysts say Trump’s warmth towards Kim sits at odds with the US government’s continued pressure campaign.

That disconnect between presidential rhetoric and bureaucratic execution is what confuses many outside observers

Lee Seong-hyon, geopolitical analyst

Trump is virtually the only figure in his administration projecting “a warm, personal image” towards Kim, according to geopolitical analyst Lee Seong-hyon, an associate-in-research at Harvard University Asia Centre.

“His national security and Treasury teams remain clear-eyed and hawkish towards North Korea’s illicit threats, especially cyber-financial crime,” he said.

“That disconnect between presidential rhetoric and bureaucratic execution is what confuses many outside observers.”

Andrew Yeo of the Brookings Institution, a Washington-based think tank, said Trump’s comments playing down a meeting with Kim and the recent sanctions suggested the president and his administration “may be a bit more aligned” on engagement with Pyongyang.

He said Trump was “not bothered by inconsistency or holding contradictory positions” and would likely “make it happen” if the chance for a meeting arose, sanctions or not. Yeo is a senior fellow and the SK-Korea Foundation chair of Korea studies at the think tank.

Lee said Kim had long ago concluded that a “pure photo-op summit” carried diminishing returns without concrete concessions, but predicted that a Trump who was emerging politically weakened from the US midterm elections “may grow far more eager for a dramatic foreign-policy spectacle on the Korean peninsula”.

‘Isolation obsolete’

Analysts say Washington’s latest round of measures are unlikely to hurt Pyongyang too much.

Gabriela Bernal, non-resident fellow at the European Centre for North Korean Studies, said Kim “probably isn’t losing much sleep over them either, since he’s got the support of Moscow and Beijing”.

China is North Korea’s largest trading partner and Russia provides Pyongyang with security and military support. Both regard North Korea as a buffer state and a regional partner to counter US influence and maintain stability on their borders.

Cybercrime is central to the Kim regime’s finances. Intelligence agencies and blockchain analysts, who trace cryptocurrency transactions, say theft and online fraud generate between one-third and one-half of the regime’s total budget. The operations run to multiple billions of dollars and help North Korea evade international sanctions and fund its weapons programmes.

Yeo described the recent sanctions as punitive and “an important signal” that Washington “will not tolerate illicit activities targeting US businesses”. But he also called it “a cat-and-mouse game”, with new hackers constantly emerging and adapting to keep money flowing to the regime.

Bernal said Pyongyang excelled at cyber operations and the scale of its scams was probably “only now being discovered”.

“As one loose end is tied, more will pop up, it’s not something that will be disappearing any time soon,” she said, adding that most operatives worked from China and Russia, neither of which cooperated on sanctions enforcement.

China accounted for about 98 per cent of North Korea’s official external trade, Lee said, blunting the “strategic bite” of targeted sanctions.

On October 15, China and North Korea officially opened the long-stalled New Yalu River Bridge to vehicle traffic. A little over a week later, Kim crossed the bridge to meet with Chinese officials in the border city of Dandong, visit war memorials and tour a historic vehicle factory.

Such links, Lee said, would expand cross-border commerce “on an expressway scale that renders traditional financial isolation obsolete”.

item.title: [SCMP] Israel deepens Somaliland ties with first ambassador, testing Horn of Africa balance
item.description:
Last week, Somaliland, a breakaway region that declared independence from Somalia in 1991, welcomed its first ambassador from Israel.

Diplomat Michael Lotem presented his credentials in Hargeisa, while officials laid the cornerstone for an Israeli embassy. The ceremony, announced by Israel’s foreign ministry on Sunday, formalised a relationship that began with mutual recognition in December.

Somalia, the African Union, Arab states and China strongly oppose the move, reaffirming Somaliland as Somali territory. Beijing has been particularly vocal, viewing recognition as separatism, a breach of its one-China principle and a threat to its naval presence in Djibouti.
item.content:encoded:
Last week, Somaliland, a breakaway region that declared independence from Somalia in 1991, welcomed its first ambassador from Israel.

Diplomat Michael Lotem presented his credentials in Hargeisa, while officials laid the cornerstone for an Israeli embassy. The ceremony, announced by Israel’s foreign ministry on Sunday, formalised a relationship that began with mutual recognition in December.

Somalia, the African Union, Arab states and China strongly oppose the move, reaffirming Somaliland as Somali territory. Beijing has been particularly vocal, viewing recognition as separatism, a breach of its one-China principle and a threat to its naval presence in Djibouti.

Somaliland, whose main port, Berbera, sits just a few hundred kilometres from the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a narrow waterway that carries about 10 to 12 per cent of global trade, is now set to shape the balance of tension in the Red Sea and Horn of Africa.

Last month, Beijing and Djibouti jointly reaffirmed Somalia’s territorial integrity, opposing recognition of Somaliland and objecting to its cooperation with Taiwan. They also stressed the importance of freedom of navigation in the Red Sea and Bab el-Mandeb Strait.

Somaliland maintains mutually supportive ties with Taiwan, which Beijing considers part of China and has not ruled out using force to bring under its control. Most countries, including Israel and the US, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state. However, Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-governed island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons.

Samir Bhattacharya of the New Delhi-based Observer Research Foundation noted that China’s concerns extended beyond its opposition to separatism.

“The Bab el-Mandeb Strait, linking the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden, is a critical chokepoint for Chinese trade and energy flows under the Maritime Silk Road,” he wrote in a December 2025 commentary.

Beijing has repeatedly described the route as a “jugular vein” for global commerce.

China’s first overseas military base, established in neighbouring Djibouti in 2017, was built “precisely to protect these interests and ensure a sustained Chinese security presence near this chokepoint”, he added.

For most of the past three decades, Somaliland’s strategic location attracted interest from a handful of commercial and security players but carried little diplomatic weight. Israel’s recognition changed that.

In a report to the US Congress in June, the State Department said Somaliland’s strategic location near Yemen and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait positioned it as a potential partner on shared security interests.

The report said it was also geographically positioned to potentially aid efforts to monitor and counter violent extremist organisations, particularly connections between Houthi fighters and al-Shabab, al-Qaeda’s largest and wealthiest affiliate.

The United States Africa Command had regular engagements with Somaliland authorities and was exploring areas for potential cooperation, it said.

Israel’s move comes after years of attacks on Red Sea shipping by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis, rising tensions between the US, Israel and Iran, and growing concerns over two key maritime chokepoints: the Bab el-Mandeb Strait and the Strait of Hormuz. The latter has been severely restricted by Tehran since the US and Israel launched their war against Iran in February.

An Israeli presence near Berbera could potentially help monitor Houthi activity along the shipping corridor. But it could also draw Somaliland more directly into the wider regional conflict.

Federico Donelli, a researcher affiliated with the University of Trieste in Italy and the Washington-based Wilson Centre, said the recent developments could “establish precedents for the international recognition of contested territories”.

He said that even without further countries recognising Somaliland or having a substantial Israeli security presence on the ground, the move could have “far-reaching implications for the regional balance of power and the evolving security dynamics of the Red Sea and Horn of Africa”.

Donelli noted that Somaliland’s “strategic value primarily derives from its geographical position along the Gulf of Aden, close to the Bab el-Mandeb Strait and Yemen’s coastline”, while the port and airport at Berbera could support maritime surveillance, intelligence gathering and a better understanding of security developments in the region.

However, he cautioned against confusing this strategic potential with evidence of an established Israeli military presence or formal access to facilities – greater strategic importance did not automatically mean greater security.

“For Somaliland, the main risk is becoming more directly exposed to regional rivalries. The recognition could increase its visibility to the Houthis and other anti-Israeli actors, potentially generating security threats and political pressure,” he said.

Donelli also said the move could make it harder for Gulf states and other regional players to maintain shipping security and stability. “The recognition risks adding another layer to existing regional rivalries,” he said.

Any disruption or rise in tensions near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait would put further pressure on a shipping route already affected by Houthi attacks and the wider Iran-related conflict and could extend to commercial shipping and energy supplies.

The implications also differed across the region, according to Donelli, who said Turkey was concerned about the impact on its strategic partnership with Mogadishu and its broader interests in Somalia, while Egypt viewed the development through the lens of its tensions with Ethiopia and regional rivalry in the Horn of Africa.

He said Saudi Arabia was focused on maintaining stability along the Red Sea and preventing further escalation, and the United Arab Emirates faced a more complex calculation because of its economic and strategic interests in Berbera, particularly its investment in port infrastructure.

“The main concern is not necessarily an immediate escalation into proxy conflicts, but the growing overlap between local political disputes, external security interests and competition over maritime access and strategic infrastructure,” he said.

Looking ahead, Donelli said further recognition by other countries could not be ruled out, but was unlikely to follow automatically. Most governments would have to weigh potential strategic benefits against the diplomatic costs of challenging Somalia’s territorial integrity and the African Union’s position on existing borders.

“The most plausible trajectory is one of bilateral consolidation accompanied by continued diplomatic contestation,” he said.

item.title: [SCMP] Why some EU and Chinese firms are keen to cooperate – even as tensions simmer
item.description:
While trade tensions between Beijing and Brussels remain elevated, some European businesses are pointing to disruptions from the United States as a bigger challenge.

Instead, they are seeking closer cooperation with China, even as Chinese carmakers scramble to front-load exports ahead of potential future trade barriers.

At last week’s 19th Europe-China Business and Technology Cooperation Fair in the southwestern Chinese city of Chengdu, the appetite for closer business ties was evident.
item.content:encoded:
While trade tensions between Beijing and Brussels remain elevated, some European businesses are pointing to disruptions from the United States as a bigger challenge.

Instead, they are seeking closer cooperation with China, even as Chinese carmakers scramble to front-load exports ahead of potential future trade barriers.

At last week’s 19th Europe-China Business and Technology Cooperation Fair in the southwestern Chinese city of Chengdu, the appetite for closer business ties was evident.

Hundreds of Chinese and European companies across a wide range of sectors filled a hall for matchmaking sessions, rotating between tables to exchange ideas and seek potential partners and investors.

Some European business representatives said they were not too worried about tensions, instead seeing significant potential for cooperation in sectors such as automotive, renewable energy and agriculture.

The biggest challenge facing companies from both sides, however, was “the instability coming from America”, said Nuno Orfao, managing partner at Portuguese consulting firm Stream, pointing to uncertainty over US trade policy and its impact on business planning and investment.

“America is putting [up] a wall, which is affecting not only the relations that Europe has with them,” Orfao said. As China faced greater trade friction with the US than Europe, this created an additional incentive for Chinese and European companies to explore cooperation, he added.

Jorge Marques, CEO of Spain-headquartered digital marketplace Space Mall, echoed that view, saying higher US tariffs on the EU and other markets since last year had driven up costs for European producers in North America, forcing many to look east.

The market is in Asia. We must be ready to open deals and make really good trade with Asia – in general, with China

Jorge Marques, Space Mall

Citing wine prices as an example, Marques said European wine sold in the US was now roughly 15 to 25 per cent more expensive than three years ago, partly because of US tariffs imposed last year.

Europe must “open its mind” and recognise where actual growth lies, he noted. “The market is in Asia. What we have to face is [being] ready to open deals and make really good trade with Asia – in general, with China.”

Marques also warned that EU policies targeting China could ultimately benefit American businesses. Rising costs were discouraging European buyers from sourcing goods directly from China, leaving some to turn to Amazon instead, he said. “In the end who wins? American companies.”

Some Chinese cross-border sellers are also looking to diversify into Europe as US tariffs raise their costs.

Zhang Jinlong, a Chinese manufacturer and cross-border vendor of smart-home products, said he was considering entering the EU market and setting up service hubs after gaining a foothold in the US earlier this year.

“Tariff rates in Europe are generally much lower than in the US, where tariffs on our categories hover around 50 per cent,” he said.

The comments come as China’s widening trade surplus, which is on track to hit another record high this year, sparks widespread concern in the West. Beijing and Brussels had appeared to be on the verge of a trade war last month, before reaching a deal to cap Chinese hybrid car imports into the EU for four years.

Beijing also pledged to “continue to facilitate” export licence approvals for rare earths and permanent magnets destined for the EU, while both sides agreed to explore possible tariff cuts on certain goods.

Some business representatives argued that the answer to Chinese low-cost competition was not tariff barriers but greater cooperation in local manufacturing and technology.

European firms have to realise that competition with China is “inevitable”, particularly in the automotive sector, according to Rupert Varnai, CEO of advisory firm Cathay Partners. They need to “find an answer to that – and it is not sanctions or higher customs duties, but some kind of cooperation”, he said.

The need to find new markets has become more pressing amid Europe’s energy crisis and high inflation, which Varnai linked to the Russia-Ukraine war, the US-Israel war on Iran and recent protests in France and elsewhere.

“The solution is to open the doors and try to make big electric vehicle companies in China to invest there,” Orfao said.

Chinese carmakers and other manufacturers are increasingly building factories or forming joint ventures in Europe amid higher tariffs on imports and EU efforts to encourage local manufacturing.

BYD, for example, has said its plant in Hungary will begin mass production in the fourth quarter of this year and that it plans to build more factories in Europe.

China’s broader lead in electrification could also make its companies attractive partners as European economies seek to accelerate their green transitions.

The Electrification Competitiveness Index, released on Tuesday by climate non-profit We Mean Business Coalition, assessed 16 major economies and ranked China first for deployment, with a score of 68 per cent, reflecting strong uptake of EVs across vehicle categories and extensive charging infrastructure.

By contrast, the US faces policy reversals and grid bottlenecks, while countries including Germany, Italy, Poland and the United Kingdom have yet to translate supportive policies into comparable progress on the ground, the index showed.

For some Chinese carmakers, however, the immediate priority is to take advantage of the current window to ramp up exports before potential policy changes take effect.

A representative of Sichuan-based Chuanyun Heavy Industry Group, which is involved in the new energy vehicle business, said the recent China-EU deal had pushed back the prospect of punitive tariffs, giving exporters more time to ship vehicles to Europe.

The company, which previously focused on markets in Central Asia, was now exploring opportunities in Europe, the representative said. In the longer term, it was also considering setting up an assembly plant there to meet local rules-of-origin requirements and significantly reduce tariff costs, he added.

In September, China’s hybrid car exports to the EU tripled from a year earlier to nearly 100,000 vehicles, outpacing the 142.7 per cent year-on-year growth in China’s total passenger car exports to the bloc, customs data showed.

item.title: [SCMP] North Korea’s low-cost drone push exposes South Korea’s red tape trap
item.description:
North Korea is rapidly advancing its drone warfare capabilities by drawing lessons from the Russia-Ukraine war, even as South Korea’s efforts to keep pace remain bogged down by procurement delays and bureaucratic red tape, observers warn.

They also caution that cryptocurrency theft has become a crucial source of funding for Pyongyang’s weapons programmes, following US Federal Bureau of Investigation allegations that North Korean state-backed hackers stole more than US$6 billion from Binance, the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange.

Against this backdrop, South Korea’s Ministry of National Defence has reorganised its existing drone unit into the newly inaugurated Defence Drone Headquarters.
item.content:encoded:
North Korea is rapidly advancing its drone warfare capabilities by drawing lessons from the Russia-Ukraine war, even as South Korea’s efforts to keep pace remain bogged down by procurement delays and bureaucratic red tape, observers warn.

They also caution that cryptocurrency theft has become a crucial source of funding for Pyongyang’s weapons programmes, following US Federal Bureau of Investigation allegations that North Korean state-backed hackers stole more than US$6 billion from Binance, the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange.

Against this backdrop, South Korea’s Ministry of National Defence has reorganised its existing drone unit into the newly inaugurated Defence Drone Headquarters.

“The Defence Drone Headquarters will spearhead the advancement of combat capabilities and drive innovation in force structure and technology to strengthen the drone and counter-drone operational capacities of each military branch,” the ministry said in a statement on Monday.

The move follows a weapons exhibition in Pyongyang last week, where North Korea showcased an array of unmanned combat systems alongside a large-scale display of firepower. The exhibits included stealth drones and cheap, expendable loitering munitions.

North Korean leader Kim Jong-un, who oversaw the display, highlighted Pyongyang’s growing focus on unmanned warfare. He said that achieving “absolute superiority” in the sector was an “indispensable choice”.

“North Korea has rapidly advanced its technology through information shared by Russia and by reverse-engineering drones acquired on the battlefield,” said Doo Jin-ho, a research fellow at Kyungnam University’s Institute for Far Eastern Studies.

“Through battlefield experience in Ukraine, the North has concluded that drones are the solution for a low-cost war, as missiles are costly and it is difficult to secure parts and components for them,” Doo said.

He added that swarms of unmanned vehicles – potentially equipped with AI – could overwhelm air defences, including US-supplied THAAD and Patriot systems as well as South Korea’s Cheongung interceptors.

The exhibition highlighted a widening gap in procurement agility between the two Koreas.

The asset that drew the most attention was a large, manta ray-shaped stealth combat drone displayed for the first time.

“The design of the air intakes and main wings appears to be modelled after stealth drones from the US and Russia,” said Shin Jong-woo, secretary general of the Seoul-based Korea Defence and Security Forum.

Technological progress was also evident in precision-strike capabilities. Pyongyang displayed its Saetbyol-9 (“Morning Star-9”) attack drone launching an air-to-ground tactical cruise missile.

It also displayed production facilities for both low-cost suicide drones and standardised quadcopters, showing its capacity for mass production.

The exhibition was accompanied by a live-fire demonstration featuring 600mm super-large multiple-launch rocket systems capable of carrying nuclear warheads. Simulated strike runs targeted mock-ups of key South Korean military assets, including frontline guard posts and K9 self-propelled howitzers.

Defence experts warned that Seoul must overhaul its weapons acquisition system and rethink its counter-drone strategies to withstand Pyongyang’s shift towards high-volume, low-cost attrition warfare.

While North Korea’s command economy allowed it to develop and iterate prototypes quickly, South Korea’s complicated acquisition procedures and technical specifications have hindered domestic industry adoption, analysts said.

“Even though we cannot verify their performance, North Korea’s mass production of drones is worrisome for South Korea,” Shin said.

South Korea’s military lagged behind even in deploying small first-person-view (FPV) drones, which streamed real-time targeting feeds to an operator’s headset, Shin noted.

“South Korea’s military is still operating at the level of commercially available training drones when it comes to FPV systems,” Shin said. “The biggest obstacles are the lengthy process of bringing weapons into service and the poor state of the domestic drone ecosystem.”

Meanwhile, suicide drones under development in the South – which rely heavily on costly satellite data links and high-end sensors – cost hundreds of millions of won per unit, running counter to the cheap, mass-attrition economics governing modern warfare.

Hong Min, a senior research fellow at the Korea Institute for National Unification, said Pyongyang’s drones appeared to incorporate technical lessons from Russian operations in the Kursk region.

“They pose a threat to the South Korean military, which has built its counter-drone systems primarily around jamming,” Hong said.
