Experts have urged Seoul to fast-track domestic mass production of low-cost suicide drones while accelerating the development of its planned low-altitude missile defence system.

A South Korean defence ministry official acknowledged the bottlenecks, speaking on condition of anonymity.

“We recognise that delays in introducing advanced capabilities such as drones and artificial intelligence are a serious problem,” the official said. “Delays have occurred in the process of complying with procedures under laws concerning defence acquisition programmes. We intend to accelerate legislation and the adoption of civilian technologies.”

Crypto-financing for weapons

On Saturday, the FBI identified the North Korean cyber operation behind the Binance breach as “TraderTraitor,” a group previously associated with cryptocurrency theft carried out by North Korean hackers.

The agency said the group quickly swapped the stolen cryptocurrency into Ethereum before routing funds through decentralised finance platforms and mixing services to obscure the transaction trail.

“Stolen cryptocurrency is a crucial source for bankrolling weapons development for North Korea,” Shin said. “It needs dollars to buy parts and components such as batteries and motors that are also used for commercial purposes to build drones.”

The FBI’s announcement aligns with findings published by blockchain intelligence firm TRM Labs, which tracked an estimated US$6.36 billion taken from Binance wallets across 10 separate blockchains in roughly 20 minutes.

Major stablecoin issuers and blockchain networks, however, quickly froze roughly US$3 billion of the stolen funds.

According to TRM Labs data, North Korea-backed hackers have accounted for an unprecedented 85 per cent of all stolen cryptocurrency worldwide in 2026, up from just 7 per cent in 2020. The firm noted that five major infrastructure breaches – Binance, Bybit, Ronin, Bitget and DMM Bitcoin – accounted for US$9.1 billion of the estimated US$12.8 billion stolen by Pyongyang to date.

Lim Eul-chul, a professor at Kyungnam University’s Institute for Far Eastern Studies, said cryptocurrency theft was a “national strategic asset” that financed the advancement of weapons and sustained the regime.

“The leadership sticks to the belief that only overwhelming physical strength – nuclear and advanced weapons, hacking capabilities – can protect the regime.”

item.title: [SCMP] Will ‘strategic stability’ with China go out the window if Trump loses the midterms?
item.description:
US President Donald Trump is likely to continue on a path of trying to stabilise ties with Beijing – even if the Democrats flip the House of Representatives, according to analysts.

But they said if the Republicans lost control of the House in this week’s midterm elections, the framework of “strategic stability” agreed to by Washington and Beijing could be put to the test.

One Chinese academic warned that other Republicans could pose the biggest risk to Sino-American ties in Trump’s final two years in office if they demanded stronger curbs on technology and more support for Taiwan.
item.content:encoded:
US President Donald Trump is likely to continue on a path of trying to stabilise ties with Beijing – even if the Democrats flip the House of Representatives, according to analysts.

But they said if the Republicans lost control of the House in this week’s midterm elections, the framework of “strategic stability” agreed to by Washington and Beijing could be put to the test.

One Chinese academic warned that other Republicans could pose the biggest risk to Sino-American ties in Trump’s final two years in office if they demanded stronger curbs on technology and more support for Taiwan.

Trump has been able to handle China following his own playbook for much of the past two years, with the US Congress – under a unified Republican grip – barely standing in his way.

But there are numerous forecasts that the Democrats will win control of the House, if not both chambers of Congress, this week – though the contest for the Senate remains tight.

It comes as the Trump administration has been working with Beijing to keep strategic rivalry on a manageable track. The midterms are being held just weeks before Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping are due to meet in Shenzhen – their third face-to-face talks this year – and ahead of another expected meeting in Miami in December.

Ali Wyne, a senior research and advocacy adviser on US-China relations at the International Crisis Group, said given that Trump had paid little heed to congressional counsel on China thus far, the outcome of the midterms would be unlikely to change his approach.

“If anything, as he starts paying more attention to his prospective legacy, he is likely to invest more in strengthening his rapport with President Xi and consolidating the tactical thaw that presently exists between Washington and Beijing,” he said.

“With wars convulsing Europe and the Middle East, Trump will want to claim that he helped preserve a semblance of calm in Asia – the fulcrum of the global economy.”

Sun Chenghao, a fellow with Tsinghua University’s Centre for International Security and Strategy (CISS), also expected Trump could use negotiations with Beijing to demonstrate his ability to govern, and that he could pursue gains with China in procurement, investment and market access.

But he added that the next Congress could also question whether Trump was trading security restrictions for commercial benefit – potentially raising the political cost of carrying out any agreements reached with China.

“High-level engagement between China and the US is likely to continue but implementation by departments and specific cooperation could be more susceptible to interference,” Sun said.

He added that whether Trump could “translate stable relations with China into domestic political gains” would be key for ties, along with his willingness to “constrain hardliners within his own administration”.

Over the past two years, the Republican-controlled Congress has been seen as a junior partner to Trump, failing to provide an effective check on a series of controversial foreign policy moves, particularly the war against Iran.

Trump has also appeared to overrule China hawks in his administration and on Capitol Hill, notably stalling the announcement of a US$14 billion arms sale to Taiwan that was informally cleared by Congress in January.

There has been growing debate in recent months about whether a Democratic-led House – if not a Congress controlled by the party – would lead to renewed volatility in the US-China relationship by pushing more confrontational legislation targeting Beijing.

Wu Xinbo, dean of the Institute of International Studies at Fudan University in Shanghai, said the midterms were likely to affect US policy towards China and bilateral relations more “indirectly” than directly.

If the Democrats returned to power, China might not rank highly on their foreign policy agenda, according to Wu.

He said they could instead prioritise securing an agreement with Iran to help bring down oil prices, putting greater pressure on Israel over the conflict in Gaza and preventing Trump from striking a deal with Russia over the war in Ukraine at Kyiv’s expense.

Still, a Democratic comeback would weaken Trump politically, leaving him more reliant on the backing of Republican lawmakers, many of whom are China hawks and could then set conditions for their support.

Wu expected that they could press for more arms sales to Taiwan, greater US support for Tokyo amid its current tensions with Beijing and tighter tech restrictions on the Chinese side.

He said Trump might then feel compelled to take a harder line on those issues in exchange for support within his own party.

Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-governed island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons.

“If Trump takes a tougher line on China, that will undermine stability in China-US relations,” said Wu, who also heads Fudan’s Centre for American Studies (CAS).

He said the Democrats could also pile pressure on China if human rights issues surfaced, and they could push back if the new Board of Investment sought to ease restrictions on Chinese investment in the US.

China has not been a focus in the American midterms race. A poll conducted earlier this month by The Associated Press-NORC Centre for Public Affairs Research found that lowering the cost of living and winding down the war in Iran were among what voters most wanted from the next Congress.

Still, a bipartisan consensus in favour of a more competitive approach to China appears to have firmed up in the US.

The number of China-related bills introduced in Congress has risen in the past decade, ranging from trade, technology and education to Taiwan, Xinjiang and Tibet, according to separate studies published by Fudan’s CAS, Tsinghua’s CISS and Service Outsourcing, a journal affiliated with the commerce ministry.

Sun from Tsinghua noted that if the Democrats won control of either chamber, or both, it was likely they would more closely scrutinise Trump’s deals with China while continuing to back restrictions on technology, investment and supply chains.

He expected Trump would rely more on executive tools to advance negotiations and exert pressure on China.

“The elections will affect how policy is pursued more than it will change the direction of competition with China,” Sun said.

Wyne from the International Crisis Group did not expect congressional activity on China to change significantly but noted that a combination of factors could “create more political space for members of the next Congress to advocate alternative approaches”.

Those factors included “Trump’s unorthodoxy on China policy, warming American sentiment towards China, and growing anxiety among US allies and partners over Washington’s unreliability and unpredictability”.

During Trump’s first term as president, the Republicans lost control of the House in the 2018 midterms. The following two years saw US-China relations swing from a trade war to a trade deal before they deteriorated again in 2020.

Recent signs show strategic competition between the two powers remains fierce, including Washington designating Confucius Institutes as a national security threat and rolling out more sanctions and bans on Chinese companies in the past two weeks.

But a survey released earlier this month by the Chicago Council on Global Affairs found that 57 per cent of Americans polled in 2026 said the US should seek to work cooperatively with China rather than try to contain it – up from 40 per cent two years ago.

After they met in Beijing in May and in Washington in September, Trump and Xi agreed to build “a constructive relationship of strategic stability on the basis of respect, fairness and reciprocity”, according to statements from both sides.

Beijing has linked this vision to Trump’s presidency, saying it hopes the framework will guide bilateral ties “over the next three years and beyond”.

According to Wu, the midterms outcome could affect whether the Trump administration would continue to mention this concept. “US domestic politics has always been the biggest source of instability in China-US relations,” he said.

Still, he expected Trump would continue to seek stability in ties for the rest of his term. “This is in his interests,” he said.

Sun also said there was room to maintain the consensus on strategic stability.

“Trump needs a manageable external environment and also wants to preserve room for making deals through head-of-state diplomacy,” he said.

But Wyne noted that efforts to operationalise that commitment could falter if Trump perceived that Xi had “disrespected” him – as he did after the outbreak of Covid-19 – or if Xi believed that Trump was quietly preparing to launch a new assault on China’s economy.

item.title: [SCMP] How South Korea can play pivotal role in Philippines’ military modernisation drive
item.description:
The Philippines’ military modernisation drive could offer South Korea an opportunity to transform its role as a major arms supplier into a deeper defence partnership, analysts have said.

This prospect gained fresh momentum after Philippine Defence Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jnr and his South Korean counterpart, Kang Shin-chul, agreed to deepen cooperation in military modernisation, defence technology and joint training on the sidelines of an Asean security summit in Cebu last week.

Teodoro reaffirmed Manila’s readiness to work with Seoul last week, describing both countries as having “brother-and-sister” ties.
item.content:encoded:
The Philippines’ military modernisation drive could offer South Korea an opportunity to transform its role as a major arms supplier into a deeper defence partnership, analysts have said.

This prospect gained fresh momentum after Philippine Defence Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jnr and his South Korean counterpart, Kang Shin-chul, agreed to deepen cooperation in military modernisation, defence technology and joint training on the sidelines of an Asean security summit in Cebu last week.

Teodoro reaffirmed Manila’s readiness to work with Seoul last week, describing both countries as having “brother-and-sister” ties.

During his visit in September for the Seoul Defence Dialogue, he praised South Korea as a defence industry partner.

“The most important thing is that our countries are strategically aligned, which is why we have confidence in the Republic of Korea as a reliable partner for our defence modernisation,” he said in an interview with The Korea Herald that month.

As it strengthens its maritime posture, the Philippines has increasingly acquired South Korean defence equipment, including Korean-made FA-50 light combat aircraft and warships. “Almost all” new frigates and corvettes in the Philippine Navy were made in South Korea, Teodoro confirmed in Seoul, but stressed that the relationship between Manila and South Korea should move beyond acquisition towards co-production.

Ripe ground

Seoul has long viewed Manila as an attractive defence industry market.

“The Philippine economy is growing, and as the country faces increasing challenges from China, it requires more advanced weapon systems,” said Dongkeun Lee, a policy fellow at the Asia-Pacific Leadership Network. “This means that the Philippines is no longer simply seeking transfers of ageing, decommissioned vessels from South Korea but is increasingly interested in acquiring sophisticated weapons systems.”

History also plays a part. The Philippines was one of the few Southeast Asian countries that sent troops under the UN Command during the Korean war.

“When South Korea considers potential partners for military cooperation, their historical contributions during the Korean war often become an important factor. Given the Philippines’ historical role, this has helped strengthen military ties between the two countries,” Lee said.

The Philippines accounted for 18 per cent of South Korea’s arms exports between 2021 and 2025, making it the second-largest destination after Poland, according to Sanghun Seok, a senior associate fellow at the Royal United Services Institute.

And as exports to Poland mainly involved land-based weapons systems, the Philippines was an important hub for South Korea to showcase its naval and air platforms to wider export markets in the region, the security analyst said.

“These interests align with the Philippines’ need to strengthen its maritime and island defence capabilities, creating momentum for deeper, longer-term cooperation.”

Frequent leadership meetings this year, as well as an elevated bilateral strategic partnership in 2024 that included the inclusion of maintenance in the procurement arrangement, “all provide a framework for moving beyond one-off sales towards cooperation throughout the equipment’s life cycle”, Seok added.

Submarine potential

Two major developments worth watching were the Philippines’ future frigate and submarine acquisition programmes and the modernisation of the Subic Bay shipyard by Hyundai Heavy Industries, Lee said.

Both Hyundai Heavy Industries and its fellow South Korean firm, Hanwha Ocean, are in the running to supply the Philippines with warships and diesel-electric submarines.

“Considering that Hyundai Heavy Industries operates a shipyard in Subic Bay, its bid could also involve using the facility for future MRO activities. Hyundai Heavy Industries has already expressed interest in developing its Subic Bay shipyard into an MRO hub earlier this year,” Lee said, referring to maintenance, repair and operations.

Hanwha Ocean recently upgraded its submarine proposal to the Philippines, offering its Jangbogo-III PN, a Philippines-specific design based on the KSS-III submarine, as well as the construction of a submarine base, maintenance facilities and training for Filipino personnel.

“The success of the Philippine submarine programme will ultimately depend on whether it can go beyond a one-off arms sale to build a strategic partnership,” Seok said. “This is also why Hanwha Ocean, Hyundai Heavy Industries and competitors from other countries are offering packages that include not only submarines but also support for building the capabilities needed to operate and maintain them.”

The key consideration was “not simply the submarines themselves but the broader ecosystem required to build, operate and maintain them”, Lee said. “From this perspective, Hanwha Ocean has put forward an attractive proposal.”

Hanwha Ocean was more eager for a deal because, unlike Hyundai Heavy Industries, it did not have an established shipyard in the Philippines or a previous track record of delivering warships to the Philippine Navy, he added.

The outcome of the submarine procurement programme could influence which partner the Philippines worked with over the medium to long term, Seok said. “It could create the potential for South Korea-Philippines defence cooperation to move beyond existing platform sales and MRO towards a higher level of strategic and industrial cooperation.”

This could pave the way for technology transfer and training between South Korea and the Philippines – as Seoul has done with other countries.

In 2024, Hyundai Heavy Industries signed a US$463 million agreement to build four naval vessels locally in Peru, with the Korean side providing design and production know-how and technician training, while working with local equipment suppliers.

In Southeast Asia, Daewoo Shipbuilding & Marine Engineering, Hanwha Ocean’s predecessor, provided the technology for the local assembly and construction of Indonesia’s KRI Alugoro submarine. Delivered in 2021, it was the third submarine export to Indonesia.

“The extent to which these models can be applied directly to the Philippines would depend on the level of agreement that the two governments and the companies involved can reach. However, the current direction of bilateral defence cooperation suggests that there is growing potential,” Seok said.

However, Lee was more sceptical, believing that South Korean firms were more likely to “prioritise commercial shipbuilding, including merchant vessels such as oil tankers, rather than defence-related shipbuilding projects”.

“In fact, Hyundai Heavy Industries has already launched its first vessel built at the Subic Bay shipyard,” he said.

item.title: [SCMP] US midterm elections 2026: all you need to know
item.description:
Americans go to the polls on Tuesday, November 3, in midterm elections that could reshape the final two years of Donald Trump’s second term as president.

Control of both chambers of Congress is in play, along with 36 governorships. Polls suggest Democrats go into the vote with an advantage, but the outcome will hinge on a few dozen closely fought races.

More than 100 million people are expected to vote if turnout matches the 2022 midterms. By October 12, a record US$3.8 billion had been spent on political advertising, according to Reuters.
item.content:encoded:
Americans go to the polls on Tuesday, November 3, in midterm elections that could reshape the final two years of Donald Trump’s second term as president.

Control of both chambers of Congress is in play, along with 36 governorships. Polls suggest Democrats go into the vote with an advantage, but the outcome will hinge on a few dozen closely fought races.

More than 100 million people are expected to vote if turnout matches the 2022 midterms. By October 12, a record US$3.8 billion had been spent on political advertising, according to Reuters.

What are the midterms?

US presidents serve four-year terms. Midterm elections are held halfway through, every four years, in November. The president is not on the ballot.

Voters instead choose members of Congress, the national legislature that passes laws, approves federal spending and confirms the president’s top appointees, including judges and cabinet members. They also elect governors, state lawmakers and thousands of local officials.

The midterms are often treated as a referendum on the sitting president. The president’s party usually loses ground.

In 2018, during Trump’s first term, Democrats gained a net 40 seats in the House of Representatives and took control of the chamber.

What is being decided?

Congress has two chambers, and Republicans currently control both.

The House of Representatives has 435 members, all elected for two-year terms, so every seat is on the ballot. Republicans currently hold 218 seats and Democrats 214, meaning Democrats need a net gain of four seats to take control.

The Senate has 100 members serving six-year terms, with about a third elected every two years. This year, 35 seats are being contested. Republicans hold 53 seats and Democrats 47, so Democrats also need a net gain of four.

The House has two vacancies and one independent who sits with the Republicans. The Senate’s 47-member minority includes two independents who caucus with the Democrats.

If the Senate ends up split 50-50, Vice-President J.D. Vance casts the deciding vote, so Republicans would keep control.

This year’s Senate contests include two special elections in Ohio and Florida to fill seats vacated by Vance and Marco Rubio, who became secretary of state.

Voters in 36 states will also choose governors, who run state governments and oversee much of daily policy, from policing to healthcare. In 15 of those states, no incumbent is on the ballot.

Why it matters: if Democrats win either chamber, they can block Trump’s legislation and use congressional committees to investigate his administration.

Who runs the election?

Unlike Hong Kong, India, Britain or most other democracies, the US has no national body that organises or oversees its elections.

The US Constitution gives the 50 states primary authority over the “times, places and manner” of elections. Congress has some power to set national rules and has used it for landmark laws such as the 1965 Voting Rights Act. But the states and their counties do the actual work of holding elections.

The Associated Press counts more than 10,000 separate voting jurisdictions across the country, each operating under its state’s laws and, in some places, local rules too. Most are counties, where an elected official such as a county clerk typically oversees the vote with a mix of paid staff and volunteer poll workers.

That means rules differ from place to place. Some states require photo identification at polling stations, and others do not. Some mail a ballot to every registered voter, while others allow postal voting only with a valid reason. Voting machines, ballot designs and deadlines all vary.

In most states, the official who oversees elections is the secretary of state, an elected post that has nothing to do with foreign affairs.

Election security experts say the patchwork system makes large-scale fraud very difficult. Rigging a national result would require many officials in many counties, often from both parties, to break the law together and keep quiet.

The question of who controls elections has become a political flashpoint this year. In March, Trump signed an executive order directing the US Postal Service to deliver mail ballots only to voters on government-approved lists. Trump has said, without evidence, that mail voting enables fraud.

States challenged the order in court. In September, the US Supreme Court refused to let the Postal Service restrictions take effect for this election, meaning mail voting will work largely as it has in the past.

Why won’t we know the result on election night?

US television networks and news agencies such as the Associated Press “call” or project winners on election night using partial counts from local electoral authorities and statistical models. Those projections are not official results. Close races can take days to call, and certifying the official results takes weeks.

Several factors contribute to the wait.

Postal ballots take longer to process: officials first record each returned envelope and compare the voter’s signature with the one on file, a check that also guards against anyone voting twice. Only then can officials open the envelope and scan the ballot.

Some states cannot start early: about half of the states allow officials to process postal ballots days or weeks before election day, so those votes can be released soon after polls close. Others, including the swing states of Pennsylvania and Wisconsin, do not let officials open postal ballot envelopes until the morning of election day.

Ballots can arrive after polling day: in California, postal ballots count if they are postmarked by election day and arrive within seven days. In June, the US Supreme Court confirmed that states may count such late-arriving ballots.

Voters can fix mistakes: in Arizona, for example, voters whose signatures are questioned have up to five days after the election to confirm or correct them.

Some races need extra rounds: Maine and Alaska, both with competitive Senate races, use ranked-choice voting. Voters rank candidates in order of preference, and if no one wins a majority, the count continues in subsequent rounds. In Georgia, a race in which no candidate wins a majority goes to a run-off, which could push the result into December.

The order in which votes are counted can also cause dramatic swings. Republican supporters tend to vote in person, while postal ballots counted later often favour Democratic candidates. Early returns can therefore favour Republicans before the lead shifts, a pattern analysts call the “red mirage”.

Trump has seized on slow counts before, accusing Democrats, without evidence, of trying to “steal” California’s primary election in June, for example.

The final balance of power may not be clear for some time. California, which has several competitive House seats, gives counties until December 3 to certify their results. If Alaska’s Senate race is close, NPR reported, the whole country could wait weeks to learn which party controls the Senate.

What are the big issues?

The cost of living: in a recent Reuters/Ipsos poll, about one in two registered voters said rising costs would weigh most heavily on their vote. Asked which household expenses Congress should focus on, respondents most often pointed to healthcare, petrol, groceries and housing.

Tariffs: Trump’s import levies have become unusually prominent in the campaign. A conservative think tank, the National Taxpayers Union Foundation, estimated they would cost the average household US$820 this year.

Democrats blame tariffs for rising prices. Republicans have run advertisements accusing Democrats who oppose the tariffs of siding with China over American workers.

Immigration: voters have tended to trust Republicans more on border security, according to Fox News polling this year, which also found 59 per cent of voters thought Immigration and Customs Enforcement, the federal agency carrying out Trump’s deportation drive, had been too aggressive.

Redistricting: the boundaries of House constituencies are normally redrawn once a decade, after the census. But after Trump urged Texas Republicans last year to redraw their map to win more seats, both parties joined an unusual mid-decade scramble. Ten states now have new maps.

An NBC News analysis in June found the new boundaries could give Republicans up to 16 seats, against six for Democrats. Forecasters have since suggested the effect may be small. The national mood favours Democrats strongly enough to offset much of the gain, Decision Desk HQ, an election data firm, said in September.

Where the race stands: Democrats lead by about 8.7 percentage points on the “generic ballot”, a poll question asking which party voters prefer for Congress, according to the PollCheck average on October 27. A Reuters/Ipsos poll the same day put Trump’s approval rating at 32 per cent.

item.title: [SCMP] Let them play: the Hong Kong playgrounds teaching children to take risks
item.description:
A climbing frame, a two-metre slide and a handful of seats made to resemble animals that bounce around on a spring: Hong Kong playgrounds often leave children – and their guardians – underwhelmed, but those championing a new era of play hope to fix that.

Spanning 15,000 sq ft, the OC Commons Playground, situated next to the Olympian City shopping complex in Tai Kok Tsui, is part of a recent wave of playgrounds in Hong Kong – both public and private – that hark back to the free, unstructured play that was briefly encouraged during the late 1960s and 70s. Its bamboo-shaped poles with footholds, trampoline-helmed hills and metal plates that chime when stepped on have been designed to develop mobility, cognition, sensory awareness, problem-solving skills and tolerance for risk. But this example remains an outlier, and unless greater diversity in design is encouraged across the city, play areas may remain shackled to a predictable homogeneity that fails to ignite the imagination of children or test their appetite for risk.

Introduced in 1929, Hong Kong’s first urban playgrounds were havens for rowdy, unsupervised children amid economic hardship. After the Pacific War (1941-45) during World War II, as the colonial government began building housing estates for a mushrooming population, playgrounds opened at the bases of residential blocks, many offering little more than the four “S”s: slides, see-saws, swings and sandpits. Although they were prominent fixtures across the city’s public-housing developments, playgrounds were often treated as an afterthought by architects and engineers.
item.content:encoded:
A climbing frame, a two-metre slide and a handful of seats made to resemble animals that bounce around on a spring: Hong Kong playgrounds often leave children – and their guardians – underwhelmed, but those championing a new era of play hope to fix that.

Spanning 15,000 sq ft, the OC Commons Playground, situated next to the Olympian City shopping complex in Tai Kok Tsui, is part of a recent wave of playgrounds in Hong Kong – both public and private – that hark back to the free, unstructured play that was briefly encouraged during the late 1960s and 70s. Its bamboo-shaped poles with footholds, trampoline-helmed hills and metal plates that chime when stepped on have been designed to develop mobility, cognition, sensory awareness, problem-solving skills and tolerance for risk. But this example remains an outlier, and unless greater diversity in design is encouraged across the city, play areas may remain shackled to a predictable homogeneity that fails to ignite the imagination of children or test their appetite for risk.

Introduced in 1929, Hong Kong’s first urban playgrounds were havens for rowdy, unsupervised children amid economic hardship. After the Pacific War (1941-45) during World War II, as the colonial government began building housing estates for a mushrooming population, playgrounds opened at the bases of residential blocks, many offering little more than the four “S”s: slides, see-saws, swings and sandpits. Although they were prominent fixtures across the city’s public-housing developments, playgrounds were often treated as an afterthought by architects and engineers.

A major advancement in playground design came in the 60s, when features such as cement bridges, mazes and tunnels were fitted into the play areas of residential developments in Kennedy Town and Tsuen Wan, and on the Kai Tak Estate, writes arts practitioner Helen Fan Lok-yi, in her book The Abstract Playscapes of Hong Kong (2023). But the most representative sculptural play space arrived in 1969, when American artist Paul Selinger’s Shek Lei Playground introduced Kwai Chung to monumental forms that resembled a perforated belt, toppled chess pieces and cylinders stacked like waves: installations that were intended to stimulate free play and exploration. Although Selinger “failed in replicating his Shek Lei Playground model in Hong Kong”, writes Fan, “he influenced subsequent Hong Kong designers to experiment with mixing art, landscaping and play”.

In the late 70s and early 80s, however, mounting lawsuits over playground injuries in the United States cast doubt on the safety of sculptural playgrounds, a cautiousness that spread to Hong Kong. As the city tended to import its play equipment from the West, standardised, certified, mass-produced equipment prized for durability and ease of maintenance became the norm. Shek Lei Playground met its unheralded end in the 90s.

According to Fan, the shift suited Hong Kong families, who were increasingly hiring foreign domestic helpers to care for their children. In a rapidly developing city where parents were rarely supervising playground time, creativity came second to safety.

Nonetheless, in 1987, the non-governmental, non-profit Playright Children’s Play Association was established to promote and safeguard children’s right to play. Soon after, in 1989, Playright opened Hong Kong’s first “accessible” play area, King’s Park Children’s Playground, in Yau Ma Tei. Designed to include children with physical, sensory or developmental disabilities, it brought a rack of tubular audio instruments, a “touch wall”, strong sculptural qualities and diverse textures to engage young visitors.

In 2018, Playright introduced the city’s first “inclusive” playground – one that fosters shared social integration as well as multi-ability play – in Tuen Mun. Here, the recreational facilities include a water-play zone, an undulating area, trampolines and musical playthings, such as percussion instruments. Between those two openings, the term “free play” had become popular among parents and educators, who believed benefits such as enhanced concentration and interest in learning would follow when children could choose their own tools, ways to play, playmates and activity areas.

One year later, then-chief executive Carrie Lam Cheng Yuet-ngor announced the revitalisation of more than 170 public play areas managed by the Leisure and Cultural Services Department (LCSD) by 2024, “to make [Hong Kong’s] public play spaces more innovative and fun as well as to meet the aspirations of local residents”. Only 18 have been revamped so far, though, officials having cited the Covid-19 pandemic and the time needed to consult residents and process their requests as reasons for the delays.

Jacky Chan Wai-hin, head of play-environment development at Playright, which has been a consultant on at least one of the government’s 170 projects, says playgrounds support social well-being and resilience, and they also make sense for property developers eager to extend the duration of customer visits to shopping centres.

Since its Playright-designed OC Commons Playground opened earlier this year, Olympian City has seen a 10 per cent rise in footfall, attracting families from as far away as Tung Chung, says Bella Chhoa Peck-lim, chief commercial officer at Sino Group.

“OC Commons is in a great location because it’s right next to a mall that, in this case, acts more like a community living room, where people do more than just shop, but hang out,” says Chan. “Olympian City also has indoor bathrooms and resting spots that are paramount to a good playground.”

Other shopping plazas banking on the appeal of playgrounds include the Tsz Wan Shan Shopping Centre, where, in 2020, a water-play zone and climbing nets were added to the fifth floor. A year later, the 18,000 sq ft Moko Park reopened in Mong Kok’s Moko mall, boasting Hong Kong’s longest climbing wall and slides of varying heights.

Alan Cheung Kwok-lun, co-founder and managing director of One Bite Design Studio and the creative mind behind T Town’s The Wonderful Town of Play, in Tin Shui Wai, says the growing involvement of private developers with strict marketing goals adds pizzazz: “Private sectors’ No 1 priority is the ‘wow factor’; they want Hong Kong’s tallest, longest something whereas government playgrounds don’t care for marketing gimmicks.”

T Town’s 32,000 sq ft, Hong Kong Wetland Park-themed playground opened in December last year on the roof of the mall. Since its debut, footfall on the building’s second floor, connecting to the playground, has doubled, according to Katherine Lo Yan-kay, director of asset management (Hong Kong) at Link Asset Management, the developer behind T Town, drawing unprecedented numbers of visitors from nearby Yuen Long and Tuen Mun.

Like OC Commons, The Wonderful Town of Play has an adventure tower, a rope pyramid, a trampoline and a tyre swing. Cheung’s design also incorporates facts and graphics about the nearby conservation park and its wildlife: a large model of a black-faced spoonbill is perched above the vertical climber, for instance, and a three-dimensional hopscotch game, Mudskipper Jump, is paired with an information plaque about the amphibious fish.

While Cheung understands children are unlikely to visit a playground to learn about wetland species, the theme gives the space a distinct identity and offers guardians something to read while they are supervising their charges. Such intergenerational touches – even those as simple as increased shade and seating areas – are crucial to sustaining the relevance of a playground, he says. “Why can’t teenagers and adults play as well? We have this misconception because our society hasn’t catered to this demographic in our playground designs,” he says. “For the elderly, this could mean including simple workout equipment placed in spots where they can see their grandchildren. Meanwhile, teenagers may want nooks where they can hang out.”

A sense of ownership also encourages repeat visits. Another of Cheung’s projects – Siu Hei Court Play Space, a Tuen Mun playground refurbished in 2020 – is decorated with tiles adorned with artwork by nursery-school and kindergarten students. Although the play area may not be suitable for them just yet, Cheung hopes that by “making the space feel relevant”, those children will return as regular visitors when they are older.

Ownership also informs the 2024 Well-being Design Guide, a framework launched by the Housing Bureau and the Hong Kong Housing Authority. It intends, with the aid of feedback from residents, to transform public housing from blocks of basic shelter into vibrant communities.

In some cases, the reference suggests switching out drab playground sets for what Housing Department chief architect Tim Li Man-wai calls “communal fitness playscapes”, which welcome cross-generational activities rather than serving only as a children’s playground. Li sees this shift not as a loss of play space, but as a way to maximise use. He points to Yip Wong Estate, in Tuen Mun, where, instead of a conventional basketball court, netless rims were installed at various heights against a colourful, numbered wall. “Older children come here for basketball competitions, but the lower rims also invite young kids who may otherwise be deterred by the high hoops. Here, they can see who can dunk a ball into a hoop with a higher number, or a specific colour; they can really stretch their imagination,” says Li.

Before the new initiative, Li explains, residents’ feedback was collected through district councils, and projects tended to conform to a top-down approach. Now, discussions, interviews and workshops are conducted from the ground up, to identify pain points and possible remedies. “Society is changing, and so should the way we engage with our people when designing their living spaces. Before, residents didn’t have time to engage with us – they were likely too busy making a living and were happy with just a roof over their heads. However, with more public spaces and a widespread use of social media, people are more willing to voice their concerns.

“When residents are a part of the design process, they have ownership about what appears in that space and are therefore more accepting of the final product,” he says.

Ownership implies users’ trust in the designers to improve their lives. But designers, too, must have faith that their spaces will be treated with respect. Before its relaunch in 2021, Yi Pei Square Playground, in Tsuen Wan, shared space with a four-metre-wide emergency-vehicle access. A meaningful redesign meant removing the gate that separated it from shops.

“Park-goers and nearby residents were worried that, if we removed the gate, shop owners would spill their belongings into the park area,” says Kay Chan Wan-ki, a freelance product designer and community-interaction planner who worked on the redesign. “But we believed that people’s sense of discipline and respect for the common good would improve if they had well-designed public spaces that met their needs.”

Following the redesign, frequent policing by officials kept the shopkeepers in line.

“You can’t please everyone, but ultimately, it was a change for the better,” says Kay Chan.

Despite the innovation evident in parts of the city, she laments a continuing lack of creativity, adventure and nature in play. Playright’s Jacky Chan shares her concerns, adding that the city’s acceptance of, and education around, unconventional playgrounds must keep pace with the LCSD’s refurbishments, or risk a return to boring uniformity.

“A playground is not a stand-alone place. First, the public must get used to these new designs. Asians have a concept of ‘as safe as possible’, but those in the West believe in ‘as safe as necessary’. A safe playground isn’t meant to eliminate all risks – only the lethal, seriously dangerous ones. Little bumps and bruises are inevitable when children explore.”

Chan’s optimism is fuelled by past victories: “When sandpits first appeared in Hong Kong’s playgrounds, they were littered with cigarette butts and – in some cases – needles. This rarely happens any more, which is a great example of public education making enormous strides.”

Acceptance is one challenge, but construction and administration are quite another. “We face barriers from developers, the government, management and operational teams, because when these non-conventional playground facilities malfunction, it’s not just replacing a loose nail,” says Chan. “We must also look at workmanship, construction companies and suppliers. Do they have the know-how to make these new-age playgrounds? Only a few fields are related to playground design: architecture, landscape design and engineering. We can instil these concepts of risk, adventure and free play in students [of those disciplines] early on.”

Last December, Playright opened Hung Hom’s Dream Together Playground, which is anything but ordinary. As one of a rotating theme, until October 14, the park hosted a “pirate ship”, whose wooden bow was scribbled with children’s paintings, its flag and mast a sparkly sheet of tarp and an upside-down table. Scattered throughout were arm hooks fashioned out of tinfoil and half bottles, swords carved out of wood and “cannons” made from hole-punchers and plastic lids. Its outdoor expanse included sandpits and structures that were meant to be deconstructed and reassembled for all sorts of play. High steps and slim balancing beams pushed children beyond their comfort zone.

Chan calls this style of playground “half-and-half”, wherein children are tasked with co-creating their version of fun. Colouring on the floor is as encouraged as crafting a pulley system to deliver make-believe takeaway boxes. Since every visitor is a co-creator, the settings keep refreshing. (Another thing that’s unusual about the Dream Together Playground is that there is a charge to enter parts of the 23,680 sq ft site; HK$240 for one child-and-adult pair covers on-site supervision staff, materials and the costs of periodically changing the theme of the space.)

“Playright has been pushing this project for the past 20 years,” says Chan. “A playground like this is very rare in our city, but it’s a start.”

item.title: [SCMP] TV showman Robert Chua spells out his vision for his vast collection of Chinese antiquities
item.description:
Robert Chua Wah-peng does not have the air of a stereotypical collector.

He does not demand of you the donning of cotton gloves or scrubbing of fingernails before touching his Chinese antiquities; he excitedly invites you to pick up vases and vessels with your bare hands; he encourages you to engage with his acquisitions up close. Most of them are not sequestered away behind glass or acrylic.

He also does not have an exact number for how large his collection is.
item.content:encoded:
Robert Chua Wah-peng does not have the air of a stereotypical collector.

He does not demand of you the donning of cotton gloves or scrubbing of fingernails before touching his Chinese antiquities; he excitedly invites you to pick up vases and vessels with your bare hands; he encourages you to engage with his acquisitions up close. Most of them are not sequestered away behind glass or acrylic.

He also does not have an exact number for how large his collection is.

“Could be hundreds of thousands of pieces,” he muses when asked.

Originally from Singapore, Chua began collecting in 1967 – the year he arrived in Hong Kong – but it was not until his first visit to mainland China, in 1979, that he got serious about his hobby. He became a regular presence at the antiques dealers’ shops on Hong Kong’s Hollywood Road, sweeping through new shipments twice a week for decades, like clockwork, buying entire lots – everything from late-Qing ceramics bearing illustrated foo dogs in bright orange and terracotta “stickmen” from the Han period to wooden mooncake moulds and snuff bottles.

In his home in Kowloon, he has a room dedicated to blue-and-white porcelain from the Ming and Qing dynasties to the Republic era, rows of Chinese wedding cabinets heaving with tableware, wardrobes bursting with vibrant stoneware and jars, a corridor with more than 180 horse sculptures, shelves groaning beneath fossilised dinosaur eggs and Neolithic pottery, and drawers holding delicate jade accessories and brass buttons. Neolithic, Warring States, Han, Sui, Tang, Song, Yuan, Ming, Qing – Chua’s collection reads like a chronicle. Inching along narrow pathways cleared between stacks for necessity’s sake, he is talking a mile a minute, propelled by obvious fervour, sharing historical facts, stories about how he obtained an artefact, the technique used to make it.

Chua is an oddity among his peers in the collecting community in that his incentive to collect really isn’t that deep. “Honestly, I don’t know,” he shrugs. “I just love beautiful things. Never do I buy anything and at any moment say, ‘I bought this for HK$1,000. One day, maybe it will fetch me HK$5,000.’ Never. I buy for the beauty. And if I see something that is lovely, I’ll buy 30 of them, to share with people.”

Among Chua’s extensive accumulation, one theme stands out, not only in quantity but also in peculiarity: his collection of ancient Chinese mingqi – “spirit objects”, traditionally placed in tombs as funerary items to comfort the deceased in the afterlife. As far as the eye can see, there are small-scale models of dwellings, animals, furniture and carriages, as well as figures of guardians and attendants.

For visitors familiar with Chinese customs, it might come as a shock to see Chua living among mingqi. Despite their exquisite craftsmanship and three-colour sancai glaze, keeping burial goods intended for the dead in one’s home is thought to invite misfortune and disruptive yin energy into the household.

Chua is aware of the taboo, but it doesn’t faze him. “I am a bit Western in that sense,” he says. “Western collectors don’t mind antiques like these, but Chinese collectors are too superstitious to want them, so that made it easier for me to acquire them; the demand was lower and they were not difficult to source.

I have thousands of happy spirits at home. I’m not worried about anything – there’s so much company. It’s always a party

Robert Chua

“But I’m happy. I have thousands of happy spirits at home. I’m not worried about anything – there’s so much company. It’s always a party,” he laughs.

Indeed, Chua has a penchant for entertaining and hosting. His calendar is ordinarily filled with visits, events, meetings, lunches and dinners, both personal and professional. He likes to receive guests in the sunroom. He has a talent for driving conversations, and his candour and quick wit work in tandem to put people at ease.

To understand and appreciate Chua’s gravitational pull towards people and telling stories, taking a gander at his own history pulls back the curtains.

Chua, 80, made his name in television broadcasting. His first job, as a property assistant at ADS Channel 7 in Adelaide, Australia, in 1964, sparked an enduring fascination with the industry. After rotating through several positions at the Australian network, he returned to Singapore two years later, to produce for Radio Television Singapore, gaining experience in light entertainment.

It wouldn’t be long before another door opened for Chua: he was offered the role of senior production executive at Hong Kong’s TVB in 1967, to help set up its first colour-television station. At just 21 years old, he created Enjoy Yourself Tonight, which became the city’s longest-running live variety programme, airing more than 6,610 episodes between 1967 and 1994 on the TVB Jade channel.

Colin Bednall, the then-general manager of TVB, “trusted me to do the job. Had I failed, he would have lost his job for sure. But luckily, everything went so well. I am grateful to him”, Chua says of the opportunity extended to him despite his age.

As someone who avowedly attributes his life’s trajectory to an improbable series of events and a chain of people betting on him against all odds, Chua has held up his end of the bargain to deliver on those instincts and that faith in his potential.

Enjoy Yourself Tonight garnered him acclaim, promotions and opportunities. Chua rose through the ranks to serve as the special assistant to the managing director and also brought the Miss Hong Kong Pageant to the local network in 1973, before leaving TVB to start his own production house. Back then, freelance television facilities were few and far between, due to the high upfront costs of launching one. Coupled with its founder’s established reputation, Robert Chua Production House (RCP) readily landed work with broadcasters, agencies and corporate clients to do commercials, shows, documentaries and the like.

Chua expanded his business to the mainland in 1979, brokering deals on behalf of foreign advertisers looking to gain a foothold in the market.

Over a decades-long career in television, Chua put his mark on numerous other ventures, but his success and tenacious pursuit of achieving “firsts” did not come without challenges. In March 1995, after more than three months of experimental screenings, his Chinese-language China Entertainment Television Broadcast (CETV) channel began airing around Asia, showing original productions, films, soap operas, children’s series and more through 24 hours of daily programming. CETV reached millions of households across the region over the 21 years it was in operation, but it also proved to be one of the most difficult periods of Chua’s life.

Already burdened by the stress of keeping the station financially afloat, in January 1999, he suffered from a build-up of excess blood fluid in his brain, which required urgent surgery. While recuperating at home – his first time off since his marriage, in 1974, to his former assistant at TVB, Peggy Jen Ping-ping – and spending more time among his collection, by then already formidable, Chua began to view his antiques in a different light. Damaged and incomplete pieces caught his attention in particular, planting a seed for a new artistic vision: to flip the script on the notion that, in their marred condition, these objects were useless or to be discarded, and revive them through novel methods.

The resulting “Antique Arts” is part of Chua’s mission to find new meaning for his pieces. “An antique does not lose its soul because it is broken,” he explains, and neither should they be valued only for what they once were. A shattered vessel or a shard of porcelain is not just “a remnant of the past. It is a survivor. It carries memory, human touch, craftsmanship, cultural identity and the passage of time”.

Rather than restoring them to their original state, Chua believes that transforming them into new artworks allows them to keep existing through a modern narrative. Combining periods, dynasties, shapes, textures, mediums and contexts, his “Antique Arts” tell a fresh story, simultaneously embodying a metaphor for Chua’s own journey of recovery. (He would go on to have a second brain surgery, in 2008, informing his decision to take a step back from his company.)

Where collectors, dealers and auction houses see broken antiquities as defective, Chua thinks of them as a continuation. “Antique Arts” is his attempt to symbolically collaborate with the “many hands” of bygone makers, resulting in a creative dialogue across time. A Song dynasty pot fragment is paired with Neolithic earthenware to depict the pouring of tea, bridging thousands of years; the remaining handle of an ancient jug is juxtaposed with a modern ink painting to “complete the gaps” of the one-time vessel, leading to an abstract installation.

Chua’s personal relationship with the material feeds into his creation process, too. Anonymous objects they are not. He has lived with them, studied them and cared for them across decades, forming an intimate connection with the pieces.

From a slim case, he pulls out slender sticks of ivory, their tips wrapped in thread, ending in thin brushes of fine hair. Qiancao – cricket ticklers – are tools used in cricket combat, to goad the insects into fighting each other for sport.

“When I have an antique, like this one, I wonder who it belonged to. I imagine what their lives were like. Everything I look at, everything I touch, I feel someone in my mind – the people who used these objects, these pieces that lived in their homes. Frankly, that’s better to me than something that’s brand-new.” He continues, “How much is the value of a piece? It’s not so much about the actual monetary value, but how much it really means to you. ‘Expensive’ is in the mind of the person.

“For most collectors, when something breaks, it’s gone forever. But for me, if something breaks somehow, my consolation is that I can give it a new life. What I have, what’s broken, I try to put them together anyway. I never break anything on purpose. Sometimes, it just happens. But I wait for the right moment. I find the right pieces that will come together, and if they don’t, I won’t rush it.”

As he left broadcasting behind, the “right pieces” ended up falling into place, anyway. Chua’s affinity for entertainment, connecting with an audience and shaping narratives continued to find ways to manifest through different avenues.

In 2013, Chua followed his entrepreneurial nose and snapped up the Asia-Pacific franchising rights to Tim Ho Wan, often hailed as the cheapest Michelin-star restaurant in the world, launching it in Singapore with his brother, Harry Chua Wah-eng. He credits “luck and fate” as the reason for their winning bid – at the time, neither sibling had any experience in the food and beverage industry to speak of – but it was, once again, trust that paved the way to the next chapter.

“At TVB, [Bednall] shouldn’t have given me Enjoy Yourself Tonight, and likewise with Tim Ho Wan, they shouldn’t have given it to me with all the food and beverage professionals out there, but they did,” he told the South China Morning Post in 2024.

Tim Ho Wan co-founder Mak Kwai-pui was a fan of Enjoy Yourself Tonight, and Chua’s unconventional thinking – unhampered by orthodox restaurant strategies – allowed him to be bold and brave. When Tim Ho Wan arrived in Singapore, Chua positioned the brand as an elevated dining experience, growing its footprint to more than 40 outposts. Kam’s Roast (known in Hong Kong as Kam’s Roast Goose) followed in 2016.

“Entertainment and food are the same to me,” he explains. “It’s a people’s business. I look at food as my programmes and I look at my chef as my director.”

Four years later, he founded Joy Luck Teahouse, a chain of food kiosks specialising in Hong Kong-style cha chaan teng snacks, and in 2021, he launched Sinstant, a gourmet line of ready-to-eat and -cook Asian meals designed for home consumption.

At 80, most people would slow down. But Chua, being the “ideas guy”, has not stopped thinking about the future. As he considers his collection, and the richness it holds, there is but one thing left to do with it: share it with the world.

He has laid out the blueprint for his vision, combining his passion for food and Chinese antiques: an all-day restaurant-cum-museum, where the cuisine echoes a rotating curation of pieces from his personal Aladdin’s cave. Imagined as a “cultural-dining landmark”, Treasure of China is designed as an immersive destination to close the distance between heritage, gastronomy and storytelling. Guests will indulge in refined dishes, surrounded by centuries-old artefacts, with restaurant staff providing the backgrounds behind each object to engage visitors.

“Many restaurants, hotels and clubs have their own collection, but the art is just part of the furniture. It’s not interactive. It’s not engaging. It doesn’t change,” says Chua. “Here, the artwork is part of the meal. Whatever you see and touch has a story.”

Chinese history and culture shape each pillar of the museum-restaurant, down to the beverage programme, which will exclusively feature Chinese wines, baijiu, huangjiu and teas. Chua’s “Antique Arts” creations are also planned to be part of the display, and select works – both ancient and “new” – will be made available for purchase, with a percentage of the proceeds donated to charities.

Regional Chinese flavours, ranging from Cantonese and Sichuan to Jiangsu, Fujian and more, will make up the concept’s culinary foundations. But something that is, perhaps, unexpected is that Chua intends to place the experience in the “affordable premium” bracket, offering Michelin-level dining at accessible prices, making good on his ambition to embrace and give back to the wider community.

“Bringing art to a greater audience and developing a concept that not only preserves history, but presents it as a new experience that people can engage with, breaks down barriers,” says Chua. “Antiques are precious because they are records of history, but that doesn’t mean you can’t engage with them on an interpersonal level, because that’s what really creates a connection for people to appreciate them.”

With more than 200 seats envisioned in the estimated 7,000 sq ft floor plan, interactive elements – such as hands-on “touchable history” encounters to hold fossilised dinosaur eggs – and aesthetic spatial design engineered for the social-media generation, Chua plans to appeal to residents and tourists alike.

Treasure of China feels like a natural next step for Chua, whose joy in amassing antiques is matched only by the unadulterated delight he expresses when sharing their stories. On our tour of his “home museum”, through rows of gleaming porcelain and stoic figurines, it is his enthusiasm that leaves the biggest impression.

But this project is not Chua’s alone to bring to fruition. Adviser Jacco Klip, a Dutch F&B professional with nearly 40 years of experience in opening and managing restaurants, provides guidance on the charitable arm of the business. Meanwhile, Choi Biu, a veteran of Hong Kong’s dining scene and long-time member of the Shun Tak Fraternal Association and local Shunde community, and Lawrence Chong, a property-development consultant who has held positions at Sino Land and Galaxy Entertainment Group, serve as co-founder and special adviser to Chua, respectively.

Chua’s concept is still in its early stages, and there’s a lot of work ahead. His collection needs to be catalogued, the search for a suitable venue is ongoing and most of the items he owns hold taboo connotations within Chinese cultural norms, raising questions about how guests will perceive the curated works and whether superstitions around their provenance will win out against curiosity. Not to mention, there are like-minded backers to find and convince.

None of these hurdles seem to be stopping the lifelong pioneer from forging ahead to secure interest and investors in Treasure of China. He has already mapped out a multi-stream revenue model, which includes brand collaborations, merchandising and licensing – a “gastro-tainment” approach, so to speak.

“We’re looking for people with passion,” Chua says. “When I do any business, profit is not my No 1 priority. You must make sure you do a good job. If you think profit comes first, you’ll never be successful, because you’re trying to compromise. I want the partners to feel proud of how they are contributing to society.”

Whether the museum-restaurant sets its roots down in Hong Kong or Macau is still to be determined, but Chua believes that the objective of his cultural destination – to entertain, educate and connect – aligns with either city’s broader tourism goals.

“Over the years, I have always believed in creating ‘firsts’ that change how people think and experience things”

Robert Chua

Whatever shape his new project takes, Chua’s mission has not changed. From “Antique Arts” to Treasure of China, giving the pieces in his collection a new voice remains central to his pursuits, as a poignant reminder that history can be palpably felt, reimagined and revived. “Over the years, I have always believed in creating ‘firsts’ that change how people think and experience things,” he says.

“With art, if it’s something you like, you enjoy, you appreciate, it doesn’t have to be that profound, right? I look at these objects, and some of them look so rough. But to me, they are beautiful because they hold so many stories and years of life.”

item.title: [SCMP] First Look: Yurt, Hong Kong’s ‘first modern Central Asian restaurant’
item.description:
While Hongkongers scout remote destinations for their first holiday in 2026, a journey of discovery for the palate is now on offer closer to home. Yurt, newly opened on SoHo’s Elgin Street, is bringing the hitherto unexplored flavours of Central Asia to the heart of the city, proving you don’t need a boarding pass to be an adventurous gourmand.

In a dining scene that prides itself on diversity, Central Asia has remained conspicuously absent from the many menus on offer in Hong Kong. For the founders behind Yurt, filling that gap has been a project a long time in the making.

“This idea has been in the back of all our minds for years, even before we met,” they share. The catalyst was when Xeniya Tregubenko was introduced to fellow Kazakh native Ali Nuraly through a mutual friend early last year. What started as a casual chat quickly touched on a common dream – to introduce Central Asian flavours to Hong Kong.
item.content:encoded:
While Hongkongers scout remote destinations for their first holiday in 2026, a journey of discovery for the palate is now on offer closer to home. Yurt, newly opened on SoHo’s Elgin Street, is bringing the hitherto unexplored flavours of Central Asia to the heart of the city, proving you don’t need a boarding pass to be an adventurous gourmand.

In a dining scene that prides itself on diversity, Central Asia has remained conspicuously absent from the many menus on offer in Hong Kong. For the founders behind Yurt, filling that gap has been a project a long time in the making.

“This idea has been in the back of all our minds for years, even before we met,” they share. The catalyst was when Xeniya Tregubenko was introduced to fellow Kazakh native Ali Nuraly through a mutual friend early last year. What started as a casual chat quickly touched on a common dream – to introduce Central Asian flavours to Hong Kong.

For both, Yurt marks a distinctive new life chapter. For Tregubenko, a seven-year Hong Kong resident, the restaurant is about “putting down permanent roots” for her culture in her adopted city. For Nuraly, a more recent arrival, it signals “the exciting beginning of my entrepreneurial journey”.

Although the pair were confident in the appeal of their plan, Nuraly admits that taking the first concrete step towards opening Yurt was daunting. “Introducing a completely unknown cuisine … it was a leap of faith,” he says.

The greater challenge, however, was one of cultural translation. “It’s one thing to cook the dishes; it’s another to bring the spirit,” Nuraly explains.

The man tasked with helping achieve this goal is head chef Marat Zakaryayev, another native of Kazakhstan whose culinary experience runs from Almaty to London. “My goal is for the first-time taster to understand our homeland through its flavours,” he says.

Completing this culinary bridge is pastry chef Anna Lobanova. Formerly pastry chef at Whey, she now works from her base in Kazakhstan to create desserts that are authentically Central Asian yet designed to resonate locally.

Diners walking into Yurt get an immediate sense of Central Asia with a warm, cosy dining room featuring atmospheric decor and lighting along with objects from the region. As Tregubenko explains, it is filled with gifts and mementos brought by members of the city’s Central Asian community who have come to support the space. The result is an atmosphere that feels deeply personal – less like the opening of a commercial venture and more like the founding of a communal home.

The opening menu offers a concise, narrative-driven tour of the steppes through dishes from Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan. A meal begins with baursak – the essential welcome of home-made, fluffy fried dough. Its name translates to “striving for unity”, and it’s a staple of the dastarkhan or traditional banquet table in Kazakh and Kyrgyz culture.

Zakaryayev is keenly aware of the differences in topography between Hong Kong and Central Asia: “One shaped by the sea and rivers, the other by mountains and endless steppe.”

The head chef has embraced this opportunity to work with ingredients that would be less familiar back home – even if featuring seafood on the menu does not come naturally. One thoughtful appetiser of sea bass with pumpkin and mung bean purée, for example, incorporates local ingredients while remaining rooted in Central Asian spices and palate.

Mains present the pillars of Central Asian cuisine, starting with beshbarmak. Described as “the dish of celebration”, it features hand-pulled noodles and tender meat in a soulful broth. It is joined by pilaf, a fragrant rice dish with beef, raisins and quail eggs that serves as a flavourful ode to Uzbekistan.

The final act is a dessert that bridges the vastness of Asia, balancing the sweet-tart flavour of Kazakhstan’s famed Aport apple against a rich, umami-forward home-made cheesecake and cheese caramel, thoughtfully adapted to a “sweet but not too sweet” profile suitable for local palates.

Yurt’s founders have taken to publicising the concept as the “first modern Central Asian restaurant” in Hong Kong – and they are aware of the responsibility that comes with claiming such a mantle. “We’re the first chapter of this cuisine for many, and we take that very seriously,” says Tregubenko.

The team’s determination to present an authentic version of their native cuisine is what led them to include horse meat on the menu – a traditional and respected protein across the steppe. The founders initially grappled with the decision, aware of the potential for misunderstanding. Ultimately, they chose cultural integrity over compromise, offering it as an add-on sausage served with their signature beshbarmak.

“We felt like if we shied away, if we didn’t showcase this one key element of our cuisine, we’d be watering down our own culture,” Tregubenko explains. “It’s an act of cultural honesty and integrity for us.”

That same commitment has led Nuraly and Tregubenko to operate Yurt as a halal establishment, positioning it as one of Hong Kong’s few refined halal dining spots. That commitment extends beyond the preparation of the food to the drinks menu as well. They “focus on crafting exceptional non-alcoholic pairings”, ensuring the experience remains celebratory and inclusive, even if it can be a “challenge” to explain to certain guests why they don’t serve alcohol.

An initial positive response suggests a healthy appetite for this previously unfamiliar cuisine. Nuraly says they’ve seen “overwhelming support” from the local Central Asian community, who have been introducing friends and inquisitive local explorers. Their target audience, he says, is simply “the curious”.

Looking forward, the founders hope Yurt will evolve into a broader cultural hub – a “living bridge” for music and art from the region. For now, they’ve built a different kind of destination. As they put it: “If the yurt in the steppe is a movable home, then Yurt the restaurant is a home that found its place.”

It’s a home that invites Hong Kong’s ever-curious diners to pull up a chair and embark on a journey to Central Asia, no passport required.

item.title: [SCMP] EU plans high-level China currency talks as fears of new trade shock mount
item.description:
After convincing China to accept a cap on its hybrid car exports, a stream of top-level European finance and banking officials will descend on the Chinese capital in the coming months on a far trickier mission: persuading Beijing to stop holding down its currency to help save the bloc’s struggling industry.

In the week of November 23, top European Union economy officials led by director general Maarten Verwey will sit down in Beijing for a “macroeconomic dialogue” with their Chinese counterparts.

Plans are in the works, meanwhile, for a heavyweight trio – from the European Central Bank, Eurogroup and European Commission – to follow them there around the turn of the year, though no final date has been set, according to multiple people familiar with the planning.
item.content:encoded:
After convincing China to accept a cap on its hybrid car exports, a stream of top-level European finance and banking officials will descend on the Chinese capital in the coming months on a far trickier mission: persuading Beijing to stop holding down its currency to help save the bloc’s struggling industry.

In the week of November 23, top European Union economy officials led by director general Maarten Verwey will sit down in Beijing for a “macroeconomic dialogue” with their Chinese counterparts.

Plans are in the works, meanwhile, for a heavyweight trio – from the European Central Bank, Eurogroup and European Commission – to follow them there around the turn of the year, though no final date has been set, according to multiple people familiar with the planning.

This would be the first formal meeting in over a decade for a revived format with People’s Bank of China governor Pan Gongsheng and Finance Minister Lan Foan. The talks were kick-started on the margins of global financial meetings in Bangkok earlier this month.

The European delegation – comprising the three institutions responsible for managing the euro zone’s monetary policy and coordinating its economic policies – will likely be led by ECB President Christine Lagarde, along with EU economy chief Valdis Dombrovskis and Kyriakos Pierrakakis, president of the Eurogroup, a coalition of euro-using EU members.

It comes amid frenzied political interest in Europe about the perceived undervaluation of the Chinese yuan, which EU leaders say is making the country’s products cheaper for European buyers, contributing heavily to what is now commonly described as a “China shock 2.0” to European industry.

The Chinese currency is not freely floated, meaning its value is not entirely determined by market forces. For decades, this has led trading partners to suspect it is undervalued in order to boost the country’s exports, a vital engine for economic growth.

Estimates on the currency’s comparative valuation vary wildly. The International Monetary Fund suggested this year that it could be up to 21 per cent undervalued, while researchers at the Centre for European Reform put that figure at closer to 30 per cent.

Research by Chinese think tank CF40 also suggests the yuan has considerable room to strengthen in the coming years, based on its analysis of Chinese and American prices.

BusinessEurope, Brussels’ umbrella corporate lobby group, said last week that China “actively restrains the appreciation of the renminbi that a surplus of this size would normally trigger, keeping exports artificially competitive”. This factor “compounds direct state support”, the chamber said.

But both publicly and behind closed doors, Beijing has pushed back, pointing to official data showing that the yuan has strengthened by almost 10 per cent against the euro in 2026.

“Global imbalances cannot be resolved through exchange rate adjustments,” Pan said in an official PBOC account of the October 16 meeting, insisting there was “no straightforward relationship between exchange rate and current account”.

While the yuan has made gains in 2026, “any appreciation has really vanished in real terms” due to flat inflation and years of falling producer prices in China, which have run counter to rising prices elsewhere in the world, said Alicia Garcia-Herrero, chief Asia-Pacific economist at French bank Natixis.

Pan and Lan came to Bangkok extremely well-prepared, according to people familiar with the discussions. The PBOC governor is well-liked in EU circles and seen as a pragmatic operator. In recent weeks, he has met a flurry of senior European officials, including governors of the central banks of France and Sweden, as well as Emmanuel Bonne, French President Emmanuel Macron’s diplomatic adviser.

Nonetheless, in Bangkok Pan politely drew on a long paper published a week earlier by the PBOC that said the Chinese central bank did not agree with analysis that the yuan was manipulated to boost exports.

“China has no need or intent to gain competitive advantages through currency devaluation,” said the paper, published on October 8.

The European side, meanwhile, broached the topic carefully, lest it appeared that they were ganging up on China along with the United States. The delicate issue was couched in the diplomatic language of “global imbalances”, with acknowledgement that China’s underconsumption was an issue when placed alongside European underinvestment and American overspend.

There was an effort not to appear confrontational – instead officials highlighted how the parties could work together to address these imbalances, with currency being one area to tackle. Ideally, the Europeans would like a glimpse of Beijing’s internal financial numbers to make fresh assessments on the yuan, even if that is seen as unlikely.

The dialogue “is aimed at enabling discussions on all relevant economic policies in a holistic manner, including global imbalances and their deep causes and the need for an orderly rebalancing in the interest of both sides and the global economy”, an ECB spokesperson said.

The Bangkok talks, then, did not achieve a breakthrough, but were seen as the gateway to technical discussions on the topic, in which technocrats will engage on the numbers, rather than getting bogged down in political bickering.

In Europe, however, the issue has boiled over into messy, mainstream political discourse. German media reports suggest that Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s dramatic pivot on China policy this month came directly from research linking an undervalued yuan to his country’s industry woes.

“Anyone who disrupts the functioning of the markets through unfair subsidies, overcapacities, aggressive pricing, or artificially undervalued currencies must expect a response,” Merz said at an event in Berlin last week.

In June, he pointed to the Plaza Accord as a model for today’s issues with manipulated currencies, referring to a 1985 pact that saw the US pressure Japan into accepting a sharp rise in the yen to curb its trade surplus.

Merz’s comments were anathema to Beijing’s official organs. In China, the accord is popularly seen to have crippled Japan’s export prowess, contributing to decades of perceived economic stagnation.

“China will not accept using exchange rates as a pretext for oppression, nor will it return to the old era of great powers coordinating the fate of a few countries. Today’s China is not the Japan of the past,” fumed Global Times, a tabloid under the official mouthpiece People’s Daily, in the days after Merz spoke.

European analysts believe, however, that allowing the yuan to strengthen would be a salve to Europe’s struggling manufacturing heartlands and help avert a potential broader trade war.

“If it’s a sizeable revaluation, of course it will [move the needle],” said Sander Tordoir, chief economist at the Centre for European Reform and co-author of a paper that reportedly helped convince Merz of the need to change tack on China.

“Most models would suggest that a 10 per cent real effective exchange rate change shifts real net exports by 1.5 per cent of GDP on average,” he said.

“Beijing faces a real choice here: either revalue the currency to lower pressure from trading partners ranging from the EU to India or accept that said partners will ratchet up the trade ramparts.”

Garcia-Herrero from Natixis said expectations were being managed as to how much ground Beijing would give on this front, since “Chinese companies’ profits are small” and an appreciation “would only reduce them further”.

The economist suspects that for China, currency talks with Europe may have a different objective. The country is on a drive to globalise its currency and the buy-in of the EU would be a big help.

“I think renminbi internationalisation is also very important, and I do think China wants some support,” Garcia-Herrero said. “I think they want to exchange with the Europeans on a multipolar world of currencies.”

But she doubted whether Europe alone could convince Beijing to change course on currency intervention, saying such a mission would be “doomed” without US support. “This not something we can achieve without the dollar.”

item.title: [SCMP] China and Oman unite in Mideast peace call on sultan’s ‘historic’ Beijing visit
item.description:
