China and Oman have called for a peaceful resolution and full ceasefire between the US and Iran, stressing that safe passage through the Strait of Hormuz must be restored.

The call came during talks in Beijing on Monday between Chinese President Xi Jinping and Oman’s Sultan Haitham bin Tariq.

In their joint statement, Beijing and Muscat encouraged the United States and Iran to resume dialogue and reach a “comprehensive agreement that includes the nuclear issue”.
item.content:encoded:
China and Oman have called for a peaceful resolution and full ceasefire between the US and Iran, stressing that safe passage through the Strait of Hormuz must be restored.

The call came during talks in Beijing on Monday between Chinese President Xi Jinping and Oman’s Sultan Haitham bin Tariq.

In their joint statement, Beijing and Muscat encouraged the United States and Iran to resume dialogue and reach a “comprehensive agreement that includes the nuclear issue”.

The two sides also affirmed that “normal and safe navigation” should be restored through the strait, agreeing to maintain communication on issues concerning the strategic waterway.

In the meeting, Xi said the Middle East and Gulf region should not become an “arena for major-power rivalry and geopolitical conflict”.

“China is ready to strengthen communication and coordination with Arab and Gulf countries to jointly strive for the early restoration of regional peace and tranquillity and the realisation of long-term stability,” he said.

He added that Beijing would continue to push for diplomatic resolutions to disputes, adding that the two countries should improve mutual political trust while expanding practical cooperation.

Haitham urged both sides to strengthen cooperation and coordination, describing the state visit as a “new starting point” for bilateral ties, according to Oman’s foreign ministry.

“We call for continued coordination with the People’s Republic of China in a manner that serves our shared interests and contributes to strengthening international security, stability and cooperation,” he said.

“We also express our great appreciation for China’s positions on key issues affecting our region.”

The Omani leader’s two-day trip, which began Sunday, is the first visit to China by the country’s monarch in their 48 years of diplomatic ties.

Xi greeted the Omani monarch with a formal ceremony featuring a 21-gun salute, a military march-past, and a welcoming banquet at the Great Hall of the People.

The trip comes as Oman – strategically located along the Strait of Hormuz – steps up efforts to move away from oil dependence and expand more into global supply chains.

Oman reportedly proposed to Iran in July that the two jointly manage the critical global oil chokepoint, with shipping firms paying voluntary fees, only to turn down a similar suggestion from Iran in September, according to the New York Post.

The sultan’s visit also came amid heightened tensions in the Red Sea, where Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels have repeatedly traded strikes with a Saudi Arabia-led coalition that supports Yemen’s internationally recognised government.

On Monday, the two sides urged all parties to prioritise the welfare of the Yemeni people.

Beijing also said that its special envoy on the Middle East would visit Iran, Oman, and Saudi Arabia this month to encourage peace talks and ease regional tensions.

Haitham was accompanied on his trip to China by a delegation of business heavyweights, including the Oman Investment Authority president, the minister of transport, communications and information technology, the minister of commerce, industry and investment promotion, and Oman’s central bank governor.

The summit talks also covered bilateral cooperation in technology, artificial intelligence, energy, logistics, digital commerce, food security, and integration between ports and special economic zones, according to Oman’s foreign ministry.

The two sides signed 14 memorandums of understanding spanning central bank digital currencies, the BeiDou navigation system, satellite technology, and supply chain investment.

Writing in state-run People’s Daily on Saturday, Chinese ambassador to Oman Lu Jian described the trip as “a historic milestone”.

He said the two sides would outline a blueprint for future bilateral cooperation, noting their new focus on renewable energy, advanced manufacturing, the digital economy, aerospace and artificial intelligence.

Omani ambassador to China Anwar bin Ahmed Muqaibil called the visit a pivotal moment, telling the Oman Daily Observer that it reflected a shared political will to elevate strategic ties.

He pointed to the convergence between the Oman Vision 2040 development plan and China’s Belt and Road Initiative, which he said provided a long-term strategic dimension for relations, according to the report on Friday.

The two nations in 2018 signed a memorandum of understanding on the belt and road plan, which aligns with Oman’s socioeconomic blueprint from 2021 to 2040 that aims to foster sustainable and private sector-led growth.

According to the report, Haitham’s visit could renew interest from China to invest in Omani infrastructure and industrial projects.

Commercial links between the two countries have expanded steadily. China has ranked as Oman’s largest trading partner since 2018, while Oman is China’s fourth-largest trading partner among Arab nations.

Omani sales to China are led by crude oil, liquefied natural gas and petrochemicals. In return, China exports machinery, electrical appliances, construction materials, batteries and solar panels.

The Oman-China Joint Committee – an intergovernmental body that oversees economic, trade and industrial ties – met in Beijing in late 2025 to discuss further Chinese investment in Oman’s non-oil industrial base.

Beyond commercial deals, Haitham’s trip is drawing close attention for its geopolitical subtext. Positioned on the southern flank of the Strait of Hormuz, across from Iran, Oman holds a critical vantage point over the world’s most sensitive maritime energy bottleneck.

Transit through the waterway has remained disrupted since the US and Israel launched strikes on Iran in February.

Addressing regional concerns, Muqaibil said the potential to strengthen joint coordination – with the aim of settling disputes by peaceful means – could expand into energy security, maritime corridor security and to other global challenges.

Omani Foreign Minister Sayyid Badr Albusaidi voiced a more explicit stance in a recent address at Cambridge University, arguing that regional security must ultimately rely on the Gulf states themselves forging a new framework.

Albusaidi said restoring free navigation through the Strait of Hormuz would be difficult to achieve unless Iran and the United States were both willing to compromise and reach a pragmatic understanding.

He criticised traditional Gulf security arrangements that relied on external military powers while treating Iran as an inherent adversary, saying they created an unstable architecture built on the “entirely false perception that there is a fundamental regional antagonism between Iran and the Arab states of the Gulf”.

“It is us, in the Gulf, who ultimately bear the responsibility for devising, developing and implementing a new regional security structure,” Albusaidi said, calling for an inclusive framework encompassing all eight Gulf littoral states.

item.title: [SCMP] Could a midterm defeat tame Trump? Not on foreign policy, Chinese experts say
item.description:
A potential lame-duck phase may not deter US President Donald Trump from pursuing more “transactional” or “risky” foreign policy moves after the midterm elections, Chinese experts warn, while casting doubt on expectations of a powerful Democratic wave.

Amid a season of high-stakes contests that could reshape global politics, the US vote on Tuesday stands out.

The election, which will determine who takes control of the US Congress, could result in Trump and his fellow Republicans no longer holding all the levers of power over the next two years.
item.content:encoded:
A potential lame-duck phase may not deter US President Donald Trump from pursuing more “transactional” or “risky” foreign policy moves after the midterm elections, Chinese experts warn, while casting doubt on expectations of a powerful Democratic wave.

Amid a season of high-stakes contests that could reshape global politics, the US vote on Tuesday stands out.

The election, which will determine who takes control of the US Congress, could result in Trump and his fellow Republicans no longer holding all the levers of power over the next two years.

Multiple models and ratings project that Democrats are on track to flip the House of Representatives, although forecasts differ on what the net seat gain will be.

There have also been signs in recent months that the party’s once narrow path to sweeping both chambers has widened, even though most of the Senate seats regarded as toss-ups are in traditionally red states, meaning the Democrats must win in Republican territory.

Observers in China agree that the US midterms on November 3 are likely to usher in a divided government.

They expect that such a shift could expose Trump to increased investigative oversight, raise the odds of impeachment led by House Democrats, and induce congressional gridlock for his administration’s legislative, personnel and budget priorities for the rest of his second term.

“The next two years could be a lame-duck [period for Trump],” said Diao Daming, an international relations professor specialising in US politics at Renmin University in Beijing.

Still, Diao said Trump had been consistently expanding presidential power and was likely to continue his approach of bypassing Congress through a barrage of executive orders to advance policies, leading to the prospect of more legal disputes.

As of October 22, Trump had already signed 292 executive orders during the first half of his second term – outpacing the 220 signed during his entire first term – according to the American Presidency Project.

Of those, more than 140 were signed in his first 100 days back in the White House, dwarfing the total issued by any predecessor over the same time frame.

US policy towards Russia, Iran, Europe and China could swing rapidly between heavy pressuring and partial bargaining.

Zhao Zhijiang

Although Trump might emerge from the midterm elections with less room to advance legislation, he could remain active on executive and foreign policy actions, Meng Weizhan, a social sciences researcher at Fudan University in Shanghai, wrote in a social media post late last month.

“He can still decide a lot of things,” Meng wrote.

Even if lasting only a few months, a single decision on tariffs, corporate licences, sanctions enforcement, military deployments or senior official appointments could have real-world consequences, he noted.

“He still has the capacity to change policy direction, although some policies will be hard to sustain,” Meng added.

Zhao Zhijiang, a research assistant at Beijing-based independent think tank Anbound, also expected Trump to retain considerable latitude in areas such as trade, tariffs, sanctions, immigration enforcement, administrative regulation, diplomacy and national security.

While Trump himself would enter the later stage of his presidency after the midterms, “Trumpism will not necessarily decline in tandem”, Zhao said, adding that younger Republicans were taking up the movement’s political line.

“The so-called lame duck problem is more about Trump’s personal term in office. Whether Trumpism can endure over the long run is the more important variable for gauging the future shape of American politics,” he said.

Republicans are heading into the midterm race with slim majorities in both the House and Senate, at a time when several polls show Trump’s domestic approval ratings at record lows.

The vote on Tuesday has been widely framed as a referendum on the US president, even though the man – who has been perceived as a mercurial leader upending the post-World War II order that the US helped build – is not on the ballot.

His first presidency saw Republicans yield about 40 seats, losing their House majority in the 2018 midterms, although they expanded their Senate majority with a two-seat net gain.

What followed were two years of investigations, subpoenas and impeachment.

The global spotlight is fixed on whether the elections can galvanise Democrats to repeat such a scenario to keep Trump in check.

All 435 House seats, 35 of the 100 Senate seats and 36 of the 50 state governorships will be decided in the midterm elections.

A Democratic takeover of the House is “almost a high-probability event”, said Diao, adding that the outcome in the Senate remained harder to call but the likelihood of Republicans losing their grip there was “continuing to rise”.

However, he expected that winning one chamber, or even both, would not necessarily secure Democrats the power to dominate the agenda.

“Even if the Democrats come back, it may feel like a fragile, even narrow, even ineffective majority,” Diao said.

If Democrats get a thin House majority, they might have to adjust some policies to accommodate the party’s rising democratic socialist wing, whose views often diverge from those of the party establishment, Diao said.

Even if Democrats flipped the Senate, they would probably hold only a razor-thin majority, which would be either insufficient to end a filibuster or difficult to hold together, given that Pennsylvania’s Democratic Senator John Fetterman could align with Republicans on many issues.

The assessment was echoed by other Chinese analysts.

“Even if Democrats controlled both chambers, they would still find it difficult to get around the presidential veto to enact a full slate of new policies on their own,” Meng wrote in his note.

He noted that Republicans might narrowly hold the Senate while Democrats could take the House.

He also noted that several states’ redrawing of congressional maps since last year could leave the scale of any Democratic House win in question, while some Republican candidates could outperform the polls in some tight districts due to campaign spending, voter turnout and local footprint.

Zhao from Anbound said that recent Republican efforts to shore up campaign mobilisation and defences, together with some candidates distancing themselves from Trump on specific issues, had made a Democratic landslide in earlier projections more uncertain.

He cited surveys showing that Americans lacked confidence in either party’s ability to solve the country’s problems. “The current situation looks more like a punishment of the [Republican] party in power than strong support for the Democrats,” he said.

Diao also said Democrats had offered no clear solutions beyond criticising Republicans, when inflation, higher oil prices driven by the conflict in the Middle East and the fallout from the trade war with Canada had fuelled public frustration with the Trump administration.

“Even if the Democrats win both chambers, is that a so-called blue wave? You don’t have a political platform … so what would the wave be made of?” Diao said. “That’s why some people say it’s not a blue wave but a red undertow.”

As a new balance of power looms over Washington, there has been discussion on Chinese social media over whether Trump will enter “garbage time” for the remainder of his presidency.

Experts said the characterisation missed the mark. The widely used sports term refers to the closing stretch of a game when one side has such an insurmountable lead that the outcome is not in doubt and players tend to become passive. The term has recently taken on a more political hue on Chinese social media.

Zhao said Trump’s final two years in office “would not be a period of policy stagnation”.

He expected the US president to maintain a hard line on immigration while pressing ahead with issues such as energy production, deregulation, manufacturing investment and trade talks.

“Diplomacy may become even more transactional. US policy towards Russia, Iran, Europe and China could swing rapidly between heavy pressuring and partial bargaining,” he said.

Meng also expected Trump to keep up his frenetic governing style over the next two years, although the gap between announced measures and eventual delivery could widen, adding that affordability, border policy and AI would also be among his priorities.

“Foreign policy is what is really worth watching more closely,” he wrote.

He noted that Trump appeared to have fallen out with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky recently, although Meng considered that the US leader had spent the last two years trying to maintain an “equal” distance from both Moscow and Kyiv.

“The split in US-Europe ties is likely to deepen,” he wrote. “This is something that may not be influenced by Congress.”

Meng added there was a “high degree of unpredictability” over Iran and Cuba.

Diao expected Trump to become more “legacy-driven” in foreign affairs and seek to do more in this field.

“On the other hand, [in areas] he believes he can control or achieve results quickly, he may also take some risky actions,” he said.

item.title: [SCMP] Could Taipei’s unexpectedly tight mayoral race add to cross-strait tensions?
item.description:
Taipei Mayor Wayne Chiang Wan-an faces an unexpectedly tough re-election fight in a race closely watched for its potential to damage the main opposition party Kuomintang and further strain the island’s relations with Beijing.

Just five months ago, Chiang appeared comfortably positioned for a second term in a city where the KMT has traditionally enjoyed an advantage over the ruling Democratic Progressive Party.

A poll by local cable news network TVBS in late May put him 28 percentage points ahead of DPP challenger Puma Shen, reinforcing expectations that the incumbent could coast to a second term.
item.content:encoded:
Taipei Mayor Wayne Chiang Wan-an faces an unexpectedly tough re-election fight in a race closely watched for its potential to damage the main opposition party Kuomintang and further strain the island’s relations with Beijing.

Just five months ago, Chiang appeared comfortably positioned for a second term in a city where the KMT has traditionally enjoyed an advantage over the ruling Democratic Progressive Party.

A poll by local cable news network TVBS in late May put him 28 percentage points ahead of DPP challenger Puma Shen, reinforcing expectations that the incumbent could coast to a second term.

By October, however, the gap had shrunk to eight points. And on Wednesday, a poll by Taipei-based United Daily News put Shen at 45 per cent against Chiang’s 41 per cent – a difference within the poll’s margin of error.

Another poll by digital news outlet ETtoday last week produced a different result, putting Chiang at 48.6 per cent against Shen’s 41.1 per cent. Taken together, however, the surveys point to a far more competitive contest than anticipated earlier this year.

The mayoral race is part of Taiwan’s November 28 “nine-in-one” midterm elections – island-wide contests in which voters cast ballots simultaneously across nine distinct tiers of local government offices.

The stakes are high for cross-strait relations: Beijing placed Shen on its sanctions list over what it called his pro-independence stance. The lawmaker is a vocal advocate for Taiwan’s civil defence against the mainland.

Beijing regards Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the United States, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-ruled island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons.

According to Chang Yuan-hsiang, a professor of political science at Soochow University in Taipei, Chiang has gone from being seen as an almost certain winner to facing a campaign with the scale and intensity of an island-wide leadership race.

Chang attributed the reversal in part to a succession of municipal controversies since May, ranging from flooding and school lunch food safety concerns to cases involving childcare and other city services.

None individually amounted to a major scandal, he said, but taken together had chipped away at Chiang’s reputation for steady, relatively trouble-free governance.

More consequential is the phenomenon Shen’s supporters call yangliu, or “ocean current” – throngs tailing the candidate through night markets and scooter convoys, with the packed appearances captured and amplified on social media.

Shen’s team has used the imagery from various Taipei neighbourhoods to create highly visual campaign events that have spread rapidly online and projected a sense of grass-roots enthusiasm.

Chang said what had begun as a deliberately constructed campaign device had ended up attracting wider attention, particularly among younger and centrist voters.

TVBS polling illustrated the shift, he said. In late May, Chiang led Shen among centrist voters by 57 per cent to 14 per cent. By early October, the advantage had narrowed to 40 per cent against 36 per cent.

“The large-scale loss of centrist voters is the main reason Chiang has fallen into difficulty,” Chang said.

The phenomenon has energised DPP supporters in the traditionally KMT-leaning capital.

Johnny Chiang Chi-chen, the KMT’s candidate for Taichung mayor and deputy speaker of the island’s legislature, said the “ocean current” had produced a spillover effect and had been effective in consolidating the DPP’s core support.

He warned that KMT supporters appeared to have become quieter or less willing to voice their preferences publicly, and that the party needed to generate momentum of its own in the final month.

Shen’s rise has also involved a striking change in political presentation.

Previously best known as a Taiwan security specialist, founder of the civil-defence organisation Black Bear Academy and a combative legislator focused on Beijing’s cognitive warfare, Shen, 44, has recast himself as a warmer, more approachable mayoral candidate focusing on municipal and livelihood issues.

The transformation has become a major KMT line of attack, with Chiang and other party figures questioning whether Shen has moderated long-held positions to broaden his electoral appeal.

Hu Yu-wei, a journalism professor at Chinese Culture University in Taipei, said an important question was whether voters saw Shen’s current presentation as a natural evolution of the politician they previously knew.

“Which is the real Puma Shen – the one they saw before or the one they see today?” Hu said.

As for Chiang, he has been forced to rethink a campaign initially centred on incumbency and his municipal record.

His first term has included the opening of the Taipei Dome and Nvidia’s decision to establish its Taiwan headquarters in the city. All the while, Chiang has cultivated a moderate, low-conflict political image.

But analysts said those strengths could become limitations if Shen succeeded in transforming the election from an assessment of municipal competence into a broader contest over political identity, values and generational change.

The implications extend well beyond Taipei City Hall.

“Taipei and neighbouring New Taipei together account for more than a quarter of Taiwan’s population,” noted international relations and strategic studies scholar James Yifan Chen, who said this made both cities’ mayoral races crucial to the KMT’s hopes of returning to power in 2028.

Conversely, a DPP breakthrough in northern Taiwan would strengthen Taiwanese leader William Lai Ching-te’s position ahead of his expected re-election bid, Chen said.

KMT chairwoman Cheng Li-wun has mostly kept her distance from the highly competitive metropolitan races, he added, with the candidates largely operating independently of the party leadership.

A loss in either Taipei or New Taipei could expose Cheng to criticism over the absence of a comprehensive party-wide electoral strategy and weaken her own political standing, he said.

For Chiang, 47, defeat would interrupt the trajectory of one of the KMT’s most prominent younger politicians.

Wang Kung-yi, director of the Taiwan International Strategic Study Society, a Taipei-based think tank, said Chiang combined island-wide recognition, central-level political experience, governance of the capital and an ability to appeal beyond the party’s traditional deep KMT base.

“A second term would strengthen his standing as a leading KMT figure, while defeat would cost the party more than control of [Taipei].”

Meanwhile, a Shen victory could further complicate already strained cross-strait relations, Wang said.

Beijing placed Shen on its list of “diehard Taiwan independence separatists” in 2024 and imposed sanctions barring him and his family from entering mainland China, Hong Kong and Macau.

Wang said Shen becoming mayor would immediately raise questions about the Taipei-Shanghai Twin-City Forum, one of the few remaining institutionalised channels of local-level dialogue across the Taiwan Strait.

“If the Twin-City Forum is hosted by Shanghai next year and Shen goes to Shanghai to attend, are they going to arrest him?” he asked.

There would also be questions about whether exchanges between Taipei and Shanghai and other mainland cities could continue, presenting “a major test for both sides”, Wang said.

More broadly, a KMT defeat in Taipei could prompt Beijing to reassess political trends on the island and whether its policies aimed at winning Taiwanese support were having the desired effect, he added.

If a Shen victory boosted DPP momentum towards 2028, Wang questioned whether Beijing might respond by taking a tougher approach.

“Would cross-strait relations become even worse? These are all questions that need to be considered,” he said.

Analysts noted that for an incumbent once expected to glide to re-election on his record, the campaign’s final month is poised to be an uphill fight, with stakes reaching far beyond Taipei City Hall to the KMT’s future and possibly across the Taiwan Strait.

item.title: [SCMP] How the Zhuhai air show charted China’s path from catching up to flying high
item.description:
When Zhuhai hosted its inaugural air show in November 1996, the event showcased the J-8IIM fighter, a second-generation fighter equipped with Russian radar and weapons, alongside a limited line-up of home-made aircraft.

Imported planes were the focus and Chinese audiences curiously studied the much more advanced foreign designs. They crowded around two Russian fourth-generation Su-27 fighters and were wowed as the jets performed their famous cobra manoeuvre, sharply braking in mid-air.

At the time, China had yet to build its own fourth-generation fighter.
item.content:encoded:
When Zhuhai hosted its inaugural air show in November 1996, the event showcased the J-8IIM fighter, a second-generation fighter equipped with Russian radar and weapons, alongside a limited line-up of home-made aircraft.

Imported planes were the focus and Chinese audiences curiously studied the much more advanced foreign designs. They crowded around two Russian fourth-generation Su-27 fighters and were wowed as the jets performed their famous cobra manoeuvre, sharply braking in mid-air.

At the time, China had yet to build its own fourth-generation fighter.

But over the next three decades, China went from being heavily reliant on Russian technology to becoming the only country other than the United States to have flight-tested sixth-generation fighters.

The Zhuhai air show – officially the China International Aviation and Aerospace Exhibition – has charted this journey year by year, becoming a major global event and a showcase for the nation’s growing military might.

This year’s edition has drawn extra attention, not only because it marks the event’s 30th anniversary but also because it comes ahead of the People’s Liberation Army’s centenary on August 1 next year, described by Beijing as a key milestone for the military’s modernisation.

International participation has doubled since 1996, with nearly 50 countries taking part this year. More than 1,100 exhibitors are expected for the December 7-13 event in the southern Guangdong city, up from around 400 at its debut.

The scale of the exhibition has also grown – from 8,000 square metres (86,110 square feet) 30 years ago to 135,000 square metres this year. More than 3,000 pieces of equipment will be on display, including 170 aircraft. There will also be a dedicated naval section for the first time.

The event mirrors China’s growing aviation confidence, showcasing advanced systems earlier than in the past for both domestic enthusiasts and prospective foreign buyers.

For example, the show did not feature China’s J-10 until 2008, 10 years after the fourth-generation fighter jet conducted its initial flight. The J-20, China’s most advanced stealth fighter in service, was first displayed five years after its 2011 maiden flight.

Now, China is not only exhibiting its most advanced operational aircraft but also offering static displays of platforms still in development.

In 2024, an airborne drone mother ship called Jiutian debuted at the air show, a year ahead of its maiden flight.

“Why could a drone that has not been flight-tested be shown at the air show? It’s because China has every confidence to send it into the sky,” military expert Fu Qianshao was quoted as saying by state broadcaster CCTV on October 14.

Overcoming underestimation

In July 2009, then US defence secretary Robert Gates said in a speech that the US should cap its production of fifth-generation stealth fighters because China would not have a fifth-generation jet by 2020. A week later, the US Senate voted in support of this policy.

At the time, the Chinese military’s most cutting-edge planes were the fourth-generation J-10A and J-11.

But less than two years later, in January 2011, while Gates was meeting with then Chinese president Hu Jintao in Beijing, the J-20 fifth-generation stealth fighter performed its maiden flight.

On his flight back, Gates admitted that US intelligence had underestimated how quickly China was developing stealth technology.

“What we had seen was that they were working on a stealth aircraft. What we didn’t know was how far along they were. They were clearly further along than our intelligence suggested,” Gates said.

Beijing may be hoping to surprise Washington once again with its sixth-generation fighters.

The US and China remain the only countries flight-testing such fighters. While there is no concrete sign of who is ahead, US Air Force Brigadier General Timothy Helfrich said last month that the US F-47 would be “the world’s first sixth-generation fighter”.

Meanwhile, China’s two tailless next-generation fighters, commonly known as the J-36 and J-50, have been observed undergoing test flights since December 2024.

General David Allvin, chief of staff of the US Air Force, said in 2025 that two prototypes of the American sixth-generation F-47 had been flying for five years. Beijing went further by releasing what is believed to be official footage of one of its sixth-generation fighters in June.

Fu said the competitiveness of China’s military aviation had undergone “earth-shaking” changes in the last 30 years, citing engines as an example.

“Compared to the US, it’s basically a tie. Even though the US is still ahead of China because it started engine installation much earlier, it has been moving quite slowly in the past few decades.”

He said China held the leading position in terms of radar, avionics and air-to-air missiles.

China’s fleet of advanced fighter jets has expanded rapidly in recent years. According to a January report by the London-based Royal United Services Institute, the PLA Air Force operated an estimated 320 to 350 J-20 fifth-generation stealth fighters by late 2025, up from around 50 in 2020.

Its fleet of J-16 advanced fourth-generation multi-role fighters grew from around 90 to 100 to around 450 over the same period, according to the report.

China is also seeking to expand its arms exports. The customer base for its fourth-generation J-10CE fighter has grown to include Uzbekistan and Pakistan, while Bangladesh is poised to become the third buyer.

Power projection

The transformation of the Chinese air force is also evident in its increasingly assertive deployments.

Xu Anxiang, then deputy commander of the PLA Air Force, said at the 2018 Zhuhai air show that China aimed to build a world-class strategic air force by the middle of the century – a goal in line with Beijing’s pledge to build a world-class military by that time.

In response to the August 2022 visit to Taiwan by then US House speaker Nancy Pelosi, Beijing mounted large-scale joint military exercises around the island.

The operations integrated PLA fighters, bombers, naval vessels and missile forces to rehearse blockade scenarios, air dominance and coordinated strikes against land and sea targets.

In October 2023, a Chinese J-11 fighter came within about 10 feet (3 metres) of a US B-52 bomber over the South China Sea, according to the Pentagon. While Washington called the nighttime encounter unsafe, Beijing countered that US military flights near China were the real cause of security risks.

According to Japan’s defence ministry, there were 1,000 take-offs and landings from China’s Liaoning and Shandong aircraft carriers in May and June last year.

The two carriers have repeatedly conducted drills in the western Pacific, the latest of which began last month and remains under way.

The PLA has also conducted long-range bomber patrols, such as when two Chinese H-6 bombers and two Russian Tu-95 bombers entered Alaska’s air defence identification zone in July 2024 in their first joint bomber operation.

China has also demonstrated its growing ability to project air power through back-to-back joint exercises with Egypt in 2025 and 2026.

For the inaugural Eagles of Civilisation exercise last year, China sent J-10C fighters, KJ-500 airborne early-warning aircraft and YY-20 aerial-refuelling tankers to Egypt, marking its first deployment of an integrated air force detachment to Africa.

Some observers, however, note that operational hurdles remain before Beijing can mount sustained global operations.

Lyle Goldstein, Asia programme director at Washington-based think tank Defence Priorities, said that while the PLA Air Force was advancing “by leaps and bounds” and was “truly formidable” close to home, it could still find it hard to operate far from China as it “lacks a robust refuelling capability or distant bases”.

“It’s very difficult to know how the US and Chinese air forces would compete in head-to-head combat.”

item.title: [SCMP] Will losing US midterms see Trump double down or signal beginning of the end?
item.description:
Tuesday’s US midterm election is both hugely consequential and not so consequential even as the world waits to see the American voters’ verdict on Donald Trump’s presidency – and the impact that verdict will have on his temperament, plans and possible petulant response, analysts and former government officials said.

On the one hand, an expected strong showing by opposition Democrats could bring more Congressional scrutiny over some of the most unconventional, maximalist and disruptive policies generated by an American president in the nation’s 250-year history.

At the same time, he is not on the ballot and little is likely to change structurally. No matter who wins or how reinvigorated lawmakers become, Trump will almost certainly retain his ability to block legislation that challenges his agenda.
item.content:encoded:
Tuesday’s US midterm election is both hugely consequential and not so consequential even as the world waits to see the American voters’ verdict on Donald Trump’s presidency – and the impact that verdict will have on his temperament, plans and possible petulant response, analysts and former government officials said.

On the one hand, an expected strong showing by opposition Democrats could bring more Congressional scrutiny over some of the most unconventional, maximalist and disruptive policies generated by an American president in the nation’s 250-year history.

At the same time, he is not on the ballot and little is likely to change structurally. No matter who wins or how reinvigorated lawmakers become, Trump will almost certainly retain his ability to block legislation that challenges his agenda.

“The stakes are not as consequential as a lot of people think because Trump still has the veto power,” said Jeffrey Moon, head of consultancy China Moon Strategies.

“But you’re not going to be able to turn off the Iran war. You’re not going to be able to turn off the tariff policy,” added Moon, formerly with the National Security Council and a US consul general in Chengdu.

“What you can do is have hearings that ask probing questions and cause embarrassing implications and make it very unpopular for him.”

A related outcome as Trump eases into lame-duck land and his clout erodes is more anti-Beijing legislation and louder rhetoric from lawmakers less intimidated or beholden to the president.

Over the past year, Trump has turned far less hawkish than many in Congress or his cabinet, forging a US-China trade truce; meeting President Xi Jinping twice in person; easing fentanyl tariffs; suspending reciprocal tariffs; moving closer to Beijing on Taiwan policy; and weakening export controls on advanced semiconductors.

Beijing has welcomed the change. “They love Trump. If anything, they want him to stay on forever,” said Jeremy Chan, senior analyst with Eurasia Group. “They want him to have a third term. I mean, hey, our guy does.”

Freed up, however, this previously supine Congress could start pushing back and flexing more muscle. The current 119th “do nothing” Congress has enacted just 121 laws compared with those in the 1990s that routinely enacted between 350 and 600.

“I don’t think that Republicans in the Senate have been favourable towards these loosening export controls. But they’ve kind of gone along with it,” said Sarah Kreps, government professor at the Cornell Brooks School of Public Policy.

“And I think we’re going to see that shift if and when the Democrats take control of one or both houses of Congress. The Trump reputation has been sun setting a little bit,” the former US Air Force officer added.

Another concern is how the notoriously thin-skinned president might react if his party gets walloped. Betting site Kalshi gives Democrats a 92 per cent chance of winning the House and a 68 per cent chance of winning the Senate.

Although US-China relations have stabilised since the two leaders met in South Korea a year ago, the mercurial US leader has a history of quick turnarounds that could put Beijing in his crosshairs.

“The midterm election, we don’t know what will happen. But I think everyone is quite sure that it’s going to ruin Trump’s mood for a lot of things, and he might be looking for scapegoats,” said Yun Sun, the Stimson Centre’s China director.

“Will he blame China for not giving him a bigger diplomatic victory so that he could turn the midterm election around? There’s no guarantee.”

Others see him turning elsewhere given Beijing’s leverage over Washington with strategic rare earth minerals.

“I don’t think he’s going to pick that fight,” said Chan. “The greater risk is 2027 when the two leaders have less opportunity to meet in person as Xi focuses on the 21st Party Congress.”

In private, Chinese interlocutors are saying they know that bilateral irritants will boil over at some point, Chan said.

“Taiwan arms sales can’t be deferred forever,” he added. “And unless we have a release valve for those bilateral pressures, then you could see this heading to a materially worse place, almost through inertia.”

As the unpopular president’s grip on the three arms of US government wanes, he is also likely to focus even more on executive orders and foreign policy, where he faces few constraints, analysts said. In recent days, he has already threatened to resume attacks on Iran after the election.

“We did a little ceasefire, which I never liked very much,” he said this week. “It was just a waste of time.”

These are powers he has used extensively. During his six years in office, he has signed 510 executive orders, compared to previous record setters, former presidents Ronald Reagan at 381 and Bill Clinton at 364 – over their full eight years.

And foreign capitals can expect further disruption from an “America first” president who started the Iran war, driven up oil prices globally; alienated long-standing US allies; dislodged Venezuela’s leadership and its oil, launched trade wars, cosied up to Moscow and slapped tariffs on nearly every economy on earth.

Amid the noise and policy churn ahead, however, a transactional leader known for rarely admitting mistakes or backing down voluntarily is likely to make more strategic retreats, even if he does not acknowledge them, analysts said.

Late last Friday, the White House quietly eased its highly unpopular Canadian tariffs in the state of Maine, where Republican Senator Susan Collins faces a tough race that could determine which party controls the Senate.

“Trump has been telling us that it’s the foreigners that are paying the tariffs,” said Moon. “But in this case, the Republicans are pretty much openly admitting or tacitly admitting that … rather than making America great again, the tariffs are actually damaging the local economy.

“He hasn’t admitted the failure of his tariff policy, but that’s what this is all about,” Moon added. “I do not think he will openly change his philosophy. This will be like cracking or breaking down a wall. This is the first brick.”

item.title: [SCMP] South Korea’s latest chart sensation has a secret: the singer isn’t human
item.description:
A little-known South Korean music act has climbed the charts with a viral hit that has caught listeners off guard – not just for its sudden popularity, but because its vocals were generated entirely by artificial intelligence.

Meomuru’s single, “Have You Become the Adult You Dreamed Of?”, climbed to No 2 on Melon’s Top 100 – South Korea’s flagship streaming chart – earlier this week. The track’s popularity has turned Meomuru into one of the country’s most-talked-about acts.

The song was created by Glorywave, a songwriting and production duo comprising Lee Yong-seok and Choi Sung-hyuk, who have worked with South Korean artists for more than a decade.
item.content:encoded:
A little-known South Korean music act has climbed the charts with a viral hit that has caught listeners off guard – not just for its sudden popularity, but because its vocals were generated entirely by artificial intelligence.

Meomuru’s single, “Have You Become the Adult You Dreamed Of?”, climbed to No 2 on Melon’s Top 100 – South Korea’s flagship streaming chart – earlier this week. The track’s popularity has turned Meomuru into one of the country’s most-talked-about acts.

The song was created by Glorywave, a songwriting and production duo comprising Lee Yong-seok and Choi Sung-hyuk, who have worked with South Korean artists for more than a decade.

The pair developed the concept, wrote the lyrics and used the generative AI music platform Suno to produce the melody, arrangement and vocal track. They then edited, mixed and mastered the final cut themselves.

The song’s success has renewed calls for mandatory labelling of AI-generated music, with South Korean lawmakers now examining whether the country’s AI Basic Act needs expanding to address the issue.

What makes an artist?

On Meomuru’s social media, which features AI-generated images and videos, one question has filled the comments section: “Is this AI?”

“The song sounded very familiar when I first heard it,” said Lee Sun-mi, a 41-year-old housewife in Daejeon. “When I shared it with my husband, he immediately suggested it might be AI-generated.”

After listening to Meomuru’s other songs, Lee found the novelty wore off quickly.

“The other songs [are] a bit too generic. The melodies sounded familiar, and the lyrics felt like something I had heard many times before,” she said. “I don’t think I’ll actively seek out AI-generated music in the future.”

But younger listeners see things differently. For Shin Ji-hye, a university student in Jecheon, knowing Meomuru used AI did not change her view that the music was “moving and catchy”.

“Depending on the prompts and the person using the technology, AI-generated songs can come together as a cohesive genre, sounding like music created by human artists,” the 19-year-old said.

Shin, who has experimented with AI music tools herself, sees platforms such as Suno as lowering the barrier to entry for aspiring musicians.

“Someone might be interested in composing but lack the ability to sing or the money to produce a song,” she said. “Others might enjoy writing lyrics but struggle to turn them into a finished track. AI can help bridge those gaps and allow more people to create music.”

A global debate

Technology-driven acts are not entirely new to K-pop. The five-member virtual boy band Plave uses real-time motion-capture and facial-tracking to control its animated characters, though human performers sing, dance and interact with fans.

The strategy has paid off: Plave’s album HYPERDRIVE topped Billboard’s Top Album Sales chart last week, and the act sold out Seoul’s 18,000-seat Gocheok Sky Dome last year.

In the United States, the largest music market in the world, AI R&B artist Xania Monet has also entered the mainstream. Monet’s vocals are generated by Suno over lyrics written by American poet and designer Telisha “Nikki” Jones.

Monet signed a multimillion-dollar deal with Hallwood Media last year and has appeared on several Billboard charts, though her success has drawn criticism from established musicians – including Grammy Award-winning singer Victoria Monet – who argue that AI acts undercut the work and livelihood of working performers.

Within the music industry, the rise of AI acts has coincided with growing intellectual property rights clashes. Suno faces infringement lawsuits in the US from major labels, including Universal Music Group and Sony Music Entertainment, over allegations its models were trained on copyrighted recordings without authorisation or compensation. Songs by South Korean artists, including Psy and BTS, are among those allegedly used without permission.

Similarly, generative AI developer Anthropic was sued last week by Authentic Brands Group – owner of the rights to Elvis Presley’s catalogue and likeness – over the alleged unlicensed use of 274 songs by the late singer.

Under South Korea’s Copyright Act, a work must demonstrate human creative input to qualify for legal protection. But where machine generation begins and human contributions end remains legally ambiguous.

In an interview with the Kyunghyang Shinmun daily, Glorywave said they had not registered “Have You Become the Adult You Dreamed Of?” with the Korea Music Copyright Association (KOMCA) and were not collecting standard songwriting or arrangement royalties.

KOMCA introduced criteria in August allowing registration for AI-assisted music where human creators demonstrated a substantial and leading role, but withdrew the guidelines just 22 days later amid pushback from the creative community and a lack of clear legislative direction.

Can AI music become art?

South Korea’s experimentation with virtual acts dates back nearly three decades. In 1998, Adam debuted to heavy fanfare, selling roughly 200,000 albums. But high production costs and technological limitations, including expensive 3D rendering, curtailed the project, and Adam disappeared from the charts within a year.

Yoo Seung-chul, a professor of media studies at Ewha Womans University specialising in consumer psychology, said another factor behind Adam’s failure was the difficulty of building an emotional connection with fans.

“But seeing the popularity of Plave, we can see that a relationship between artists and fans is possible even with virtual performers,” Yoo said. “As AI services such as ChatGPT and Gemini have become mainstream, people increasingly feel that these virtual agents are their friends. This is particularly true among younger generations.”

Yoo does not believe AI acts will be able to fully replace live performers, but he expects AI music to carve out a distinct genre of its own.

Music critic Kim Sung-hwan sees the phenomenon as an inevitable progression in the recording industry’s drive to reduce production costs, but stresses that creative ownership still depends on human intent.

“The most important thing is the original idea behind an AI-generated song,” Kim said. “What matters is whether that initial idea – the concept that led to the song’s creation – came from a human.”

Kim warned that as AI tools made music production easier, the quality of creative work could suffer if too little human effort goes into the process.

“The real question is whether AI music will remain a mechanical output created simply for commercial purposes and financial returns, or whether it can become a work of art that people can enjoy together and appreciate for its artistic value,” Kim said. “We need a proper institutional framework to develop guidelines for how AI should be used in music creation.”

item.title: [SCMP] Southeast Asia’s EV boom sidelines local car parts suppliers
item.description:
Southeast Asia’s electric vehicle boom risks leaving the region’s smaller companies behind, as Chinese automotive giants bypass local part-makers in favour of imported components and locked-in supplier networks.

Local manufacturers across Indonesia, Thailand and Malaysia are facing a double squeeze: demand is weakening for parts used in petrol and diesel cars, collectively known as internal combustion engine (ICE) vehicles, while steep barriers to entry also keep them out of EV supply chains.

Analysts say repair and servicing work plus hybrids, which pair a petrol engine with an electric motor, could offer a lifeline, but without stronger government support and better access to Chinese manufacturers, the EV transition threatens to hollow out the region’s established supply base.
item.content:encoded:
Southeast Asia’s electric vehicle boom risks leaving the region’s smaller companies behind, as Chinese automotive giants bypass local part-makers in favour of imported components and locked-in supplier networks.

Local manufacturers across Indonesia, Thailand and Malaysia are facing a double squeeze: demand is weakening for parts used in petrol and diesel cars, collectively known as internal combustion engine (ICE) vehicles, while steep barriers to entry also keep them out of EV supply chains.

Analysts say repair and servicing work plus hybrids, which pair a petrol engine with an electric motor, could offer a lifeline, but without stronger government support and better access to Chinese manufacturers, the EV transition threatens to hollow out the region’s established supply base.

Chinese EV investments have so far generated minimal business for established local component makers, according to Indonesian economist Bhima Yudhistira Adhinegara.

“The supply chain is very different between Japanese autos and Chinese EVs,” said Bhima, executive director of the Centre of Economic and Law Studies in Jakarta. “The biggest barriers are financing, technology and access to manufacturers.”

Similar concerns have emerged in Thailand, long seen as the backbone of Southeast Asia’s auto sector. Krungsri Research, the research arm of Thailand’s Bank of Ayudhya, said in its 2026-28 industry outlook report that local suppliers were struggling to enter Chinese EV supply chains.

Manufacturers either imported major components or relied on existing Chinese suppliers, it said, with Thai vendors at a disadvantage on both cost and hi-tech proprietary know-how.

Hybrid hopes

Continued demand for ICE cars and hybrids could, in theory, generate the income needed to fund the switch to electric, but Bhima said the financial strain was already limiting smaller Indonesian firms’ ability to invest.

Sluggish domestic consumer spending and rising fuel costs have sapped demand, forcing smaller suppliers to respond by downsizing, cutting product quality or seeking credit restructuring just to stay afloat.

“There are no transitional incentives from the government for small ICE suppliers,” Bhima said.

He called on Indonesia’s government to help smaller manufacturers connect with EV brands and assembly plants, and to use local-content rules – requirements that a certain share of a vehicle’s value be sourced domestically – to ensure firms were brought into the supply chain.

“The government can ensure that investment and sales of EVs to meet local content requirements must absorb local small manufacturers,” Bhima said.

In Thailand, Krungsri Research found that hybrid production supported demand for both conventional engine parts and electrical systems, with Japanese hybrid manufacturers sourcing substantial volumes of their parts from within the Southeast Asian nation.

An automotive master plan published by the Economic Research Institute for Asean and East Asia on October 13 took a similar line, advocating support for lower-emission vehicles and hybrids in the near term while preparing for wider electrification in future.

Other Thai manufacturers are diversifying away from the automotive sector entirely. Sompol Tanadumrongsak, president of the Thai Auto-Parts Manufacturers Association, has previously urged local suppliers to repurpose for rail, medical equipment, aviation and agricultural machinery.

This Week in Asia contacted Sompol and the association for comment on this article, but had not received a response at the time of publication.

Replacement parts offer another potential market. Drivers holding onto their old ICE cars could prop up demand for aftermarket replacement parts in Thailand, Krungsri Research found, even as technological disruption accelerates and competition from abroad intensifies.

In Malaysia, Chinese EV pioneer BYD recently dropped plans for a proposed assembly plant in Tanjung Malim following a dispute over export quotas and pricing conditions set by the Ministry of Investment, Trade and Industry. The ministry defended the requirements as non-discriminatory.

Earlier this month, BYD changed tack, partnering with local contract assembler Inokom to assemble passenger vehicles at an existing facility in Kulim, in Malaysia’s northwestern Kedah state.

Still, local value add remains modest. Malaysian media reported in March that domestically assembled EVs comprised just 20 to 30 per cent local content, compared with up to 70 per cent for foreign-branded ICE cars.

Malaysia has attempted to link up its suppliers with Chinese supply chains. In May last year, the Malaysian Investment Development Authority brought together 23 domestic parts suppliers and 12 technology suppliers with the Chinese carmaker Chery, resulting in four commercial agreements covering components, technology transfer and joint investment.

Aiman Abdullah, managing editor of Motoring Malaysia and a long-time industry watcher, said domestic carmakers’ electrification programmes were gradually building up local engineering and manufacturing expertise, adding that experience working with the high-voltage systems in hybrids could help vendors move into EV components.

But suppliers still needed clearer planning from both the government and carmakers, he stressed, because vendors typically required six to 18 months to prepare for full-scale production,while investments often took about a decade to pay off.

“Investors need to see stability and focus in terms of policy before they take out their chequebooks,” Aiman said.

Smaller businesses might have the vision and some amount of technical expertise, but lacked the financial means to break into EVs, he said, proposing a fund to help them expand and scale up production.

The aftermarket route

Servicing and reconditioning cars offers an alternative way into the wider EV economy, though this again has limits.

Teoh Jiun Ee, co-founder of regional used-car platform Carsome and CEO of its training arm, Carsome Academy, said Malaysia already had a well-established ecosystem for conventional services such as body repairs, tyres and suspension.

But when it came to high-voltage systems, battery assessments and model-specific components, the work became more specialised, he said.

“The key distinction is between work we can carry out here and the parts, data and specialist systems we can access to carry it out.”

Carsome, which operates its own inspection centres and refurbishment facilities, is able to inspect EVs, but it cannot repair or replace individual battery modules and refers such cases to manufacturers, especially for cars still under warranty.

Technicians could build on their existing knowledge of vehicle systems and fault-finding by adding skills in electrical systems, high-voltage safety and EV diagnostics, Teoh said.

Yet access to such retraining depended partly on who bore the cost, he said, adding that employers, government and industry partnerships could help.

“If the cost falls entirely on individual technicians, there is a risk that the people who most need to upgrade their skills may be the least able to access it [training],” Teoh said.

“For us, the broader opportunity is to develop a more mature used-EV ecosystem here, where vehicles can be assessed consistently and safely, and buyers have greater confidence in the condition of the cars they purchase.”

item.title: [SCMP] Dark past of Japan’s Unit 731 buried under airport expansion
item.description:
A village that sent hundreds of men to one of imperial Japan’s most notorious wartime units is being demolished to make way for a runway at Tokyo’s Narita International Airport.

Unit 731 carried out lethal experiments on captives, many of them Chinese, to develop biological weapons during the second world war. Around 300 of its roughly 3,000 personnel came from Kamo, a neighbourhood in Shibayama town, Chiba prefecture, east of the capital. Its founder and commander, Lieutenant General Shiro Ishii, grew up there.

Demolition began in August, about 5km (three miles) from the southern perimeter fence of Narita’s main runway. Ishii’s family home is among the buildings that have already been flattened.
item.content:encoded:
A village that sent hundreds of men to one of imperial Japan’s most notorious wartime units is being demolished to make way for a runway at Tokyo’s Narita International Airport.

Unit 731 carried out lethal experiments on captives, many of them Chinese, to develop biological weapons during the second world war. Around 300 of its roughly 3,000 personnel came from Kamo, a neighbourhood in Shibayama town, Chiba prefecture, east of the capital. Its founder and commander, Lieutenant General Shiro Ishii, grew up there.

Demolition began in August, about 5km (three miles) from the southern perimeter fence of Narita’s main runway. Ishii’s family home is among the buildings that have already been flattened.

Around 651 hectares (1,606 acres) of the neighbourhood were compulsorily purchased for the airport expansion, town officials confirmed, with some residents moving elsewhere in Shibayama and others leaving altogether.

Among them was at least one man whose father served under Ishii, the Asahi newspaper reported on Tuesday.

Unit 731 was supposedly tasked with “epidemic prevention and water supply”, suggesting a sanitation service for troops, but its true purpose was much darker.

From its base in Pingfang on the outskirts of Harbin, in occupied northeast China, the unit researched, developed and tested biological and chemical weapons by conducting gruesome human experiments on prisoners and civilians without their consent.

Historians estimate that as many as 3,000 died at its Harbin headquarters. Thousands more lost their lives in experiments at other sites across Asia and tens of thousands, mostly civilians, were killed by the unit’s weapons.

Ishii recruited heavily from Kamo, apparently in the belief that men from his own community would stay loyal to him. Historians say he was correct.

“No other single region in Japan produced such a concentrated and large number of unit members,” said Masataka Mori, a former history professor at Shizuoka University who spent many years studying the unit. “Ishii sometimes referred to Unit 731 as the ‘Kamo Unit’, after his hometown.”

Almost everyone in Shibayama knew Ishii was in command, but only unit members were aware of what the work truly involved. “The unit’s true nature was kept strictly confidential because it was engaged in human experimentation and biological warfare, acts that violated international law,” Mori said.

As Japan’s defeat drew near, Ishii and nearly all of his senior officers tried to destroy the evidence and fled back home. Ishii gave members three orders, according to Mori: never reveal you served in the unit, do not run for public office and take what happened to your grave.

Many returned to Kamo and were “placed under surveillance” to ensure they complied, he said.

Immunity and silence

American occupation forces took Ishii into custody soon after their arrival in 1945 – but went on to offer him and his senior colleagues immunity from prosecution in return for their research data, which US scientists could not have gathered legally.

The unit was consequently barely mentioned at the Tokyo War Crimes Trials, the Allied tribunal that tried Japan’s wartime leaders over a two-year period, and few of its members ever faced justice.

As a result, the public abroad and in Japan remained largely ignorant of its horrific work until 1981, when the writer Seiichi Morimura published The Devil’s Gluttony, a two-volume account of the unit’s crimes.

In Kamo, as in other small pre-war communities, many residents shared a surname and were distantly related. Among them was Shinichiro Ishii, who served in the unit. His son Junichiro told the Asahi that his father “didn’t like to talk about” his wartime experiences in occupied China.

After Morimura’s book appeared, Shinichiro reportedly shut himself in his bedroom and refused to speak with journalists, angry that other veterans had talked. Junichiro’s mother, who had lived in China with her husband, described good pay, homes with flush toilets – a luxury at the time – as well as help from Ishii in evacuating the family to Japan near the war’s end. Her husband often had nightmares, she said.

“It’s not a story I particularly want to tell, and I don’t know the whole truth myself,” Junichiro told the Asahi. He declined an interview with This Week in Asia.

A Shibayama town official confirmed there were “several historical sites” in the airport expansion area, but said there was no complete list. The town wanted to promote the project, which it expected to bring business opportunities and jobs, the official added.

Tokyo has been equally cagey about Unit 731. In a written statement to Japan’s parliament in 2003, then prime minister Junichiro Koizumi acknowledged the unit’s existence but said “no evidence” had been found that it conducted biological warfare.

The government confirmed the unit had a base at Pingfang, but said the documents describing its work there were “essentially private records”, whose contents it could not objectively verify. It said none were held in government archives and that, given the passage of time, further investigation would be “extremely difficult”.

Keiko Suenaga, a history professor at Fukushima Medical University who has researched the unit, said many Japanese might “have vaguely heard of Lieutenant General Ishii” but the school curriculum did not sufficiently teach about his actions.

She said the internet was “awash with historical revisionist information” and conspiracy theories denying the unit’s crimes, including claims that it never existed or that it was “literally a unit for disease prevention and water supply”.

Such rewriting of history left people without accurate knowledge of their past, Suenaga said, with successive Japanese governments facing dwindling amounts of scrutiny as public awareness had waned.

Washington’s decision to grant immunity had also allowed many of those responsible to escape prosecution, she said, making it harder for Japan to criticise American wartime air raids or the atomic bombings.

“As a result, it can be said that those responsible for war crimes within the ruling elites of both Japan and the US entered into a ‘win-win’ relationship with one another,” Suenaga said.

Today, the site of the Ishii family home is taped off, with signs warning that construction work will begin soon. The men who came home to Kamo after the war are now largely forgotten and their community will soon lie under a thick layer of runway asphalt.

item.title: [SCMP] Asian scientists are looking to South Korea as it becomes harder to stay in the US
item.description:
As tightening US visa restrictions and geopolitics lock out Asian researchers from Western institutions, South Korea is emerging as a new academic sanctuary for top talent.

According to Yoo Ji-beom, president of Sungkyunkwan University (SKKU) in Seoul, that reflects a broader trend that has seen the West giving way to Asia after decades of dominance – particularly in the field of applied technology in China, Japan and South Korea.

“Technological competition and global talent mobility are reshaping the knowledge ecosystem. Competition to attract and retain the very best researchers has become far more intense than before,” Yoo said during an interview in Hong Kong.
item.content:encoded:
As tightening US visa restrictions and geopolitics lock out Asian researchers from Western institutions, South Korea is emerging as a new academic sanctuary for top talent.

According to Yoo Ji-beom, president of Sungkyunkwan University (SKKU) in Seoul, that reflects a broader trend that has seen the West giving way to Asia after decades of dominance – particularly in the field of applied technology in China, Japan and South Korea.

“Technological competition and global talent mobility are reshaping the knowledge ecosystem. Competition to attract and retain the very best researchers has become far more intense than before,” Yoo said during an interview in Hong Kong.

“[South Korean] students who want to stay or study in the USA have a very hard time getting a visa and they have to wait longer than before,” he said, adding that Chinese students faced similar hurdles.

“Instead of going abroad, they say ‘let’s study in our land’,” he said, noting that the popularity of K-culture in Asia, America and elsewhere was also helping to bring more students to South Korea.

SKKU – the oldest university in East Asia with 628 years of history – is capitalising on that shift.

In June, the university secured 13.5 billion won (US$10.08 million) in government funding over five years to recruit “outstanding scientists from abroad in energy, biomedicine, nanotechnology and quantum materials” through South Korea’s Brain Pool Plus programme.

Under the initiative, researchers will be employed on a tenure track and receive up to 600 million won annually in personal and research allowances.

The university said it aimed to recruit six international researchers at a time, mainly from the US and leading Asian research hubs.

SKKU said it had “already welcomed several researchers through the programme this year, with additional recruitment currently under way”.

After Washington proposed a US$100,000 fee for the H-1B visa last year, South Korean ministries were tasked with finding ways to take advantage of the tougher US immigration policy and lure scientists and engineers from abroad.

“We are working to create an environment in which they can settle in and concentrate on their research,” Yoo said, adding that South Korea should try to attract more international researchers to its science and engineering graduate programmes and support their career development.

Data from South Korea’s Ministry of Education shows that the total number of international students in higher education reached more than 307,000 this year, up 21 per cent from 2025.

Around 223,000 of them are enrolled in degree programmes – a rise of almost 25 per cent from a year ago – with Chinese students making up the largest group at nearly one-third of the total, according to a report released in August.

Asian students accounted for 92 per cent of South Korea’s international student population across both degree and non-degree programmes, such as Korean language courses.

Vietnam led with almost 100,000 students at 31.5 per cent, followed by China at 25.7 per cent, and Uzbekistan at 6.8 per cent, Nepal at 6.5 per cent and Mongolia at 5.6 per cent.

Yoo, a materials scientist, has bachelor’s and master’s degrees from Seoul National University. He completed a PhD in materials engineering at Stanford University in 1989.

Following his doctoral studies, Yoo returned to South Korea and spent five years conducting research at the Electronics and Telecommunications Research Institute in Daejeon before joining SKKU in 1994.

He has led research on carbon-based materials, including graphene. He served as vice-director of the SKKU Advanced Institute of Nanotechnology and as dean of the College of Engineering before beginning his four-year term as university president in 2023. He is now set to serve a second term.

Yoo described the pace of change in China’s universities and research ecosystem as “remarkable” with significant advances in almost every field of research.

“I see this growth as the result of sustained, long-term investment in research, a deep pool of young researchers and the capacity to translate research quickly into industrial application,” he said. “There is much that Korean universities can learn from this experience.

“I believe Chinese and Korean universities can be partners in a shared knowledge ecosystem – competing and cooperating at the same time, and growing together,” he added.

According to Yoo, energy materials offered the most promising avenues for joint research. He listed as examples next-generation solar cells and batteries, environmental materials for carbon neutrality, nanomedicine and biomaterials, and fundamental nanoscience such as two-dimensional materials.

“These fields have a large basic-research component, and they benefit greatly when researchers bring complementary strengths together,” he said.

While US-China tech decoupling has rattled global industries such as semiconductors and rechargeable batteries, Yoo said universities should remain neutral and prioritise open collaboration built on trust, transparency and shared challenges such as climate, energy and health.

“Over the past several years, even as geopolitical tensions have risen, SKKU’s international joint research and people-to-people exchanges with the United States, China and many other countries have expanded,” he said.

“Nature Index data show that research collaboration between Korea and China grew by more than 80 per cent in 2024, while Korea-US collaboration reached its highest level in a decade that same year.

“To me, this suggests that scientific cooperation need not be a matter of choosing one partner over another.”

Yoo said SKKU was focused on developing joint research partnerships and exchanges across Hong Kong, mainland China, the US, Japan, Europe and Southeast Asia.

In the Greater Bay Area, the university has agreements with institutions such as City University of Hong Kong, Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen, and Sun Yat-sen University in Guangzhou.

It also has long-standing partnerships with Peking University, Tsinghua University, Fudan University and the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, including a regional governance forum run by its think tank with Chinese partners for the past 20 years.

He said universities were about academic work, not politics. “Instead of deep tech or hi-tech [we need to] focus on fundamental science and try to find new phenomena, new materials and new ways to do something,” Yoo said.

“Basic studies take more than 10 years, and that is one of the ways to avoid conflicts.”

item.title: [SCMP] Will AI-powered open-door vending machines reshape Hong Kong’s retail landscape?
item.description:
Sherry Shum has embraced a new shopping routine after finding a smart vending machine near her home in Chai Wan in Hong Kong.

The 37-year-old retail worker uses her phone to scan a QR code, opens the smart machine’s door, picks up a bottle of Coca-Cola, an oolong tea and a pack of potato chips, closes it and walks away with HK$60 (US$7.70) worth of goods. The whole process is so seamless that the bulk of the time is spent deciding what to buy.

The moment Shum takes an item from the shelf, the machine detects the product based on its appearance and debits her account. Once she shuts the door, the bill is settled via the payment method she selected before opening it.
item.content:encoded:
Sherry Shum has embraced a new shopping routine after finding a smart vending machine near her home in Chai Wan in Hong Kong.

The 37-year-old retail worker uses her phone to scan a QR code, opens the smart machine’s door, picks up a bottle of Coca-Cola, an oolong tea and a pack of potato chips, closes it and walks away with HK$60 (US$7.70) worth of goods. The whole process is so seamless that the bulk of the time is spent deciding what to buy.

The moment Shum takes an item from the shelf, the machine detects the product based on its appearance and debits her account. Once she shuts the door, the bill is settled via the payment method she selected before opening it.

“I buy things basically every day … I can grab multiple items at once after just opening the door,” she said. “The open-door machines are more convenient because you do not have to wait for items to drop one by one from traditional machines that sometimes get stuck.”

Over the decades, vending machines have evolved from simple dispensers of bottled or canned drinks into smart retail points that combine digital payments and data-driven consumer insights. They now offer a low-cost retail channel for third parties such as local charities, selling products like flowers and daily necessities – from disposable underwear to sanitary towels.

These artificial intelligence-powered open-door vending machines have been growing in popularity in Shenzhen in the past couple of years, but they remain uncommon in Hong Kong.

Some operators have pledged to install more of them across the city in the coming months, with one reporting higher sales revenue during the trial stage.

IVM Technology is one of Hong Kong’s largest operators, managing about 800 AI vending machines alongside 1,500 traditional ones in Hong Kong, the firm’s founder and managing director Leo Lui told the South China Morning Post.

Hong Kong had an estimated 15,000 to 17,000 vending machines, with the number expected to increase as the lower capital costs of AI machines attract new market entrants, Lui said.

“It will not surprise me if there are 30,000 to 40,000 machines later,” he said.

Lui pointed to Hong Kong’s exorbitant logistics, labour and parking costs – such as paying HK$200 just to park a delivery van for restocking at major commercial sites – as a major bottleneck.

Unlike mainland Chinese operators who could rely on low delivery expenses to sell low-margin goods, Hong Kong vending businesses faced fixed transport costs of about HK$2 per item, forcing them to focus on higher-priced, premium inventory, Lui said.

While the new open-door models generated 20 to 30 per cent more revenue in closed environments such as offices, traditional machines still outperformed them by 30 per cent in transient public spaces like bus stops, Lui explained.

“On the streets, some consumers might find the new machines are too slow, whereas with an Octopus card on a traditional machine, the product drops in a second after a purchase is made,” he said.

While nearly 90 per cent of new vending machines deployed on the mainland were AI open-door models, Hong Kong’s adoption remained significantly slower due to distinct local economic factors, said Rex Leung, general manager of IVM Technology.

The offline nature of the Octopus card contactless payment system presented a significant hurdle for AI machines, which required post-purchase settlement after the door was closed, Leung said.

“The physical Octopus card is an offline payment method where users tap and leave immediately, which is incompatible with this machine that charges users only after they finish shopping,” Leung added.

To resolve this issue, Octopus Cards was expected to launch an integration allowing users to scan a quick response (QR) code and settle payments online via the Octopus application, Lui said.

Leung added the company aimed to evolve into a platform that allowed a wider range of organisations to sell goods in their machines.

FreshUp, another local vending machine operator with a network of more than 5,000 machines, had set up more than 500 smart coolers that allowed customers to open the door, take products and be charged automatically through visual recognition technology, said David Lam, the group’s founder and CEO.

The smart models were generating 10 to 20 per cent more revenue per transaction than traditional push-button machines because the open-door design encouraged consumers to buy multiple items at once, Lam explained.

“People might have pressed buttons for individual items in the past, but now, since they have already opened the fridge to buy a drink, they might take chocolate or potato chips if they find them interesting, increasing the overall basket value or unit items per transaction,” Lam said.

The AI models required an upfront hardware cost of HK$20,000 to HK$30,000, which was similar to the price of traditional machines, he added.

While the local smart retail sector was projected to grow steadily at an annual rate of 5 to 10 per cent, operators had to pay a recurring fixed back-end computing fee to software providers for data processing every time the cabinet door was opened, Lam said.

Beyond commercial retail, the elimination of mechanical coils and rigid size restrictions has allowed open-door cabinets to serve as low-cost “micro-retail platforms” for non-governmental organisations and local brands seeking physical exposure without traditional overheads.

The new technology provided a low-cost retail alternative for charities such as the Po Leung Kuk, which sold products made by people with disabilities, said Choi Kai-yin, a social worker and service manager at the organisation.

Listing items in physical retail stores incurred high rental and administrative costs, making it difficult for charities to generate sufficient revenue to support their disabled creators, Choi said.

“Renting a shop is [costly], as we are selling bottled drinks for about HK$10 each, and it is hard to calculate how many bottles we need to sell to cover the rent,” Choi added.

By selling bottled tea at HK$12 through vending machines, the Po Leung Kuk hoped to create a reasonable profit margin, which would directly benefit individuals with disabilities in recognition of their contributions and participation in vocational training, Choi said.
