Swire Coca-Cola has been rolling out smart vending coolers on the mainland in recent years, as retail formats incorporating digital payments increase in popularity following the pandemic. Its Hong Kong bottling business has now begun introducing these coolers, which allow customers to open the door and select drinks, adapting technology and operating processes proven on the mainland.

The coolers are easy to operate: shoppers select a payment method before opening the door, choose their products and close the door. When the door is closed, the bill is settled.

“Consumers today expect to see it, want it and get it almost instantly, and Hong Kong is no exception. People want a cold drink close to where they live, work, study and play, and they want paying for it to be quick and simple,” said Hunter Jin, Greater China CEO of Swire Coca-Cola.

“Smart vending coolers meet that expectation by combining cashless payment with product-recognition technology, so the whole purchase feels seamless.”

Swire Coca-Cola has set up more than 150 coolers across sports and entertainment venues, workplaces, residential communities, educational institutions and industrial settings to reach locations unsuitable for conventional machines.

The new coolers would not completely replace the company’s network of about 6,000 conventional vending machines in Hong Kong, but would serve as a smart alternative offering a seamless digital experience, Swire Coca-Cola said.

“As Hong Kong continues to welcome major events and visitors, vending can do more than sell drinks,” Jin said. “We are exploring Hong Kong-themed vending and digital experiences at venues, transport hubs and tourist destinations that showcase local culture and add to the city’s vibrancy.”

item.title: [SCMP] Six legendary libraries, where architecture and academia meet
item.description:
Libraries are hard drives containing the memory of the world in an ancient form. Less pocketable than anything digital, but in many cases far prettier, these buildings are also sometimes works of art in their own right and cathedrals of humanism, whether erected four centuries ago or by a still-living architect of global acclaim.

Their beauty is inessential to their function but celebrates the knowledge they contain, the power and wealth or taste and intellect of those who commissioned them, or plays a role in preserving the essence of cultural identity.

You might visit one to see the masterful carpentry of ornate shelving, elaborate spiral staircases and walkways, stained glass, trompe l’oeil frescoes, carved marble and art, in addition to displays of rare and ancient books, maps, treaties, manuscripts and other historic documents. To the atmospheric silence and the smell of wax polish found in churches is added the warm aroma of ancient leather bindings.
item.content:encoded:
Libraries are hard drives containing the memory of the world in an ancient form. Less pocketable than anything digital, but in many cases far prettier, these buildings are also sometimes works of art in their own right and cathedrals of humanism, whether erected four centuries ago or by a still-living architect of global acclaim.

Their beauty is inessential to their function but celebrates the knowledge they contain, the power and wealth or taste and intellect of those who commissioned them, or plays a role in preserving the essence of cultural identity.

You might visit one to see the masterful carpentry of ornate shelving, elaborate spiral staircases and walkways, stained glass, trompe l’oeil frescoes, carved marble and art, in addition to displays of rare and ancient books, maps, treaties, manuscripts and other historic documents. To the atmospheric silence and the smell of wax polish found in churches is added the warm aroma of ancient leather bindings.

You might enter for some relief from the haste, heat and hustle of a big city, or because the libraries themselves have become popular meeting places, with cafes and places to sit.

Here are six institutions whose collections or buildings should not be overlooked, whatever reason you have for being in town.

The Real Biblioteca del Monasterio de San Lorenzo de El Escorial, Madrid, Spain

Philip II of Spain (1527-98) ruled one of the greatest empires in human history and did so much of the time from El Escorial, creating here the national library of the Kingdom of Spain in a room intended to be one of the most magnificent in the palace, and a rival for the richest libraries elsewhere in Europe, particularly cultural competitor Italy.

The main royal collections were transferred to the new building in 1566, even before the rest of the complex was ready for Philip to move in, although his advisers regretted that such magnificence was created in a remote spot, rather than in one of the university cities of the time.

Today, its improbable out-of-town location is part of the attraction, just a short local-train journey northwest from Madrid, followed by a stroll through pretty countryside that’s a pleasant relief from the capital’s intensity. The palace is ever more imposing as approached, and the heavily frescoed ceiling of its library, by a Milanese master referencing Michelangelo’s Sistine Chapel, is worth the trip in itself, even without taking into account what’s beneath it.

This includes ornate shelving and displays of ancient maps, coins, medals and scientific instruments. Philip’s giant armillary sphere, like a skeletal globe and representing the great circles of the heavens, has stood in the same spot here since 1593, when it was still thought that the sun and the rest of the heavens revolved around the Earth.

And there’s still the great church and the labyrinth of palace chambers, with their tapestries, art and furniture to see, before a reflective journey back to Madrid.

Veneranda Biblioteca Ambrosiana, Milan, Italy

Italy’s fashion capital is home to at least five historic libraries, of which the 18th century Biblioteca Nazionale Braidense is perhaps the most beautiful. But in terms of its collection, the Ambrosiana is the greatest of all, with more than a million volumes, including thousands of incunabula: printed books from before 1501, which are now very rare.

It was also one of the first in the world to open its doors to anyone who could read or write, and its users included mathematician, inventor and astronomer Galileo Galilei (1564-1642) – not your everyday influencer – who called it “heroic and immortal”. He may turn out to be right; opened in 1609, it has lasted for more than four centuries so far.

The hush of its long red-carpeted main room, with an ornate arched ceiling and dark bookcases in two tiers, is home to the world’s greatest collection of drawings and writings by Leonardo da Vinci (1452-1519), much of it on open display. Here, the polymath painter of The Last Supper (1495-98) and the Mona Lisa (1503), who was also an architect and engineer, can rather thrillingly be seen thinking out loud about geometry, anatomy, physics and assorted inventions, with many detailed illustrations in his own hand.

The Ambrosiana complex also incorporates an art gallery with masterpieces by Caravaggio, Botticelli, Raphael and many others, spanning four centuries.

You’ll need at least half a day here.

The Real Gabinete Português de Leitura, Rio de Janeiro, Brazil

While beautiful ancient libraries are most numerous in Europe, the 16th century voyagers to the New World took their ideas with them, and Rio’s Real Gabinete was founded in 1880 as a memorial to modern Brazil’s Portuguese roots, and to that country’s era of maritime dominance, by then already a fading memory.

While the library’s calm and cool interior is a welcome break from the swimwear parades of Rio’s beaches, there’s vibrant colour and decorative detail enough almost to match the city’s famous carnival. The eye scarcely knows where to rest, and many visiting photographers seem unsure where to point their lenses first.

Spiralling wooden pillars with gilded bosses support three galleried tiers of shelves. The heavily ornamented Manueline style of Portuguese cathedrals from 350 years earlier has been adapted to new purpose, but the interior is colourfully illuminated by a stained-glass dome in a cast-iron frame that was hi-tech for its day.

This is certainly memory in built form, harking back to past cultural ascendancy. The facade is a copy of a Lisbon monastery – carved limestone panels were created in Portugal and shipped out – and the library’s most prized possession is a first edition of poet Luís de Camões’ epic Os Lusíadas of 1572, widely considered Portuguese literature’s greatest work.

The library’s luxurious pseudo-antiquity is an almost shocking discovery in a humdrum Rio backstreet, although it’s far from merely a monument. The Real Gabinete still receives copies of every book published in Portugal, and so holds the largest overseas collection of Portuguese works.

The Morgan Library and Museum, New York, United States

Modern Madison Avenue may hardly seem the place for quiet contemplation, but here in 1906, the fabulously wealthy banker and industrialist J. Pierpont (JP) Morgan built himself a library that’s now part of a modern complex by “starchitect” Renzo Piano (he was behind the modern glass atrium and expansion completed in 2006), who also designed The New York Times Building (opened in 2007) and the Whitney Museum (current location opened in 2015).

But entering the Morgan Library makes you feel as though you’ve stepped through a time portal, as the building is in a style that was popular in the early 20th century, called American Renaissance, which harks back to the Europe of three centuries earlier. There are triple tiers of walnut shelving beneath a coffered ceiling copied from a Roman villa, murals of literary figures and walls hung with tapestries, which, with an ornate fireplace, manage to give it an air of domesticity.

The main draw, though, is Morgan’s acquisitions, which include the original manuscript of Charles Dickens’ A Christmas Carol (1843), the original score of a Mozart symphony, the only surviving complete draft of a Jane Austen novel (the early Lady Susan of 1794) and original prints by English poet, painter and printmaker William Blake (1757-1827).

It’s all highly restorative before a return to New York’s bedlam.

The Qatar National Library, Doha, Qatar

Although we’re now in the era of the e-reader and the on-demand download of just about anything, the age of great library-building is not over.

Doha’s Rem Koolhaas-designed building of 2018, with its 45,000 square metres of floor space, is supposed to resemble two folded pieces of paper, emphasising the importance of the written word in Qatari heritage. But on first impressions, it looks like a UFO about to launch itself into the sky.

The library’s vast and airy interior, well supplied with spaces in which to sit and read, is a haven against Doha’s often scorching heat. It’s more like a town square, and is a popular place to meet, with access to 3D printers and other tech as well as more than a million volumes in 16 languages available for loan. The interior is so vast that it looks ready to hold hundreds of millions more.

Only the basement recalls ancient European libraries, its warren of smaller spaces containing a magnificent display of Arabic calligraphy and illuminated manuscripts, very early maps of Arabia and accounts of both European exploration and the French invasion of Egypt, in 1798.

Yururi Yusuhara, Yusuhara, Japan

Libraries can be great without being grand or intimidating, and even the biggest architectural stars sometimes involve themselves in small projects.

Yusuhara, a sleepy community of 3,300, high up in the central mountains of the Japanese island of Shikoku, well away from the hordes tramping the famous 88-temple pilgrimage around the coastline, has almost become a second home to Kengo Kuma.

The architect is known for his large-scale projects, such as the Japan National Stadium, in Tokyo, but at Yusuhara, he’s indulged himself with local materials and a desire to develop traditional Japanese styles and techniques to produce something fresh. Amid typical Japanese domesticity, he’s built six wooden buildings, including a corridor bridge, a hotel that faintly resembles a haystack and an extraordinary library.

To enter from the wooded hills of the surrounding countryside is to seem to arrive at a forest rather than leave one. From a smooth cedar-wood floor (shoes must be removed, of course), pillars fork as they rise and end in a tangle of criss-crossing branch-like structures that descend again from the ceiling.

At floor level, the building is constructed of shelving that doubles as seating and as stairs forming multiple levels that also seat audiences for public events.

This isn’t a library in which to escape the pressures of the outside world, but a fully functional modern community service – complete with more than 70,000 volumes – unlike any other you may have visited.

item.title: [SCMP] Hong Kong bar trends in 2026: comfort, classics and mindful drinking
item.description:
Hong Kong’s drinks scene is one of the world’s best – but also one of the world’s most diverse and volatile. Every year, the city has had to navigate – to varying degrees of success – trends and shifts in what bargoers enjoy, resulting in celebrated openings and sombre closures alike. Speakeasies (The Old Man, Please Don’t Tell, Room 309, Stockton) in the 2010s gave way to neighbourhood bars in the 2020s. Publications like Time magazine, Fortune and Drinks International all note that Gen Z drinks less overall than their predecessors, swapping evening bar crawls for daytime coffee raves.

As we ease into 2026, we sat down with some of Hong Kong’s leading mixologists to explore the latest trends shaping the industry – showing how our bars are adapting to the way we drink and how that, in turn, is redefining our nights out.

Neighbourhood bars are still in, so keep it simple
item.content:encoded:
Hong Kong’s drinks scene is one of the world’s best – but also one of the world’s most diverse and volatile. Every year, the city has had to navigate – to varying degrees of success – trends and shifts in what bargoers enjoy, resulting in celebrated openings and sombre closures alike. Speakeasies (The Old Man, Please Don’t Tell, Room 309, Stockton) in the 2010s gave way to neighbourhood bars in the 2020s. Publications like Time magazine, Fortune and Drinks International all note that Gen Z drinks less overall than their predecessors, swapping evening bar crawls for daytime coffee raves.

As we ease into 2026, we sat down with some of Hong Kong’s leading mixologists to explore the latest trends shaping the industry – showing how our bars are adapting to the way we drink and how that, in turn, is redefining our nights out.

Neighbourhood bars are still in, so keep it simple

“I think of neighbourhood bars as focusing on simplicity and character, with an interior design that isn’t too elaborate,” says Antonio Lai, co-owner of Tastings Group, whose bars include Quinary, The Opposites and Draft Land.

A significant portion of bars that opened in the last two to three years have embraced some blend of relaxed atmosphere, simple drinks and a focus on community – think Socio, which upcycles surplus and waste ingredients from other venues, or Sugar King with its standing-room-only approach to Cuban-inspired cocktails. Hong Kong’s biggest success on the world stage, 2025 World’s Best Bar, Bar Leone is founded on similar tenets: accessible drinks and a convivial, casual atmosphere.

“Neighbourhood bars, to me, are places to have a drink in comfort,” says Samuel Kwok, who co-founded The Opposites with Lai. “Some places, like hotels, give the impression that you have to dress up a bit, or act or sit in a certain way,” he adds. “Sugar King and Mius [founded by Shelley Tai] have an atmosphere where you can just go in and have a drink, and the staff won’t bother you too frequently.”

Timeless, refined and classic flavours are in

If keeping it simple is at the root of the neighbourhood bar movement, classics are just one of the ways to get started. “People have always been wowed by bold, boundary-pushing innovation,” Singular Concepts and Tell Camellia co-founder Gagan Gurung says, “and we love serving [that need], but there’s been a noticeable shift to where guests are craving comfort. They’re reaching for those everyday, go-to cocktails that feel familiar, timeless and satisfying.”

Many of Hong Kong’s bars have pared back some part of their service to this effect. Both Sugar King and Montana opened on the strength of their daiquiris, also known as the “bartender’s handshake” (the cocktail represents a test of skill in producing the perfect balance of rum, lime and sweetness). Likewise, Kwok cites Bar Leone’s selection of classically inspired drinks as key to its success: “They are cocktails you could probably make at home and understand easily. Younger, newer bartenders these days are increasingly interested in the classics – a sort of return to form.”

“Trends come and go,” Gurung continues, “but the truth is everyone needs their all-time favourite, whether it’s a negroni, a daiquiri or a perfectly balanced Old Fashioned. Innovation excites, but comfort keeps people coming back.”

Less is more – comfort and moderation are key

For Ajit Gurung (no relation to Gagan Gurung), co-founder of The Savory Project, a part of this comfort lies in the way drinks are presented – especially when it comes to bars like his, which continue to find success with bold and innovative flavours. “I think tasting menu-style cocktails will dominate a lot of markets,” he says. “Small portions of multiple courses for cocktails is a great way to showcase new ideas and flavours without overwhelming guests.”

Draft Land and Bar Oasis are two examples of bars boasting exceptional cocktails on tap, allowing guests to sample before they order. “We’ve already pushed the boundaries of food and cocktail innovation – the real differentiator is in how we make people feel,” Gagan Gurung says. “It’s about the entire guest experience.”

Guests are becoming more selective when it comes to those experiences, seeking out spots they trust for drinks they are comfortable with. “Refined drinking is the way forward,” says Ajit Gurung. “Guests are more health conscious and are drinking less. They are selective about where they drink, how much sugar is in their drink, what spirits are used. They are following the bartenders as each has a different style of experiences they provide.”

“The younger generation may prefer to drink quality over quantity, just sipping a couple of glasses at any one bar,” Lai says. “They may also bar hop or prefer a low- or no-ABV style of drinking, and may start earlier in the day with coffee. The earlier they start, the earlier they can sleep, and the less they’ll be affected the next day.”

“People today are far more health conscious,” Gagan Gurung notes. “Whether it’s about wellness, mindfulness or just opting for a more balanced lifestyle, drinking habits are clearly shifting.”

Local ingredients for well-travelled guests

If bargoers are to step outside their comfort zone, it may well be to try a local ingredient far from home. “Guests now are well travelled and constantly looking for new experiences,” Ajit Gurung says. “Bold, culinary-driven ideas are the perfect category of cocktail for guests with more sophisticated palates.”

He is referring mainly to the resurgence of savoury cocktails, but Lai and Kwok see the same spirit of exploration extending to greater interaction with China. For Lai, Chinese-produced wines and spirits, including non-alcoholic sparkling spirits, will be more ubiquitous. Kwok adds that more bartenders from mainland China will go overseas for guest shifts.

“The new generation of [Chinese] bartenders is getting better in terms of language and communication, which has always been the biggest barrier,” he says. “China also has a lot more to show the world in terms of techniques and ingredients.” Kwok points out that China’s eight great cuisines are distinct and ripe for discovery. “Yunnan has great teas. Some areas have great herbs, while others have great spices and chillies. Every time I go to China, I see things I’ve never seen before thanks to this diversity.”

The reverse is also increasingly true – over the last few years, Bar Leone, Coa and Penicillin have opened branches in Shanghai. Lai hopes to open a branch of Quinary on the mainland, but obstacles remain.

“A surprising barrier is toilets, especially in second- and third-tier cities – even Hongkongers don’t know how to navigate the situation,” Kwok says. “We went to Chengdu once and every toilet was a squat toilet. If you’re hosting guests in China, taking them to truly local places requires them to navigate those toilets.”

“If I open a bar in China,” Lai says emphatically, “I will require sitting toilets!”

item.title: [SCMP] New Everest film hopes to nudge US-China relations into a higher altitude
item.description:
The film Everest: The Other Side, a collaborative US-China project that opened on Friday in 515 US cinemas and that will premiere at 700 IMAX theatres in China on November 6, starts with a majestic shot of the world’s tallest mountain. Then the music builds and more challenging weather rolls in, foreshadowing what is at stake.

The film invokes a well-trod narrative for fans of the mountaineering genre: a mix of the grit and sacrifice driving world-class climbers, along with no small amount of tragedy among these extreme humans driven to take on epic risks.

What is different is that this ascent finally succeeded on its third attempt by master climber Jim Morrison, not on more conventional Nepal and Tibetan routes, where we are told that 13,000 climbers have reached the pinnacle.
item.content:encoded:
The film Everest: The Other Side, a collaborative US-China project that opened on Friday in 515 US cinemas and that will premiere at 700 IMAX theatres in China on November 6, starts with a majestic shot of the world’s tallest mountain. Then the music builds and more challenging weather rolls in, foreshadowing what is at stake.

The film invokes a well-trod narrative for fans of the mountaineering genre: a mix of the grit and sacrifice driving world-class climbers, along with no small amount of tragedy among these extreme humans driven to take on epic risks.

What is different is that this ascent finally succeeded on its third attempt by master climber Jim Morrison, not on more conventional Nepal and Tibetan routes, where we are told that 13,000 climbers have reached the pinnacle.

Rather, it took place on China’s Hornbein Couloir route, which only five climbers have reportedly ascended, with a twist. Morrison was also the only one ever to ski back down, a feat that took over four hours on incredibly steep slopes with no margin of error.

Morrison is driven by grief and harrowing memories as we learn not only that his wife and two children crashed and died in a plane that she was piloting in 2015.

But after meeting fellow world-renowned ski mountaineer Hilaree Nelson four years later, he then watched her die in 2022 in an avalanche as they prepared for their shared Everest attempt.

“I hope that it inspires people to get through their Everest, their hardship, whether that’s a big goal in life or a sickness of a family member,” Morrison said at a premiere at the Asia Society in New York. “We’re all going to go through difficult times.”

Much of the film is focused on how to cope with the death of loved ones, the cost of embracing life on the edge and his desire to memorialise Nelson by successfully carrying out their shared dream.

Interwoven is also the cold calculus of life at the extreme as Morrison skis down to get experts – who ultimately took two days to recover Nelson’s body after bad weather set in – rather than try and dig her out. This is followed by his resolve a few months after her death to resume his quest, convinced she would have wanted him to forge ahead.

The documentary, backed by National Geographic and the Walt Disney Company, was directed by award-winning filmmakers and climbers Jimmy Chin and Elizabeth Chai Vasarhelyi, friends of Morrison and Nelson, who are both directors and characters in the narrative.

The film took six years to make, weathering personal setbacks, the pandemic, two failed attempts and very narrow weather windows before Morrison’s successful ascent.

“This movie is a miracle on top of a miracle on top of a miracle,” said Janet Yang, the film’s producer, in an interview in New York’s famed Chelsea Hotel, briefly the city’s tallest building that has hosted the likes of Bob Dylan, Mark Twain, Janis Joplin and Andy Warhol over the years.

Yang was the project’s principal bridge between the US and China, the problem solver and cultural whisperer, overseeing the endless coordination required to secure permits and approval during years when the two nations grew increasingly wary of each other.

But she had an ally, however unfortunate, in the Covid-19 outbreak.

“We had more time than we thought we would,” she said. “There were a lot of Zooms and a lot of different departments that had to get involved. It just is not that interesting to talk about. It’s also a lot about the cultural sensitivity.”

Yang has been here before, in a long career introducing Chinese film to the West and Hollywood productions to China.

In 1986, she brought Chen Kaige’s Yellow Earth to the US. The following year, she worked with director Steven Spielberg on Empire of the Sun, one of the first major productions filmed on the Mainland since 1949, before partnering with Oliver Stone on The Joy Luck Club in 1993, with its hallmark all-Asian cast.

Along the way, the native New Yorker became the first Asian-American president of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences before assuming the chairmanship of the Committee of 100 earlier this year.

Yang sees film as a way to bridge the enormous gaps separating the US and China. The US side often has a highly simplistic, monolithic and inherently suspicious view of China, she said, although the recent personal ties between President Donald Trump and President Xi Jinping have helped.

“This kind of reductive, absurd mentality about China is what I’ve been fighting,” she said. “It’s much more multidimensional and complex and layered and human.”

China, meanwhile, could benefit by acting with greater confidence, she added, rather than reacting in ways that can be misunderstood overseas where there is little knowledge of its history of exploitation by Western powers.

Everest: The Other Side has incredible footage and a heartwarming narrative. Nature as a lowest common denominator can act as a cultural bridge far from politics or polemics.

But the decidedly safe topic contrasts with some of Yang’s past projects that grappled with history, rural poverty and crumbling dynasties.

“There’s again nothing controversial, nothing sensitive, not because we were going out of our way to avoid it, but just because, by the nature of the subject, it just transcends national boundaries, cultures,” said Yang. “It’s not political truth. It’s about people’s dreams, but also the lure of nature.”

Films involving foreign partners in China are either classified as official co-productions, which Beijing generally funds and distributes as Chinese films, or assisted productions like Everest that allow more leeway, though their content is still carefully vetted.

At one point, one of the Nepalese climbers gets hurt and fellow Sherpas balk at continuing, their internal differences and criticism played out on the screen.

Yang said the production team debated at length before ultimately deciding to leave this in, a rawness that depicts the power and economic imbalance in a climbing team.

“I’m very happy,” she said. “It’s very real.”

The technical challenges of shots, equipment and filming in brutal conditions were significant, and there were no second chances, said Chin, who, along with his wife Chai Vasarhelyi, shot the 2018 Academy Award-winning documentary Free Solo.

“Every extra person or extra camera up there creates a lot more exposure to risk,” he said.

“Every single one of those shots on the ski descent, those are all single takes because we weren’t going to make him go back up there to recreate it.”

At a time when US-China tensions are omnipresent, spanning trade, security, technology, Taiwan, misunderstanding and the ever-present risk of a crisis, Yang still believes film can help ease the distrust.

“This is my Everest. I want to climb it. I have to believe it’s possible. Am I deluding myself?” she said, before concluding that the needle has moved over the decades, however unquantifiable the progress often is by definition.

item.title: [SCMP] Why the Philippines remains a hotspot for transnational drug syndicates
item.description:
Transnational drug syndicates in the Philippines continue to thrive despite decades of crackdowns targeting street-level dealers, with analysts warning that regional suppliers, financiers and trafficking networks have largely eluded enforcement efforts.

Former drug officials and security analysts say the country’s drug trade remains closely connected to a wider regional supply chain, with criminal groups relying on local partners, maritime routes and established distribution networks to move methamphetamine across Southeast Asia.

A foiled attempt to smuggle US$55 million worth of methamphetamine aboard a private jet in Laos, allegedly bound for the Philippines, has brought renewed attention to these cross-border operations, prompting a House investigation into suspected Philippine connections.
item.content:encoded:
Transnational drug syndicates in the Philippines continue to thrive despite decades of crackdowns targeting street-level dealers, with analysts warning that regional suppliers, financiers and trafficking networks have largely eluded enforcement efforts.

Former drug officials and security analysts say the country’s drug trade remains closely connected to a wider regional supply chain, with criminal groups relying on local partners, maritime routes and established distribution networks to move methamphetamine across Southeast Asia.

A foiled attempt to smuggle US$55 million worth of methamphetamine aboard a private jet in Laos, allegedly bound for the Philippines, has brought renewed attention to these cross-border operations, prompting a House investigation into suspected Philippine connections.

At least five transnational drug networks operate in the Philippines, according to Mark Anthony Santos, chairman of the House committee on dangerous drugs, who cited information from an unnamed senior police official.

Chinese and Chinese-Filipino trafficking groups, as well as Mexican and West African drug cartels, including the Sinaloa cartel, dominated the country’s drug black market, Santos said.

“Drug syndicates do not operate solely through street-level distribution. They exploit private aircraft, maritime routes, financial intermediaries, and gaps in coordination among jurisdictions. Even when a shipment is intercepted, the people financing and organising the operation may remain beyond the reach of investigators,” Santos said in a statement on October 22.

“Authorities must look beyond intercepted shipments, follow the money, and work with foreign law enforcement to identify and dismantle the syndicates behind the drug trade.”

Among the major networks operating in the region is Sam Gor, an alliance of Chinese criminal groups linked to the crystal meth trade. It is estimated to control 40 per cent to 70 per cent of the regional drug market, operating through partners and criminal groups.

At a briefing earlier this month, Philippine Drug Enforcement Agency (PDEA) director general Isagani Nerez confirmed that Sam Gor comprised an alliance of five major Chinese triad groups: the 14K Triad, Bamboo Union, Big Circle Gang, Sun Yee On and Wo Shing Wo, whose leaders are believed to be based in Hong Kong and Taiwan.

This Week in Asia has reached out to PDEA for comment.

Sam Gor is reportedly also present in Vietnam, Cambodia, Laos, Myanmar, Thailand, New Zealand, Australia, South Korea, Japan, mainland China and Taiwan.

An evolution

Former drug officials and analysts said the potential Philippine connection to the foiled shipment in Laos, as well as the presence of transnational drug cartels in the country, reflected a long-standing problem dating back decades.

“These connections have existed for many years, particularly in the methamphetamine trade, where regional suppliers have historically relied on local Chinese and Filipino-Chinese groups for domestic distribution,” a former Philippine drug official, who requested anonymity, told This Week in Asia.

“The Philippines’ geographical location, extensive coastlines, maritime borders, and significant domestic demand make it vulnerable to these activities.”

Jeremy Douglas, deputy director of operations at the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime, agrees that the Philippines has long remained a major market for illicit drugs – mostly methamphetamine, known locally as shabu – from the Golden Triangle, the mountainous border region where Thailand, Myanmar and Laos converge near the Ruak and Mekong rivers.

The presence and activities of transnational organised crime groups in the Philippines have been observed for at least the past 10 to 20 years, according to Dr Rohan Gunaratna, a professor of security studies at the S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies at Nanyang Technological University.

“What we are seeing today is largely a continuation and evolution of criminal networks that have long operated across the region,” he said.

Gunaratna called the Southeast Asian drug trade ecosystem “highly dynamic, interconnected and adaptive”.

“It operates through a regional supply chain in which different countries play different roles, from manufacturing and precursor sourcing to transport, wholesale distribution and consumption,” he said.

Chinese transnational criminal organisations are significant actors in this ecosystem as their influence extends well beyond the direct trafficking of drugs, according to Gunaratna. “Their networks and business relationships enable them to connect production facilities with wholesale distributors and established criminal groups in destination markets.”

The region’s major drug markets included Thailand, the Philippines, Indonesia, Malaysia and Vietnam, Gunaratna said, although the scale and nature of consumption and trafficking varied across countries.

“Beyond Southeast Asia, Australia and other Asia-Pacific markets also remain important destinations for regional drug supplies,” he said.

The Philippines’ drug trade

The methamphetamine trade in the Philippines has historically been connected to the wider regional supply chain controlled by Chinese transnational criminal organisations, including networks associated with Sam Gor, according to Gunaratna.

He said Chinese transnational criminal groups played a significant role in establishing the meth trade in the Philippines during the 1990s. Over time, methamphetamine became the country’s dominant illicit drug market.

“At the higher levels, these networks have played a significant role in the sourcing and moving methamphetamine supplies, while local Chinese and Filipino-Chinese criminal groups have traditionally handled domestic wholesale distribution and retail networks,” he said.

Regional suppliers and local distribution networks did not necessarily work as a unified organisation, but through interconnected relationships and supply arrangements, he added.

Aside from its extensive coastline and several islands, the Philippines’ weak governance and corruption among law enforcement personnel and government officials created opportunities for organised criminal groups to operate, Gunaratna said.

He pointed to the Zamboanga-Basilan-Sulu-Tawi-Tawi corridor, which connects the southern Philippines with maritime areas bordering Malaysia and Indonesia, as an area of concern.

“Its geography, combined with informal maritime routes and limited enforcement coverage in certain areas, creates opportunities for the movement of illicit commodities across national boundaries,” Gunaratna said, adding that the Philippines primarily served as a destination and distribution market for drugs, and occasionally a transshipment point for markets such as Australia.

These operations predate former president Rodrigo Duterte’s administration, which launched a controversial war on drugs from 2016 to 2022 that left thousands dead.

But targeting lower-level players in the domestic market “does not necessarily translate into dismantling the larger regional supply chains, which operate across multiple jurisdictions”, said the former drug official.

“The drug problem was significant then, and it is now; the fundamentals of the regional drug market, the use and demand and the supply remain a major challenge the Philippines and [its] neighbours are still grappling with,” Douglas said.

item.title: [SCMP] Will diversifying fuel imports be enough to fix Indonesia’s energy shortfall?
item.description:
Indonesia is looking beyond Singapore for petrol supplies as it seeks to reduce its dependence on a single source, but analysts say diversifying imports will do little to address the country’s fuel production shortfall without faster refinery modernisation and investment in alternative fuels.

Indonesia has long sourced petroleum products from Singapore, including RON 90 petrol, which has a minimum octane rating of 90 and is marketed domestically as Pertalite. Singapore’s geographic proximity, advanced blending facilities and extensive storage capacity have made it a key supplier to Indonesia.

Jakarta is now trying to diversify away from Singapore and is looking for alternative suppliers such as China and India, according to Minister of Energy and Mineral Resources Bahlil Lahadalia.
item.content:encoded:
Indonesia is looking beyond Singapore for petrol supplies as it seeks to reduce its dependence on a single source, but analysts say diversifying imports will do little to address the country’s fuel production shortfall without faster refinery modernisation and investment in alternative fuels.

Indonesia has long sourced petroleum products from Singapore, including RON 90 petrol, which has a minimum octane rating of 90 and is marketed domestically as Pertalite. Singapore’s geographic proximity, advanced blending facilities and extensive storage capacity have made it a key supplier to Indonesia.

Jakarta is now trying to diversify away from Singapore and is looking for alternative suppliers such as China and India, according to Minister of Energy and Mineral Resources Bahlil Lahadalia.

“We know that we import RON 90 fuel from a neighbouring country, so starting tomorrow I will be leaving for several countries, including India, China and other countries, to get certainty about supplies,” Bahlil told reporters on Monday.

The ministry has yet to provide an update on Bahlil’s trips. It did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

According to Bahlil, the government does not want to “rely on a single source of supply”, considering that nearly 60 per cent of Indonesia’s fuel imports currently come from Singapore.

Data from statistics agency BPS showed that 28.36 per cent of Indonesia’s oil and gas imports in the first half of this year came from Singapore.

Bahlil said the shift to China and India was also a precaution in case Singapore retaliated against Jakarta’s decision to cut natural gas exports to the city state by 31 million standard cubic feet per day. Indonesia currently supplies gas to Singapore with a total volume of 409.5 MMSCFD.

“Before we take any step, it is impossible not to consider or take everything into account,” he said.

Bahlil revealed on October 23 that the subsidised Pertalite reserves covered consumption for just 18 days, while reserves for the non-subsidised fuel stood at over 20 days.

Insufficient refinery capacity

The move to seek alternative partnerships highlights Indonesia’s fuel production gaps, as its refining capability cannot keep up with growing domestic demand.

Indonesia’s current refinery capacity sits at about 1 million barrels per day, but daily domestic consumption requires 1.6 million barrels, according to Fabby Tumiwa, executive director of the Institute for Essential Services Reform. Singapore offset the gap by up to 400,000 barrels per day, he said.

“Singapore’s fuel production is well-suited to our fuel needs. We also know that Singapore is a regional refining and trading hub. The trading ecosystem there is very liquid, making it easy to buy fuel on the spot or long-term market,” Fabby told This Week in Asia.

“From an energy security perspective, relying on a single source with large volumes is unsafe. We must diversify, both the products and sources.”

Fabby said “not all refineries in Indonesia operate continuously”, while some new refinery projects planned by state-owned oil and gas company Pertamina “simply cannot proceed due to lack of financing or investors”.

The United States’ Energy Information Administration estimated the average utilisation rate of eight Indonesian refineries in 2024 at 79 per cent, the latest data available.

“It’s not that Indonesia lacks refineries. The question is whether the capacity and configuration of the available refineries can produce the type and volume of petrol the public needs,” said Iwa Garniwa, rector of the PLN Institute of Technology in Jakarta.

During former president Joko Widodo’s first term, Indonesia announced seven new refinery projects to boost domestic fuel production; only one, the massive refinery upgrade project in Balikpapan, has materialised.

Bahlil said last week the Balikpapan refinery, which cost Jakarta US$7.4 billion to build, would meet up to a quarter of domestic fuel demand.

Muhammad Baron, Pertamina’s vice-president of corporate communication, said in a statement to This Week in Asia that the Balikpapan refinery underlined the government’s efforts to “reduce dependence on fuel imports by increasing refinery capacity and optimising domestic resources”.

“[The Balikpapan refinery] increases crude oil processing capacity and refinery capabilities to process residues into higher-value products, producing Euro V-quality fuel,” Muhammad said.

Euro V petrol indicates a cleaner fuel standard that limits emissions of sulphur, carbon monoxide and particulate matter.

Iwa said the future of other refinery projects depended on “significant capital investment”, whether foreign or domestic.

“Investors need to take into account crude oil prices, processing margins, exchange rates, domestic fuel prices and the risk of policy changes. If the project’s economics are unattractive or the risk allocation is unclear, investors may delay their investment decision,” Iwa said.

He pointed to the long-delayed construction of the New Grass Root Refinery in Tuban, East Java, a joint project between Kilang Pertamina Internasional and Russian oil giant Rosneft. The project, expected to process up to 300,000 barrels of crude per day, has languished in the planning stage since 2015.

“The Tuban project’s experience demonstrates that changing geopolitical conditions and partner issues can affect project timelines,” Iwa said.

For now, the government could meet the rising Pertalite demand by sourcing it from countries such as South Korea, Japan, Malaysia, Thailand and the United Arab Emirates, Iwa said.

Alternative fuels

Aside from building new refineries, Muhammad said Pertamina “continues to increase domestic oil production, optimise its use as a raw material for refineries, and increase processing efficiency and reliability”.

Pertamina was also developing a domestic bioethanol supply as a petrol blending component to support the government’s implementation of the B50 biofuel programme, he added.

The B50 blend consists of 50 per cent crude palm oil and 50 per cent fossil diesel.

As Indonesia aims for fuel self-sufficiency by 2028, Fabby urged the government to begin cultivating more bioethanol-producing crops such as sugar cane, sorghum and corn.

“If we work hard, E10 might be achievable by 2028,” Fabby said, referring to a fuel blend of up to 10 per cent renewable bioethanol and 90 per cent fossil fuel.

“However, targeting E50 by 2028 will be quite difficult, as it requires a surge in bioethanol production, vast areas of land and [considerable] time since crops cannot grow overnight.”

item.title: [SCMP] Singapore tells suppliers to ‘honour commitments’ amid Indonesia’s gas cut
item.description:
Singapore expects all parties who have signed commercial contracts for gas supplies to “honour their commitments”, said Prime Minister Lawrence Wong on Sunday after Indonesia cut its exports.

Speaking at the People’s Action Party (PAP) convention, Wong added that Singapore’s gas importer will take the necessary steps to protect its rights and interests.

Indonesia began reducing natural gas exports to Singapore on Saturday. Indonesia’s upstream oil and gas regulator SKK Migas said the move was to divert more supplies to domestic electricity needs.
item.content:encoded:
Singapore expects all parties who have signed commercial contracts for gas supplies to “honour their commitments”, said Prime Minister Lawrence Wong on Sunday after Indonesia cut its exports.

Speaking at the People’s Action Party (PAP) convention, Wong added that Singapore’s gas importer will take the necessary steps to protect its rights and interests.

Indonesia began reducing natural gas exports to Singapore on Saturday. Indonesia’s upstream oil and gas regulator SKK Migas said the move was to divert more supplies to domestic electricity needs.

Singapore’s Energy Market Authority said the reduction of 31 million standard cubic feet of gas a day amounts to less than 2 per cent of Singapore’s total daily gas demand.

About 95 per cent of Singapore’s electricity is generated using natural gas and it imports a significant amount of this gas through pipelines from Indonesia.

“The gas supplies are covered by commercial contracts. We expect all parties to honour their commitments and Singapore’s gas importer will take the necessary steps to protect its rights and interests under these contracts,” Wong said.

Singapore has been readying itself for such risks, the prime minister added. It has invested in liquefied natural gas (LNG) terminals to import natural gas from different countries, without having to rely on pipelines, providing more options to manage any disruptions to supply.

However, Singapore must look beyond natural gas to cleaner sources of power that can provide reliable electricity around the clock, Wong added.

This is why authorities are studying the potential of nuclear energy, he said.

“Understandably, there are concerns about the safety of nuclear power in a small and densely populated country like Singapore. We take the concerns very seriously. Safety must come first,” Wong said.

“But we should not rule out an option simply because it is difficult or controversial. We must assess the risks and trade-offs carefully, engage Singaporeans, and eventually make the right decision to secure our energy future.”

From 2027, Singapore will be embarking on an assessment by the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) to gauge the country’s ability to make an informed decision on adopting nuclear energy.

Known as the IAEA’s Integrated Nuclear Infrastructure Review, each phase comes with key milestones that have to be reached to guide countries in their understanding of the commitments and obligations associated with developing a nuclear power programme.

Wong said: “Dealing with today’s concerns is only part of our job. We must also prepare Singapore for tomorrow – that means looking ahead, anticipating problems and acting before they become more difficult to solve.

“Consider the economy of the future. It will still be driven by ideas and talent, but computing power will become increasingly important and that requires enormous amounts of energy.”

In his speech, Wong noted that the world has become more “dangerous and troubled”, with harder challenges, but Singapore faces these difficulties from a position of strength, he added.

“We remain a trusted partner and an attractive place for businesses and investors,” the prime minister said.

In addition, Singapore is proactively strengthening partnerships across different regions of the world, with office-holders travelling more frequently to build relationships and deepen cooperation.

In the past week, President Tharman Shanmugaratnam made a state visit to Sweden, while Wong recently returned from Qatar and the United Arab Emirates.

“These countries are in different parts of the world, but they all see value in working closely with Singapore,” Wong said. “That reflects the trust and goodwill we have built over many years.”

Singapore is known as a reliable partner, a trusted hub and a country that delivers on its commitment, Wong said.

“This reputation is a vital asset, especially in today’s fragmented and troubled world. It helps us attract high-quality investments,” he added. “And the investments support growth, create jobs and enable incomes to rise.”

Some challenges are harder to tackle as they cross national borders – these include online scams or haze.

Singapore is grappling with its worst haze episode since 2015. It has sent notices to 10 Singapore-based firms and 10 Indonesian firms under the Transboundary Haze Pollution Act.

“We cannot solve these problems through our own efforts alone. We need cooperation from other countries,” Wong said.

“But that does not mean we stand by and do nothing. We are doing everything we can within our power to protect Singaporeans, strengthen our own response and work with partners to tackle these problems at source.”

Touching on governance, Wong said that the Singapore we want cannot simply be delivered by the government to Singaporeans, and has to be “built with Singaporeans”.

“That is the partnership we strive for: a PAP government that listens, acts and delivers. A people who step forward and contribute and a society where everyone looks out for one another.”

While Singaporeans have given the PAP a strong mandate to govern for another term, this mandate is not an “entitlement”, Wong said.

“It is a responsibility to deliver what we promised, tackle the difficult issues facing our country and prepare Singapore for what lies ahead. That is why we must never take the trust of Singaporeans for granted. After all, no political party has a permanent claim on that trust,” Wong said.

“Every generation of PAP leaders and activists must earn it afresh. We know what is expected of us. We must listen and deliver. We must hold ourselves to high standards and we must always put Singapore and Singaporeans first.”

Wong noted that while some sectors of Singapore’s economy are doing well, others are facing pressures.

Some workers are benefiting from new opportunities, but others are struggling to keep up. Lower-wage workers worry about keeping pace with rising costs, while Singaporeans in their 40s and 50s who lose their jobs worry about finding work again.

“We understand these concerns and we will respond to them. Our task is not just to keep the economy growing. It is to make sure that growth translates into better lives for all Singaporeans,” he said.

The government is also doing more to ease the burdens on parents and give families greater assurance, as seen by measures introduced at this year’s National Day Rally, he added.

Wong acknowledged that the government has a “full agenda”, such as continuing to tackle the cost-of-living pressures and helping Singapore secure better jobs.

Ultimately, the government will do its part, but everybody has a part to play too, the prime minister said.

“We will create opportunities and support workers through change, but workers must be prepared to learn and adapt,” Wong said.

“We will reduce the emphasis on exams and broaden education pathways, but parents must give their children space to grow at their own pace.

“We will strengthen support for families and seniors, but all of us must also look out for one another.”

This story was first published by CNA

item.title: [SCMP] US Democrats prepare to counter any Trump claim of foreign meddling in midterms
item.description:
Top Democrats on the US congressional intelligence committees say they are preparing to check and respond to any claim by US President Donald Trump that foreign powers interfered in the November 3 midterm elections, even though they say they have seen no sign of any country interfering with voting or vote counting.

The concern comes as Democrats lead by eight points among likely voters in the fight for control of Congress, according to an October 27 PBS News/NPR/Marist poll. It also follows a prime-time address in July in which Trump singled out China, alleging that Beijing interfered in the 2020 election, a claim not substantiated by the evidence he released.

“We continue to see nothing to contradict the long-standing assessment by the [intelligence community] that no adversary has attempted to interfere with the physical infrastructure or vote counting of our elections,” Representative Jim Himes of Connecticut, the top Democrat on the House Intelligence Committee, said in a statement on October 27.
item.content:encoded:
Top Democrats on the US congressional intelligence committees say they are preparing to check and respond to any claim by US President Donald Trump that foreign powers interfered in the November 3 midterm elections, even though they say they have seen no sign of any country interfering with voting or vote counting.

The concern comes as Democrats lead by eight points among likely voters in the fight for control of Congress, according to an October 27 PBS News/NPR/Marist poll. It also follows a prime-time address in July in which Trump singled out China, alleging that Beijing interfered in the 2020 election, a claim not substantiated by the evidence he released.

“We continue to see nothing to contradict the long-standing assessment by the [intelligence community] that no adversary has attempted to interfere with the physical infrastructure or vote counting of our elections,” Representative Jim Himes of Connecticut, the top Democrat on the House Intelligence Committee, said in a statement on October 27.

The statement said the committee had received its fifth pre-election briefing from senior intelligence officials, and gave no further details.

Himes and Senator Mark Warner of Virginia, the top Democrat on the Senate Intelligence Committee, previously also said the administration has not provided the statutorily required reports on foreign threats due 120, 60 and 30 days before the election.

The lawmakers also said they had asked Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton and CIA Director John Ratcliffe to be reachable by phone on Election Day so they can check any claims of foreign interference in real time, according to NPR and CBS News.

“We start with the premise that the president is going to do that,” Himes said at a briefing with reporters, according to NPR.

“We’re making the assumption that the president is not going to accept the results of what looks to be a very challenging election for him and his party.”

A spokesman for the Office of the Director of National Intelligence told CBS News that Clayton had told both intelligence committees he was available “24/7 on any issue”.

A CIA spokesman also said Ratcliffe would continue to be available to the agency’s oversight committees as appropriate.

Trump says he’ll accept results but not ‘cheating’

Asked earlier this month whether he would accept the results, Trump said he would, but added: “We don’t want cheating.”

Representative Rick Crawford, the House committee’s Republican chairman, did not respond to requests for comment on whether his party agrees with the Democrats’ assessment.

The Office of the Director of National Intelligence did not respond to a request for comment on election interference.

A White House official told the South China Morning Post that, following task force findings on what the official described as China’s “illicit acquisition” of 220 million voter files and Chinese-made parts in voting machines.

The voter files Trump cited in July were not confidential, according to people familiar with the matter cited by news agencies at the time.

Political consultants routinely buy such files. A 2021 US intelligence assessment concluded that China did not deploy efforts to change the outcome of the 2020 presidential election.

The official also cited an August 24 letter from Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin to the White House Transparency Task Force.

It cited declassified records saying China remains “the most active and persistent cyber threat” to US networks, and an October 2024 intelligence memo saying China, Iran and Russia “have the technical capability to access some US election-related networks and systems”.

The letter also said the three largest voting machine vendors, which make up more than 80 per cent of the market, acknowledge Chinese-made parts. The letter did not allege that any machine had been tampered with.

The Trump administration has also stepped up efforts to address alleged voter fraud ahead of the midterm elections.

The Department of Homeland Security is requiring funded states to audit five per cent of paper ballots after the 2026 election. The process involves manually checking a random sample of ballots against machine-reported results to verify accuracy and identify potential errors or manipulation.

The US Justice Department sent letters to election officials in all 50 states on October 29, reminding them to preserve federal election records for 22 months and warning that violations could carry criminal penalties, including prison time and fines.

No interference, but influence

Omar Noureldin, senior vice-president of policy and litigation at Common Cause, a democracy and voting rights advocacy group, said influence, such as social media bots spreading disinformation, had been seen in past election cycles, while interference targeted the mechanics and technical infrastructure of elections.

“I want to be clear that there have been no credible reports of foreign interference,” Noureldin said about the 2026 midterm.

Although there are no signs of Chinese interference with voting or vote counting, lawmakers say Beijing is conducting influence operations in the US.

NPR reported that Himes and Warner said a classified intelligence briefing detailed Chinese influence operations targeting US elections.

“China’s been more selective, oftentimes on local races or smaller issues, oftentimes with Chinese nationals involved,” Warner told NPR.

Neither lawmaker has said which races are targeted, what methods are being used or how this cycle compares with earlier ones. Their offices did not respond to the SCMP’s requests for detail by publication time.

In July, Trump cited declassified intelligence on China’s acquisition of American voter data. An SCMP analysis in July also found little evidence supporting Trump’s claims.

It found documented Chinese interest in US voter data but no specific action to manipulate votes, divisions within the intelligence community over Beijing’s intentions, and questionable claims of an FBI cover-up.

Beijing rejected the allegations Trump made in July, as it has similar accusations over the years. Chinese foreign ministry spokesman Lin Jian called the claims fabricated, malicious and long proven groundless.

He said China respected the principle of non-interference and had never meddled in US domestic affairs, and urged Washington to examine its own conduct, including global surveillance and data theft.

Noureldin also accused the administration of cutting more than US$700 million from the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency’s budget, weakening its ability to monitor such threats, and urged the next Congress to restore the funding.

He nevertheless expressed confidence in the resilience of US election systems against hacking, citing their decentralised structure.

“Our election administration system is a blessing and a curse,” he said.

“It is decentralised across tens of thousands of election jurisdictions, which makes foreign interference in the infrastructure of our election administration system very, very difficult.”

item.title: [SCMP] Can Connie Chan become San Francisco’s first Asian-American in Congress?
item.description:
On a recent warm Thursday evening, supporters drift into San Francisco’s United Irish Cultural Centre to hear Connie Chan, who is running for California’s 11th congressional district.

Born in Hong Kong, Chan attended elementary school in Taiwan before immigrating to the United States at 13. Now a San Francisco supervisor, she hopes to succeed long-time Democratic powerhouse Nancy Pelosi, who announced her retirement and endorsed her.

The 48-year-old politician would be the first Asian-American to represent the city in Congress.
item.content:encoded:
On a recent warm Thursday evening, supporters drift into San Francisco’s United Irish Cultural Centre to hear Connie Chan, who is running for California’s 11th congressional district.

Born in Hong Kong, Chan attended elementary school in Taiwan before immigrating to the United States at 13. Now a San Francisco supervisor, she hopes to succeed long-time Democratic powerhouse Nancy Pelosi, who announced her retirement and endorsed her.

The 48-year-old politician would be the first Asian-American to represent the city in Congress.

But Chan faces a strong adversary in Scott Wiener.

While she entered local politics in 2020, Wiener has been a fixture in San Francisco Democratic circles since 2004, building strong ties with Asian-Americans, championing “yes in my backyard” (Yimby) housing policies and establishing himself as a formidable fundraiser.

As Chan takes the stage, she recounts her life story, her hands moving in a slightly practised fashion for emphasis. She speaks of the hard work, love of freedom and her family’s arrival with almost nothing before finding her way as a volunteer interpreter and social activist.

“That is our job, our job for San Francisco, for the United States, to be the conscience not only for the nation but the conscience for this world,” she says to enthusiastic applause in the large, half-full hall with ageing chandeliers, parquet flooring and large Palestinian, Irish and American flags.

“We must stand in solidarity and make sure that we send, all of us in Congress, that we’re ready to pass that vote with conscience to say no more wars and no more genocide,” she adds, addressing a crowd heavily weighted towards union labour, Arab-Americans and older whites.

“We are ready to vote for peace around the world.”

Will Nancy Pelosi’s successor take a different approach to China?

San Francisco has long been a hub of liberalism and multiculturalism, and it remains to be seen whether Pelosi's successor adopts her views on China honed during her 38 historic years in Congress as the nation’s first female speaker and an outspoken critic of Beijing’s human rights record.

Some say San Francisco politics have moved on from the stance Pelosi embraced in the 1990s, with neither candidate likely to make geopolitics as central as she did.

But Chan devoted nearly a third of her speech to Gaza, Ireland and oppression. Others argue that even if US-China tensions intensify, Chan would have deeper cross-cultural roots in finessing any trans-Pacific tensions.

Pelosi was not one to hide her views. She was a long-standing critic of Beijing’s human rights record, opposing preferential trade treatment for China and speaking out against its treatment of Tibetans, Uygurs and Hong Kong activists. In 2022, she became the first sitting US House speaker to visit Taiwan in a quarter century.

Beijing was quick to react. During and after her visit, China suspended military talks; conducted unprecedented live-fire military drills, including missiles launched over the island; sent warplanes and ships across the Strait’s median line; and imposed an import ban on hundreds of Taiwanese products.

Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-governed island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons.

“Connie would be able to advocate those dynamics with a level of care and competency that other candidates would not be able to and, to be quite honest, that Pelosi wouldn’t have been able to or wasn’t able to do,” said Vincent Pan, co-executive director of the activist group Chinese for Affirmative Action.

“I just don’t think that, on this issue, Scott would be able to do so. Again, it’s not a direct criticism. It’s just stating a fact.”

Asian-American voters could prove decisive in San Francisco race

The contest is significant for several reasons, Chinese-American community members say. As enthusiastically supported as Pelosi was in winning 20 elections, San Francisco has never had an Asian-American representative in Congress, despite Asians making up a third of the city’s population.

“Our communities are super threatened by the Trump administration, so that necessitates new leadership that can address what we’re facing,” said Russell Jeung, Asian-American studies professor at San Francisco State University and co-founder of activist group Stop AAPI Hate.

“Connie Chan’s advocacy, her use of language, makes a strong statement that Asian-Americans are part of the system, have a stake in the community. And what people are realising is that Asians are not just a swing vote but actually a dominant voting bloc.”

One concern is that recent Chinese immigrants vote at lower rates than other groups, especially if they do not speak English and have little experience with democracy.

It is and was quite a hill to climb for Connie

Malcolm Yeung, San Francisco’s Chinatown Community Development Centre

“Having an Asian-American candidate sort of draws their attention and then educates them,” Jeung added. “We don’t have the socialisation into the American system.”

In June’s primary, dominated by three Democratic candidates, Wiener garnered 41 per cent of the vote against Chan’s 30 per cent.

But after tech entrepreneur Saikat Chakrabarti dropped out, lending his support to Chan, the race has tightened. Ultimately, a lot of the outcome will depend on Asian-American turnout, say local operatives.

An October 16-19 University of Southern California poll has Wiener leading by 6 percentage points, within the margin of error. Betting site Kalshi shows a wider margin, giving Wiener 79 per cent odds against Chan’s 22.

“It is and was quite a hill to climb for Connie,” said Malcolm Yeung, chief executive of San Francisco’s Chinatown Community Development Centre.

“Scott’s reputation, which is incredibly well deserved, is that he’s a monster campaigner,” Yeung added. “He works harder than virtually any other politician. He shows up at every event, talks to every constituent.”

Key issues in this heart of the Silicon Valley race include development and artificial intelligence.

Wiener is seen as more pro-growth, more aligned with property and tech firms and a long-time advocate of the “yes in my backyard” housing stance.

Chan’s base includes public sector and construction unions and opponents of data centres and gentrification.

Chan supporter Jordan Mar, a political organiser, said a Chinese-American representative in Congress is long overdue given the city’s long history of migrant workers singled out for exclusion.

He voted for Wiener in past state races, Mar said, but Chan’s concerns over artificial intelligence (AI), data centres and lost opportunities swayed him.

“I think he takes too much Anthropic money,” he said, referring to the San Francisco-based AI model developer. “It’s not necessarily about strong ethnic identity, but I think we need strong regulations to support housing.”

Given that both candidates are progressive Democrats, the advertising has been civil without the rancour seen in Texas, Ohio and other scorched-earth races.

As a long-time Yimby, Wiener has sought to paint Chan as something of a regressive Nimby – short for “not in my backyard” – while she has hit him on his ties to corporate interests.

Political insiders say Pelosi, who has ties to both candidates, endorsed Chan for several reasons, including her own long-standing support in Chinatown, her advocacy for female candidates and Chan’s backing from construction unions.

Wiener also “got ahead of the game a little bit” by announcing his candidacy and appealing to her backers before Pelosi formally bowed out, said one source.

“That’s a no-no, especially with Nancy,” he added.

Chan and Wiener divide San Francisco’s Chinese community

As always, however, Chinese communities are complex, encompassing people from mainland China, Taiwan and Hong Kong, recent immigrants and multigenerational families, and residents across the economic spectrum.

Even as Asian-Americans feel obliged to support one of their own, many prefer Wiener’s policies and more pro-business stance.

“In the Chinese community, a lot of people don’t want to speak up because Chinese are supposed to support Chinese,” said Nancy Yu Law, owner of a tea shop and active in the Chinatown History and Culture Association that has several hundred Chinese shop owners.

“A lot of people don’t necessarily agree with what she has done, but we don’t want to say we don’t support her. It’s tricky.”

Yu Law recounts a recent fundraising event attended by several of her Chinese business friends.

“Somehow Pelosi shows up. Oh, wow – and they were stunned. And when they asked for a group photo, all my friends left. But they did sponsor her US$1,500,” Yu Law said. “And they say, ‘No way, I have lots of business in China.’”

The shopkeeper added that if Chan is elected as Pelosi’s successor, business owners are concerned she could mirror her mentor’s Taiwan visits and human rights campaigns. “My friends do not want to take a picture with Nancy Pelosi.”

Back at the Irish cultural hall, as she mingles in the crowd dressed in a tweed jacket and a thick black belt, Chan counters that her lived experience makes her an ideal trans-Pacific bridge.

“Chinatown is a gateway between Asia and the diverse Asian-American population, which gives me deep understanding,” she said.

“It’s not a monolithic community. I understand our different Asian heritage, how complex we are as Asian-Americans.”

item.title: [SCMP] How a Democratic-controlled Congress could reshape US policy on China
item.description:
A Democratic takeover of either chamber of the US Congress could bring tougher scrutiny of President Donald Trump’s dealings with Beijing, even as lawmakers are likely to maintain a broadly hawkish stance towards China, analysts said.

A change in control could shift the emphasis of congressional oversight, with the Democratic Party seeking greater accountability for the administration’s China policy after Trump’s Republican Party largely gave him room to manoeuvre, said Sarah Trister, a former lead staff member on the Senate Foreign Relations subcommittee on East Asia and the Pacific.

“I would not expect congressional Democrats to come in and seek to fully reframe the China relationship,” she said.
item.content:encoded:
A Democratic takeover of either chamber of the US Congress could bring tougher scrutiny of President Donald Trump’s dealings with Beijing, even as lawmakers are likely to maintain a broadly hawkish stance towards China, analysts said.

A change in control could shift the emphasis of congressional oversight, with the Democratic Party seeking greater accountability for the administration’s China policy after Trump’s Republican Party largely gave him room to manoeuvre, said Sarah Trister, a former lead staff member on the Senate Foreign Relations subcommittee on East Asia and the Pacific.

“I would not expect congressional Democrats to come in and seek to fully reframe the China relationship,” she said.

But winning a majority in the coming midterm elections would give Democrats tools to challenge the administration’s decisions, including the power to compel testimony and obtain documents.

“They’re going to use their power if they do take the majority; they’ll have subpoena power,” said Trister, now a managing director at consulting firm FGS Global.

Trister said both parties largely agree that China poses security and economic risks, although Democrats favour what she described as “strategic decoupling”.

Technology, trade, Taiwan, artificial intelligence and tariffs are among the issues analysts expect to draw scrutiny, as Trump pursues warmer ties with Chinese President Xi Jinping.

How Democrats see the China AI question

Kyle Chan, a fellow at the Brookings Institution’s John L. Thornton China Centre, said that the Democrats are not of one mind on China right now.

There are “members of the more traditional moderate wing of the Democrats, like Chuck Schumer, who have been advocating for tougher, say, export controls and have been pretty vocal in criticising Trump for relaxing export controls or not being tougher”, he said.

But the landscape among party members differs. Some in the more progressive wing have more mixed views on this topic, according to Chan, and may be interested in “trying to work with China on AI”.

If Democrats take control of Congress, he predicts they may try a two-pronged approach on AI and technology, a hot-button issue for both parties.

“On the one hand, try to close the export control loopholes and push forward things like Match,” Chan said, referring to the Multilateral Alignment of Technology Controls on Hardware Act.

At the same time, Democrats could “build some more communication channels with China on AI and try to come up with different ideas”, he added.

Ali Wyne, a senior research and advocacy adviser on US-China relations at the International Crisis Group, thinks if Democrats take back one or two chambers of Congress, they “will be even more energised” around a US-China collaboration on AI.

“There are a number of other prominent Democratic senators who have said that the United States and China need to collaborate,” he noted.

“Not because we trust China, not because we will trust China, but just because the stakes of getting this issue wrong are too high.”

Democrats vow to rein in Trump’s trade war

The approach to tariffs, a cornerstone of Trump’s second term agenda, could see a shift under a Democratic-led Congress, according to Josh Lipsky, vice-president and chair of international economics at the Atlantic Council.

He said Democrats had vowed to try to rein in tariffs if they won control of Congress.

He predicted Democrats would pass bills seeking to restore Congress’s authority over trade, including measures requiring congressional approval to maintain tariffs and restricting the use of certain statutes to impose them.

Trump would veto any such legislation that reached his desk, Lipsky said, but the bills could establish a policy framework for 2028 and beyond.

On China, however, some tariffs could remain in place, he said.

“Look at the 100 per cent EV tariffs [President Joe Biden] put on China, right?” he said. “That prevented what Europe is experiencing right now: a flood of cheap Chinese EVs [electric vehicles] into our markets.”

The current Congress is also debating bipartisan legislation to codify a ban on Chinese-made connected vehicles.

The debate over which tariffs to retain, alongside China’s retaliation involving critical minerals, will play out over the next two years, Lipsky said.

Will the US become more aggressive on Taiwan?

Taiwan remains one of the most sensitive issues in US-China relations, with arms sales and provisions in the annual US defence bill among the key areas of congressional attention.

Bonnie Glaser, a China expert at the German Marshall Fund, said a Democratic victory could give the party greater influence over Taiwan policy through control of the defence authorisation and spending processes, as well as the Senate agenda.

That could allow Democrats to push for requirements on the delivery of previously approved weapons, notifications of new arms sales, the use of Taiwan security funds and reports on delays, as well as explanations for suspending or conditioning arms sales, she said.

“If the Democrats control both chambers, there could be a push to legislate constraints on administration policy. For example, there could be momentum to pass the Six Assurances to Taiwan Act, which has bipartisan cosponsors,” Glaser said.

Beijing views Taiwan as part of China to be reunited with the mainland, by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington opposes any attempt to change the status quo by force and is committed to supplying the island with defensive weapons.

Leadership reshuffle on key congressional committees

A Democratic majority would put the party in line to take control of key congressional committees, handing leadership positions to lawmakers with differing priorities on China.

In the House, Gregory Meeks of New York, the top Democrat on the Foreign Affairs Committee, would be positioned to replace Republican Brian Mast as chairman. Ami Bera of California would likely take over the East Asia and Pacific subcommittee from Republican Young Kim.

If Democrats also win the Senate, Chris Coons of Delaware could succeed retiring Jeanne Shaheen as the top Democrat on the Foreign Relations Committee and potentially become its chairman.

The Congressional-Executive Commission on China, currently led by Republican Senator Dan Sullivan and the congressman Chris Smith, could also come under Democratic leadership, with the congressman Jim McGovern or Senator Jeff Merkley among the potential choices. Both have long criticised Beijing’s human rights record.

One of the most closely watched changes could come at the House Select Committee on China, which is a temporary congressional body.

Glaser said it would likely survive a change in party control, though its priorities could shift towards human rights issues.

Ro Khanna of California, the committee’s top Democrat, would be positioned to succeed Republican John Moolenaar as chairman.

Wyne said if Khanna did become chairman, he could take the committee in a “potentially much more productive direction”, adding that the ranking member is clear-eyed about various challenges that China poses to US national interests.

He also argues that the overall direction of congressional policy towards China is unlikely to change significantly, though a combination of factors could give Democrats more political room to challenge the administration’s approach.

“A confluence of factors – Trump’s unorthodoxy on China policy, warming American sentiment towards China, and growing anxiety among US allies and partners over Washington’s unreliability and unpredictability – could create more political space for members of the next Congress to advocate alternative approaches,” he said.
